The SQL example highlights a stale schema column that remains in a system prompt even after it becomes useless. A maintained skill can carry revised operational understanding without preserving every old lesson as permanent prompt text, provided consolidation reflects reliable current evidence.
qualification: Thresholds are illustrative and inconsistent: about ten memories earlier, about five reviews near the ending.
title: Consolidate repeated experiences into maintained skills

explanation: Utility-informed retrieval cannot use a history it does not yet have. The speaker acknowledges an initial cold-start period in which ranking remains ordinary semantic search until enough reviews are available. Evaluation of a learning memory system should therefore distinguish initial runs from later experience-rich behavior, rather than assuming advertised feedback benefits are available immediately at deployment.
qualification: The source does not quantify how many reviews or which task diversity is sufficient.
title: Expect semantic-only behavior until outcome reviews accumulate

explanation: A memory usefulness score depends on the quality of the feedback used to credit it. The source explicitly warns that noisy review labels make utility noisy, and also names drift and a lambda parameter in credit and reranking. A feedback-driven memory system inherits judgment problems instead of eliminating them merely by using an outcome-related score.
qualification: The speaker says many problems have been reduced, but gives no controlled noise study or specified credit-assignment method.
title: Noisy outcome reviews can corrupt utility-based retrieval

explanation: The speaker reports policy-following performance rising from 66 to 76 percent with memory, then to 80 with skills. This supports extracting a claimed benefit of experience plus consolidation, but not treating the numbers as established general performance. The transcript omits configuration, sample sizes and uncertainty, and corrupts the benchmark name and later repeated figures.
qualification: Speaker-reported benchmark figures only; the caption renders the policy benchmark name as "towel bench".
title: Separate reported memory gains from reproducible benchmark evidence

explanation: In the product SQL demo, a gaming-mouse request initially returns no product. Feedback points out a wireless mouse, and a subsequent run searches more broadly and returns related inventory. Inspecting the changed tool trajectory is important: the claimed learning is not merely a different final sentence but a change in how search is performed after failure feedback.
qualification: The transcript does not show SQL text, a held-out test set or proof that the retrieved mouse satisfies every gaming requirement.
title: Use failed-search feedback to change the next tool trajectory

explanation: Token use is an input cost, not a measure of useful work accomplished. At large application volume, redundant calls accumulate both latency and compute expense. The speaker argues for extracting more useful capability from a smaller payload, rather than rewarding token consumption itself. This frames optimization as preserving or improving task outcomes while removing unnecessary computational work.
qualification: Billion-token daily scale is speaker-reported; no audited cost figures are shown.
title: Optimize completed work rather than token consumption

explanation: Connect model calls, tools and retries into a trace for each task by instrumenting the shared model client. Record prompt version, model settings, token use, latency and cost for every attempt. This creates a production behavior benchmark and lets optimization compare actual execution paths instead of isolated model-call prices or an unversioned collection of final answers.
title: Instrument every attempt through the shared model client

explanation: A candidate disagreeing with historical production labels is not necessarily introducing that much new error. Ambiguous inputs can make the existing model disagree with its own prior answers. The speaker reruns production three times on identical inputs and reports roughly seven percent self-disagreement, contextualizing an eighteen percent candidate mismatch rate. Measure that background variation before interpreting agreement as quality.
qualification: The 93 percent agreement is an empirical repeatability baseline, not a literal upper bound on candidate accuracy or agreement.
title: Measure production against itself before rejecting a cheaper candidate

explanation: The first lever in the proposed optimization sequence is structuring prompts to maximize prefix-cache reuse. It is presented as a comparatively easy way to reduce task cost before rewriting instructions or reducing model capability. The principle is to avoid repeatedly paying for stable shared context when the serving system can reuse it, while still checking actual cache behavior.
qualification: The talk supplies no provider-specific cache semantics or measured cache-hit improvement.
title: Start cost reduction with reusable prompt prefixes

explanation: Define inputs, output schema and a scoring function, then let an optimizer revise prompt instructions using benchmark failures. This turns deletion of accumulated rules and examples into a measurable search problem rather than a risky manual edit. The application contract stays stable while the prompt changes, and the resulting smaller payload must still be tested for behavioral quality.
qualification: The reported 51 percent instruction-token reduction is associated with the illustrative prompt; reduction alone is not a release criterion.
title: Search for a shorter prompt under a fixed application contract

explanation: A large prompt can sometimes be decomposed so that a cheaper model handles initial routing or extraction while a frontier model is invoked only for harder reasoning. This is one rightsizing option after observability and prompt optimization. It changes the architecture rather than merely substituting a smaller model everywhere, so the resulting end-to-end behavior must be validated.
qualification: The talk proposes this strategy but does not provide a component-level cost/quality experiment.
title: Reserve expensive models for the components that need them

explanation: A smaller model can search its own prompt space against labels produced by a larger production model. This differs from giving it the existing large-model prompt and assuming equivalent behavior. However, the speaker reports many downsizing experiments as not release-ready, warning that model compression through prompting introduces failure modes and overfitting that require separate validation.
qualification: Historical large-model answers are training targets, not independently verified truth.
title: Reoptimize the prompt for the smaller model instead of blindly swapping it

explanation: Run repeated shadow evaluations on the same inputs and measure three relationships: production against itself, candidate against itself, and candidate against production. Both systems have internal variability, so only measuring their cross-version mismatch confounds changed behavior with random answer movement. This design supplies the information needed to interpret drift before deciding whether it indicates a harmful regression.
qualification: No sample size, repeat count or deployment duration is specified for the final shadow comparison.
title: Compare production repeats, candidate repeats and cross-version outputs

explanation: The speaker proposes taking cross-version disagreement and subtracting average within-version disagreement to measure changes in decision probabilities. The purpose is to distinguish a changed distribution from answers that move even without an implementation change. Treat the result as a drift diagnostic, not evidence that one version is correct, and retain the requirement to review what the differences mean.
qualification: The talk gives a verbal relationship without specifying mathematical assumptions; it does not establish a universal error-correction formula.
title: Adjust raw mismatch for both versions' internal variability

explanation: Matching production exactly can preserve its mistakes. The speaker recommends reviewing disagreements to decide whether the candidate is better, production is better, or both outputs are acceptable for an ambiguous request. This converts raw behavioral drift into an outcome judgment and prevents treating all differences as regressions simply because historical labels came from the incumbent model.
qualification: The transcript does not specify reviewer expertise, blinding, agreement or sampling strategy.
title: Review mismatches as improvements, regressions or acceptable alternatives

explanation: Do not release solely because reviewed improvements exceed regressions in one batch. Estimate uncertainty around the net gain using paired outputs from the same requests, and keep repeated runs of the same conversation grouped. Pairing preserves the shared-input comparison, while grouping prevents repeated observations of one conversation from being treated as independent evidence about many different requests.
qualification: The transcript specifies the design and decision rule but not an exact confidence-interval estimator.
title: Use paired comparisons and grouped repeats for net-gain uncertainty

explanation: The proposed release test requires the lower confidence bound on net gain to exceed zero. If the interval crosses zero, the observed improvement is not enough evidence to claim superiority and additional evidence is needed. This makes the decision explicit rather than shipping a promising point estimate or equating token reduction with verified product improvement.
qualification: This is the speaker's proposed rule, not a complete risk policy for every application.
title: Claim improvement only when the lower confidence bound is positive

explanation: A favorable aggregate comparison can conceal a damaging decline on an important customer intent. The speaker requires running the analysis separately on critical categories before release. This preserves application priorities that are not represented by the overall average, particularly when a frequent or easy class can outweigh a smaller category whose failures have higher operational consequences.
qualification: The talk does not define critical categories or category-specific risk tolerances.
title: Check critical intent categories separately from the global average

explanation: The proposed playbook applies caching, prompt shrinkage and model rightsizing in sequence, but does not treat any cost saving as sufficient for release. After repeated comparisons and disagreement review, critical categories must remain acceptable and uncertainty must support positive net gain. Continue measuring after shipping, so efficiency gains remain accountable to the product rather than the optimization benchmark alone.
qualification: This summarizes the speaker's release workflow; the synthetic classifier is not proof that the entire process has delivered quantified production savings.
title: Sequence cost levers, then ship only after quality evidence holds

explanation: The workshop distinguishes direct user attacks from indirect instructions planted in material an agent reads. A public profile can contain invisible text that redirects later outreach. Defenses must cover the boundary between external content and executable instructions, rather than assuming that text retrieved for a legitimate task inherits the user’s authority.
qualification: Prompt constraints and sanitization are recommendations, not demonstrated complete injection defenses.
title: Treat retrieved content as data, not authority

explanation: Instead of granting an agent a whole SQL database, expose a read-only view containing only the fields required for its task. In the example, names and telephone numbers are available but home addresses are not. This reduces both disclosure scope and write capability independently of whether the model obeys instructions.
qualification: The example is architectural guidance, not a measured attack-resistance result.
title: Restrict what the agent can retrieve before relying on output filtering

explanation: An agent should receive only the permissions needed for its current job, with human confirmation for risky actions. The speaker acknowledges that approvals interrupt long background tasks and encourage users to select always-allow. Treat that usability pressure as part of the security design rather than interpreting blanket authorization as a harmless convenience.
qualification: No quantitative comparison of approval strategies is supplied.
title: Balance approval friction against the cost of excessive agency

explanation: A skill or MCP server that was safe when installed may become unsafe after a later update. Provenance and a reputable publisher therefore do not replace recurring inspection. The speaker recommends reading text skills before installation and rescanning installed tools, because agent instructions and executable dependencies can both carry malicious behavior.
qualification: Scan coverage and false-negative rates are not established.
title: Revalidate trusted components after updates

explanation: Blanket bans can move AI activity onto personal accounts or private laptops, outside organizational visibility. The workshop describes workers transferring material between work and personal devices to retain productivity benefits. Effective governance therefore needs education and workable approved paths, not just restrictions that make the underlying demand disappear from monitoring.
qualification: Workaround examples are speaker anecdotes; the quoted organizational adoption statistics are not independently substantiated here.
title: Pair governance with usable sanctioned alternatives and education

explanation: An AI inventory extends beyond software packages to models, datasets, agents, pipelines, and connected tools. Keeping this inventory current makes it possible to identify affected applications when a component acquires a vulnerability. The demo illustrates component discovery and centralized querying; an inventory is a response-enabling map, not proof that every listed asset is safe.
qualification: The inventory demo is vendor tooling; detection completeness and real incident response performance are not evaluated.
title: Maintain an AI bill of materials for impact analysis

explanation: Threat modeling starts by mapping assets, architecture, data flows, and trust boundaries, then identifying threats, choosing mitigations, and validating them. Because agent systems evolve, the process should recur with code, infrastructure, data-pipeline, or model changes. Scans and automated triggers help connect this design activity to the delivery lifecycle rather than a one-time review.
qualification: Framework names and architectural examples are explained, not benchmarked against alternative threat-modeling methods.
title: Iterate threat models with architecture and deployment changes

explanation: Traditional protection of databases, credentials, and infrastructure is insufficient to describe an agent’s attack surface. The workshop adds model artifacts, prompt templates, context windows, memory stores, and accessible endpoints. Map where external data enters and where model outputs cause downstream actions, since either transition can convert untrusted content into consequential behavior.
qualification: This expands the security scope; the talk also reuses traditional frameworks rather than demonstrating that all prior methods are obsolete.
title: Include prompts, memory, context, and tool endpoints in the threat model

explanation: Long-running agents may perform actions that users miss while multitasking or that are not fully exposed in the interface. The speaker recommends verbose file logging and a separate background monitor that flags unwanted behavior, such as accessing secret storage. This adds retrospective and real-time visibility without assuming a human continuously watches each tool call.
qualification: Monitoring is proposed operational guidance; no alert-quality or detection-latency evaluation is provided.
title: Audit agent traces beyond what is visible in the UI

explanation: MCP servers are code projects with conventional bugs and security flaws, not magic capability boxes. The workshop separates tool-poisoning inspection from scanning implementation code for issues such as command injection, path traversal, and insecure dependencies. Both surfaces matter: a server can have malicious descriptions, vulnerable execution paths, or both.
qualification: A displayed Figma-related curl example and vulnerability headlines are described; the skipped video is not an observed exploit in this transcript.
title: Assess MCP integrations as ordinary code as well as agent instructions

explanation: Use an agent hook to invoke a security scanner after code generation, repair reported issues, and scan the new version again. This turns security from an optional final action into a repeated workflow step. The relevant stopping condition in the proposed loop is absence of scanner findings, which should not be confused with absence of all vulnerabilities.
qualification: The scan-fix loop is recommended, without a measured success rate or proof that a clean scan establishes security.
title: Make generated-code security checks part of the generation loop

explanation: Separate development, staging, and production environments, and route production changes through monitored delivery pipelines. Require human approval for deployments, destructive database operations, or privilege changes, and constrain network exposure. The point is to limit the blast radius of generated actions rather than trusting a functioning demo or a polite model to avoid irreversible harm.
qualification: Production database and mailbox incidents are retellings, not independently investigated case records in the workshop.
title: Keep coding agents away from direct production access

explanation: A model may recommend a package that does not exist; an attacker can register that name and attach malicious code so later users install it. The workshop contrasts this mechanism with typo-squatting around misspelled real packages. Dependency checks must therefore consider existence and provenance, not merely whether a generated import looks plausible or can now be resolved.
qualification: The speaker reports a real incident and rough download numbers without enough detail to verify them here.
title: Verify generated dependency names before installation

explanation: Company-wide policies can disable blanket approvals and constrain data transfer, yet users may still create workarounds. The speaker argues that education must explain the concrete failures these restrictions prevent, such as deleting a mailbox or leaking a wallet. Operational policy is therefore a combination of enforcement, understandable risk, and developer practice rather than configuration alone.
qualification: The talk offers experience-based recommendations rather than measured evidence of training effectiveness.
title: Explain security controls so users do not simply route around them

explanation: The car-negotiation story decomposes a loop into gathering comparable prices and inventory, negotiating with dealers, making offers compete, and stopping when a verifiable price condition is satisfied. The transferable idea is to define the observable outcome and stopping rule along with the agent’s actions, rather than identifying repeated tool use alone as product success.
qualification: This is a retold anecdote, not a controlled evaluation of negotiation performance.
title: A useful agent loop needs a verifiable outcome

explanation: The speaker distinguishes the signals driving a worker loop from the verifier that determines whether its apparent success is correct. Stronger feedback can improve iteration, but only a calibrated verifier can establish whether the loop actually achieved the intended outcome. This distinction matters when automated feedback risks rewarding behavior that merely resembles the desired result.
qualification: No calibration procedure or measured verifier accuracy is supplied.
title: Separate signal quality from verifier calibration

explanation: The inner loop performs work and produces traces and artifacts; an outer loop analyzes what went right or wrong and proposes system changes. Improvement is not simply asking the same worker to try again. It requires deciding which artifacts are informative, how they change the feedback signal, and which candidate changes deserve evaluation.
qualification: The talk proposes a product architecture rather than reporting a comparative experiment.
title: Use execution artifacts as inputs to a separate improvement loop

explanation: A recipe packages harness profiles, evaluations, models, resources, tools, environment choices, and accumulated human judgments into an evolving artifact. Keeping it portable and versioned records both what changed and why. The proposed unit of reproducibility is therefore the configured system and its learned operating choices, not a single prompt detached from runtime context.
qualification: Portability and reproducibility are design goals of an early product, not demonstrated cross-provider equivalence.
title: Version the whole agent recipe, not only its model or prompt

explanation: Execution history should be distilled into different kinds of durable system assets. Failure patterns become judges and evaluation cases, repeated behavior becomes skills or prompts, and user frustrations can motivate harness extensions or memory changes. The distinction prevents treating every observed problem as another prompt sentence, while preserving feedback as reusable material for future versions.
qualification: The mapping is heuristic guidance and does not establish which failures are sufficiently frequent or severe to prioritize.
title: Turn recurring failures into evaluations and recurring work into skills

explanation: The speaker uses taste to mean the decisions that distinguish one service provider’s good work from another’s. A reusable agent recipe should carry these judgments, their rationale, and the evaluations that express them. This is particularly relevant where success depends on a specific operator’s preferences rather than a universally agreed task score.
qualification: Taste is the speaker’s framing; it is not shown to capture every safety or objective correctness requirement.
title: Encode the maker’s judgment as explicit evaluation criteria

explanation: A recruiting agent may repeatedly choose famous big-tech employees even when its operator wants overlooked candidates. Inspect traces, cluster common behaviors or frustrations, and use the pattern to identify a requirement that was absent from the initial instructions. The example treats user dissatisfaction as evidence for a concrete behavioral criterion rather than merely a low overall rating.
qualification: The recruiting walkthrough is illustrative; no production frequency, cluster quality, or hiring outcome is reported.
title: Discover missing requirements from patterns in real trajectories

explanation: In the recruiting example, an agent can create a trajectory-level judge for whether sourcing overemphasizes big-tech employees instead of hidden GitHub candidates. The human’s proposed role is to confirm that this is the desired distinction, not necessarily to author evaluation code. Keep criterion agreement separate from the convenience of generating a checker automatically.
qualification: The claim that generation is easy is speaker opinion; evaluation code correctness and judge reliability are not demonstrated.
title: Let agents implement evaluations while humans validate the judgment

explanation: An offline evaluation can agree with a maker’s preferred behavior while end users value something different. The speaker proposes testing recipe candidates in production using A/B tests or multi-armed bandits, then promoting a version once users also appreciate the change. Offline alignment and actual customer benefit are distinct acceptance conditions in this loop.
qualification: No experimental design details, effect sizes, or deployment guardrails are provided.
title: Promote recipe changes only after users validate the offline preference

explanation: The proposed optimization target is valuable work per watt: first determine whether the output matters to users, then determine whether its resource cost is economically sensible. The speaker frames production learning as necessary for finding useful frontier behavior and subsequent optimization as making that behavior viable, rather than minimizing cost before defining value.
qualification: Work per watt is a conceptual score here; neither physical energy measurements nor a formal value metric is specified.
title: Establish valuable work before optimizing its economics

explanation: A finance demo transforms one clean document into fluent output, whereas a decision memo combines filings, calls, broker notes, spreadsheets, and informal material that may disagree. The evaluation target is the ability to defend consequential claims under skeptical review. Plausibility and formatting are insufficient when the output supports an actual investment decision.
qualification: This is an investment reviewer’s experience-based standard, not a measured comparison of finance products.
title: Evaluate whether an output survives scrutiny, not whether it impresses briefly

explanation: An audited filing, analyst note, and group-chat estimate do not deserve identical evidential weight. The speaker describes a tool preferring a confident informal guess over a nearby audited number. Retrieval should preserve and expose source trust levels so persuasive wording or semantic closeness does not silently become a substitute for authority in financial analysis.
qualification: The expensive-tool incident is anonymized and does not identify the underlying retrieval or ranking implementation.
title: Retain source authority rather than ranking solely by textual relevance

explanation: A memo can lose trust when one page gives revenue growth as eighteen percent and another gives seventeen point four. The important failure is not just the size of the discrepancy; reviewers infer that unverified easy arithmetic may signal unverified harder analysis. The proposed control is automatic agreement checking that blocks inconsistent documents from shipping.
qualification: The speaker does not specify tolerance rules, rounding handling, or a reconciliation algorithm.
title: Treat repeated figures as consistency constraints

explanation: When an earnings call and an official filing give meaningfully different growth figures, the discrepancy itself is useful diligence evidence. A fluent synthesis that quietly chooses the nicer version removes information reviewers need. Preserve both claims and bring the conflict to a human rather than requiring accidental side-by-side reading to discover it.
qualification: The speaker’s priority is financial diligence, where reconciliation may be a decision task rather than an automatic synthesis step.
title: Expose conflicting evidence instead of smoothing it into one answer

explanation: A forecast such as approval expected soon can gradually become approval received over successive drafts without an intentional lie. Label factual evidence and estimates distinctly, using a representation that survives copying into later slides or documents. Evaluation should check uncertainty preservation across transformations, not only whether the first generated draft used cautious wording.
qualification: The draft-drift story is speaker experience, with no measured transformation error rate.
title: Keep uncertainty labels intact through rewrites and copying

explanation: The proposed thirty-second test asks whether a reviewer can select a sentence and immediately reach the exact supporting source paragraph. A generic references tab or a plausible-looking citation is insufficient if it forces live manual hunting. Attach source trust information to individual claims so evidence can be checked under real meeting pressure.
qualification: Thirty seconds is a practical usability standard proposed by the speaker, not a validated universal threshold.
title: Make exact-source verification a one-click product capability

explanation: The retold legal-brief incident illustrates that asking a chatbot whether its own cited cases are real can reproduce the original error. Formatting, realistic names, and page numbers do not establish existence. The transferable requirement is to connect a claim to actual retrievable evidence, not treat another confident model response as independent substantiation.
qualification: This is a retelling of a public incident without independent case-document verification in the talk.
title: Do not verify a model’s invented references by asking the same model

explanation: The speaker argues that software cannot absorb an organization’s accountability for a consequential decision. Design around a findable human decision-maker and record who reviewed, what changed, and when approval occurred. The approval log connects evidence and uncertainty to an actual sign-off, rather than leaving a polished machine-written document without an owner.
qualification: Human sign-off is the speaker’s requirement for live financial deals; legal incident details are retold rather than established here.
title: Make the accountable reviewer explicit and log the approval

explanation: The closing requirements are claim receipts with source trust, distinct facts and estimates, automatic numerical agreement, surfaced contradictions, and logged human approval. The speaker frames these as plumbing and honesty problems rather than benchmark deficits. A useful diagnosis asks which control is missing before attributing every trust failure to insufficient model intelligence.
qualification: The talk does not demonstrate that model quality is irrelevant; it argues these specific product requirements cannot be replaced by a smarter model.
title: Diagnose missing controls before assuming the model must get bigger

explanation: The speaker describes coding agents completing subtasks and announcing success while the resulting application still has missing or broken behavior. Without another checking mechanism, the user becomes the enforcement layer through repeated corrective prompts. Define independently checkable completion criteria rather than using the agent’s own done message as evidence of task completion.
qualification: This motivates the harness through personal experience; no measured agent failure rate is reported.
title: Treat completion messages as claims to check

explanation: Vector V1 connects a completion hook to a separate program that runs the user’s configured checks. The useful boundary is between generating a solution and invoking verification automatically, so the user does not have to remember to request tests after every session. The mechanism can enforce only the requirements actually represented in those checks.
qualification: The talk shows a prototype workflow; it does not demonstrate completeness of its test configuration.
title: Trigger configured checks when the agent finishes

explanation: A configuration file defines test cases, and failed checks return feedback that asks the coding agent to try again. The shown progression from failed tests to passing tests illustrates a machine-driven repair loop rather than manual nudging. This is a scoped success condition: the configured tests pass, not necessarily every unstated product requirement.
qualification: Retry limits, terminal failure handling, and resistance to gaming tests are not discussed.
title: Feed failing checks back into agent retries

explanation: The speaker challenges a reported claim that smarter future models will remove the need for enforcement. Better task capability does not by itself establish that a system reliably meets a particular user’s requirements. Specifications, tools, subagents, and context may improve generation, but the argument keeps these inputs distinct from observing that the delivered result works.
qualification: The opposing view is a speaker-reported conversation, not a direct claim established by the other party; no model comparison is provided.
title: Do not equate greater capability with demonstrated reliability

explanation: Detailed instructions say what should happen; verification checks whether it did happen. The talk argues that stronger specifications, context, and tool access remain useful but do not remove the need for acceptance checks. This distinction supports investing in a harness that observes outputs instead of endlessly strengthening natural-language requests after every missed requirement.
qualification: The argument is architectural guidance rather than evidence that every requirement can be expressed as a deterministic check.
title: Keep instructions and verification as separate system responsibilities

explanation: The speaker proposes exchanging harness engineering effort for lower inference cost: with more guardrails and verification, smaller or open models might satisfy tasks that otherwise require a costly frontier model. Treat this as a hypothesis to evaluate on the actual workload, because the talk gives no cost-quality measurements or evidence that arbitrary missing capability can be repaired by checks.
qualification: Explicitly framed as theory; the humorous Q&A about token spending supplies no economic validation.
title: Test whether stronger checks can enable cheaper models

explanation: Different teams enforce different requirements, so the speaker shifts from a personal tool toward a language-agnostic contract that lets each team supply its own checks. The reusable part is the mechanism for running and reporting verification, while the concrete acceptance criteria remain local. Portability should not imply every organization must use identical rules.
qualification: The contract is discussed at a pattern level; no formal schema or interoperability test is included.
title: Separate a portable enforcement interface from project-specific policy

explanation: Verification can occur after conversations, before commits, within multi-agent workflows, and for asynchronous tasks. The speaker also allows a check that invokes an LLM judge. Distinguish deterministic invocation of a verification step from deterministic correctness of its judgment: adding a model-based checker does not automatically make the result a reproducible binary fact.
qualification: The deterministic-invocation versus stochastic-judgment distinction makes explicit a limitation of the speaker’s proposed mixed-check architecture.
title: Run checks at consequential workflow boundaries

explanation: Edit prediction runs at each keystroke, using code around the cursor, recent edits, definitions, diagnostics, and errors to propose the next change. That interaction budget motivates a small model specialized for this one task. The case illustrates why model selection should consider invocation frequency and latency requirements rather than assume a frontier general model is the appropriate serving choice.
qualification: The talk does not supply measured latency or a comparison against serving a general model.
title: Match model specialization to interaction latency

explanation: Zed builds training examples from opt-in editor snapshots containing the actual context available when an edit was requested, then asks a frontier teacher what it would predict. This connects distillation inputs to the production task distribution. The speaker emphasizes that teacher prompting still needs careful tuning because a powerful teacher can produce inconsistent or undesirable targets.
qualification: The snapshot collection is described as opt-in; privacy handling, representativeness, and sampling details are not given.
title: Capture task context from opt-in production snapshots

explanation: Static checks detect teacher predictions that undo what a user just typed or exceed the allowed editable region. A failing target is sent to another frontier model with an explanation of the failure, creating a repair step before the prediction becomes a student training label. Synthetic data quality is therefore a controlled pipeline concern, not guaranteed by teacher capability.
qualification: The talk does not report repair accuracy, remaining error rates, or whether all bad predictions are captured by these heuristics.
title: Validate and repair synthetic teacher targets before distillation

explanation: Teacher predictions and their repairs can be cached across experiments, while prompt formatting changes for choices such as including diagnostics or varying edit-history length. The pipeline uses JSONL records that acquire fields at each stage. This separation reduces repeated expensive teacher work and makes feature-context experiments possible without regenerating every target from scratch.
qualification: The speaker describes the architecture and sample sizes but does not report measured cache savings or ablation outcomes.
title: Separate reusable target generation from experiment-specific formatting

explanation: Eventually the editor user writes a desired version of the code, so a later snapshot can provide feedback about an earlier prediction. However, intervening changes of intent or an agent rewriting the region can make that later state unrelated to what was predictable from the original context. Do not assume eventual user output is clean ground truth for the initial request.
qualification: The team is experimenting with this settled-data approach, not presenting it as a fully solved labeling method.
title: Treat later user code as an informative but noisy target

explanation: In the Q&A, the speaker explains that the editor snapshots a region after ten seconds without editing there; it does not currently use git commits. This is a practical collection heuristic, not proof that the user is satisfied or the code is final. Continuous editing without a sufficiently long pause delays collection, which shapes the observed data.
qualification: Git commits are suggested by the questioner and acknowledged as possible, but are not part of the described implementation.
title: Define settlement operationally and preserve its uncertainty

explanation: The team proposes generating several predictions from the original request context and comparing them with the later settled state using edit distance. If one is sufficiently close, the later result is treated as predictable from the earlier information rather than obviously unrelated noise. The mechanism is a heuristic compatibility filter, not a proof of semantic correctness.
qualification: Thresholds and validation of the noise-versus-predictability assumption are not supplied.
title: Filter settled outcomes by whether plausible predictions can reach them

explanation: Generating ten frontier predictions for each of roughly one hundred thousand examples is described as prohibitively costly. Once a student approaches teacher prediction quality, the team instead samples a student checkpoint about fifty times and applies the same proximity test. This shifts repeated data filtering to a cheaper model while retaining a diverse set of candidate edits.
qualification: Approaching teacher quality and negligible student cost are speaker-reported; no quality or financial measurements are shown.
title: Use an adequate student checkpoint to reduce teacher-filtering cost

explanation: Distances between sampled predictions and settled user edits create a spectrum: extremely far cases look noisy, extremely near cases look trivial, and an intermediate region is considered useful training material. The speaker highlights new functions beyond the student’s training cutoff as possible examples. They generally train on the prediction closest to settlement, not directly on the still-noisy settled code.
qualification: This is a heuristic selection strategy; thresholds, coverage bias, and comparative training improvements are not quantified.
title: Prefer examples that are neither obvious nor unrelated

explanation: The team keeps evaluation data separate from training and compares predictions against three distinct teacher answers because many editing contexts have no single correct continuation. A close match to any reference is treated as evidence of a reasonable prediction. Multiple references reduce one-reference brittleness but still reflect what the teacher proposed rather than exhaust all valid user intentions.
qualification: The speaker does not specify an exact multi-reference aggregation formula or show how much coverage improves.
title: Use held-out tests with multiple acceptable reference edits

explanation: The reported evaluation suite includes an n-gram-based similarity metric, a reversal ratio for predictions that undo the user’s last typing, and production kept rate. It also compares diagnostic error counts before and after an edit. These measure different failure modes, so similarity alone is not the entire quality definition for an editor-integrated model.
qualification: The similarity metric’s name is garbled in captions; diagnostic changes are only described as a quality signal, not proof of correctness.
title: Track destructive edits and local diagnostics alongside similarity

explanation: The speaker warns that offline evaluation scores do not necessarily correlate with what users want. Deployed candidates receive configurable traffic shares, and an internal dashboard tracks acceptance rate, latency, and related signals before a version becomes the default. Offline checks and production experiments serve complementary roles rather than allowing one proxy score to decide a release.
qualification: A traffic-allocation page is shown, but the metric dashboard cannot be shown; no experiment outcomes or significance analysis are reported.
title: Validate model changes with live editor behavior and latency

explanation: A working agent can drift away from requirements when its model, instructions, environment, or encountered edge cases change. Evaluation should therefore continue after initial development rather than operate as a one-time launch check. Combine monitoring and traces with repeated quality and safety checks so changes in the requirements-to-behavior gap become visible while the system is operating.
title: Evaluate changing agents throughout their lifecycle

explanation: An agent workflow contains distinct failure points that a final-response score alone cannot localize. In the weather example, first check whether the agent resolved the local-weather intent, then whether it selected the expected tool, and finally whether the response completed and adhered to the task. Separate stage-level criteria make it easier to identify which behavior needs changing when overall quality disappoints.
title: Score intent, tool choice, and task completion separately

explanation: Observability should shorten the interval between detecting a failure and explaining it. Linking an evaluation result to its execution trace lets developers compare agent versions and inspect the exact tool calls and messages behind a regression. The presenters use a model replacement that makes tool use less effective as an example: the metric identifies a problem, while the trace reveals a tool that was no longer called.
title: Connect failed metrics to the execution that produced them

explanation: When a workflow delegates to flight, hotel, and car-rental specialists, inspect the whole invocation path rather than only the final concierge answer. Per-agent traces expose which specialist underperformed and which consumed tokens, allowing a targeted replacement or optimization. This is a diagnostic benefit of the demonstrated decomposition, not evidence that splitting every task into multiple agents improves quality or efficiency.
qualification: The travel workflow illustrates attribution; no monolithic-versus-specialist performance comparison is reported.
title: Use workflow traces to attribute quality and token costs to specialists

explanation: A cheaper model or a narrower cached search source can lower token expense or tool latency, but the change may also reduce accuracy or other task behavior. Treat each substitution as an experiment and compare evaluations immediately afterward. Optimize costs against retained quality rather than accepting a lower bill as sufficient evidence that an agent version is better.
title: Re-evaluate cost-saving changes for collateral regressions

explanation: Generic traces can show that an agent ran without carrying the contextual fields needed to explain a particular failure. Add custom attributes related to the behaviors under investigation, and inspect them locally while debugging before exporting to a central backend. The workshop also notes that generative-AI tracing and message-content capture require explicit activation in its setup; deployment alone did not make all details observable.
qualification: The transcript describes console and backend tracing configuration but does not expose all code or exact environment-variable names.
title: Instrument traces with debugging-relevant attributes

explanation: An apparent agent-performance problem can originate in a service it calls. Exporting AI telemetry into the same monitoring system as search indexes and other infrastructure enables joint inspection of the agent and its dependencies. The workshop uses search telemetry as an example of how to investigate whether a performance impact arose from a called service instead of from the model alone.
title: Correlate agent traces with dependency telemetry

explanation: Running a collection of quality, safety, and agentic evaluators requires more than selecting metric names. Prepare the prompt-and-response test data, specify each evaluator and its criteria, then define how that evaluator receives fields from the dataset. This explicit mapping makes a batch evaluation runnable and interpretable; the workshop presents the process with built-in evaluators rather than validating the criteria against expert labels.
title: Map each evaluator explicitly to its required data

explanation: The prepared travel-agent results pass simple coherence and fluency checks, but a separate inspection finds an answer using August 2024 where the expected date was in 2025. Preserve these as different evaluation dimensions: readable language can coexist with contextually incorrect details. Inspect the failed example and its rationale rather than treating an aggregate or stylistic pass as evidence that the response is grounded.
qualification: A walkthrough of a simple test set, not a measured comparison of evaluator accuracy.
title: Passing language-quality checks does not establish factual grounding

explanation: An allowlist or prohibited-action taxonomy expresses what an agent should do; it does not show whether malicious prompts can circumvent that instruction. The red-team workflow gives a second agent risk categories and attack strategies, generates manipulative prompts, and observes violations. This complements normal-use quality and safety evaluations by directly challenging the enforcement of constraints rather than merely restating them.
title: Test whether adversaries can bypass specified behavioral constraints

explanation: The demonstrated scan tries leetspeak against violence, sensitive-data leakage, and task-adherence risks and finds no failures. The presenters contrast this simple transformation with a crescendo strategy that builds attacks over successive turns and takes longer to run. Treat the observed pass as evidence about the selected attack set, and choose additional strategies when the threat model includes progressive manipulation.
qualification: The comprehensive scan is not completed in the available demo. The speaker says adaptive scans determine all vulnerabilities, but the talk supplies no evidence of exhaustive coverage.
title: A passing simple scan is narrower than adaptive adversarial coverage

explanation: When a new application has no historical evaluation data, the preview observe skill inspects the agent instructions, generates a dataset, and runs an initial batch to establish a baseline. This is a way to start measuring before real usage exists. The result remains a synthetic starting point derived from the stated specification, not demonstrated coverage of the eventual production population.
qualification: Early-preview prepared workflow; the transcript does not report independent test-set review or a representative sampling process.
title: Bootstrap an initial test set from the agent specification

explanation: The coding-agent skill automates baseline evaluation, failure analysis, instruction changes, and comparison using the same evaluators. It pauses to ask whether to proceed, and the presenter emphasizes that a domain expert can guide the next experiment or request a revised dataset. Automation reduces SDK orchestration work; it does not remove the need to interpret failure reasons, supply domain knowledge, or decide when to stop.
qualification: The preview walkthrough demonstrates the interaction pattern, not general autonomous optimization reliability.
title: Automate the evaluation loop while retaining human direction

explanation: After one instruction update fixes a task-adherence failure, asking the optimizer to reach a perfect score produces additional changes that regress. The walkthrough reaches version ten but selects version five as best. Preserve the comparison history and deploy by version identifier so an earlier candidate can be restored. More optimization steps are not themselves evidence of better behavior, even on the same test setup.
qualification: Version preference is based on this prepared small evaluation; no held-out generalization result is supplied.
title: Keep the best measured version instead of assuming later iterations improve

explanation: Recognition accuracy measures whether the system hypothesis matches the request, but it does not determine how the assistant should respond to uncertainty. Holding the hypotheses fixed, a policy can choose to act, reject, or confirm, changing the errors users experience and the effort needed to recover. Evaluate this behavioral layer separately rather than making accuracy the only lever for user experience.
qualification: The satisfaction improvement is inferred through a cost heuristic, not directly measured in a controlled user study.
title: Improve user outcomes without changing recognition accuracy

explanation: The threshold example starts with spoken requests whose hypotheses have been labeled correct or wrong, then assigns each hypothesis a reasonably calibrated confidence score. Plotting correct and incorrect score distributions supports quantitative decisions about when to act. This is a simplifying condition: a real cascaded voice system contains several layers and confidence signals, so a single unvalidated score should not automatically be treated as an outcome probability.
title: Ground action gating in labeled outcomes and meaningful confidence

explanation: Different unsuccessful interactions impose different burdens. Wrong playback requires noticing the mistake, interrupting the assistant, and requesting again, whereas a rejection may only require repeating the request. The speaker proposes extra seconds until the intended song plays as a practical outcome-cost heuristic, using ten seconds for wrong playback and four for rejection. These values operationalize relative inconvenience rather than measuring recognition accuracy.
qualification: Recovery times are assigned illustrative values; alternative cost measures or empirical estimates could change the policy.
title: Score mistakes by the effort required to recover

explanation: For an act-or-stop policy, count wrong actions and stops at each candidate confidence threshold, multiply them by their respective user costs, and choose the threshold with the lowest total. This explicitly trades fewer harmful actions against more interruptions. An intuitively plausible threshold can be suboptimal because the optimum depends jointly on the score distributions and the consequences assigned to each outcome.
qualification: The illustrated optimum is dataset- and heuristic-specific, not a universal confidence setting.
title: Choose action thresholds by minimizing weighted outcome cost

explanation: Adding confirmation creates an intermediate region between stopping and acting, represented by two thresholds. A correct hypothesis that the user simply affirms incurs a different interaction cost from a wrong hypothesis that the user must correct. The example assigns two seconds to affirmation and six to correction. Evaluate both branches instead of treating every confirmation as either free safety or the same kind of interruption.
qualification: Two confidence thresholds are an explanatory simplification, not a prescribed architecture for every production policy.
title: Model confirmation as a distinct policy action with its own outcomes

explanation: The best threshold is not an intrinsic property of a recognition model. Increasing the assigned cost of wrong playback changes the minimizing policy even when the original confidence scores remain unchanged. Inspect both cost assumptions and outcome distributions when tuning behavior, and avoid presenting one optimization result as permanent when user tolerance, task consequences, or interaction conditions differ.
title: Recompute the policy when consequence estimates change

explanation: The act-confirm-stop construction explains the objective with one or two offline confidence cutoffs. The speaker explicitly distinguishes that simplification from real systems, where the decision model would be learned and operate in real time. Preserve the principle of minimizing user-outcome cost while allowing the actual policy to account for richer context rather than freezing the demonstration thresholds into a universal rule.
qualification: The talk does not provide an implemented learned policy, training procedure, or deployment results.
title: Treat fixed thresholds as a teaching model, not the full production solution

explanation: A TV can display several channel choices and let the user confirm with a remote, making clarification less burdensome than spoken correction. Conversely, launching the wrong channel may disrupt the current viewing state and increase wrong-action cost. Reuse the cost-sensitive framework across surfaces, but re-estimate costs for the actual modality and consequences; robot or digital actions can be more consequential than playing the wrong song.
qualification: TV behavior is an illustrative transfer argument; the talk does not experimentally evaluate wearables or robots.
title: Adapt outcome costs to the interface and action consequences

explanation: Each villager has a separate retrieval-backed memory namespace, so one agent does not automatically inherit what another knows. Information must move through actual communication. This state architecture matters to evaluation: a diffusion or coordination scenario would be misleading if the implementation silently gave every agent access to a shared global memory. Test social behavior against the knowledge each participant could legitimately acquire.
title: Preserve local knowledge boundaries in multi-agent evaluation

explanation: The game framework assigns each memory an importance score and stores above-threshold events in a separate cache for later retrieval. This makes salient events more available than mundane ones. The example compares an ordinary dinner with a memorable murder. It describes one memory mechanism in the architecture, not evidence that salience scoring alone solves long-horizon consistency or that its thresholds have been optimized.
qualification: No salience-scoring validation, threshold values, or ablation results are reported.
title: Distinguish memory salience from simply storing every event

explanation: An agent may recall a topic yet lose who supplied it, repeat a rumor as certain, or fail to use a known fact while planning. These are distinct long-horizon failures that a successful short conversation does not rule out. The village example motivates evaluating how stored information changes across intervening events and whether future actions remain consistent with what the agent actually learned.
title: Evaluate provenance, uncertainty, and action use across time

explanation: The speaker frames improvement as changing how agents write and retrieve memories, communicate uncertainty, attribute sources, update trust, and replan. Retrieval quality is only one part of that protocol. A system can retrieve relevant text but still misrepresent its source or fail to act on it, so define the editable behavior in terms of the state transitions and communications responsible for the observed failure.
title: Optimize the state-handling protocol, not only the retrieval component

explanation: The proposed auto-research system sits outside the village, reads complete traces, compares events with scenario ground truth, and asks whether society-level behavior improved. Individual agents still operate with local perspectives. This separation allows an evaluator to know the full experimental state without accidentally making agents omniscient, and shifts the evaluation unit from one answer to an extended interaction trajectory.
title: Use an outside observer to score whole multi-agent runs

explanation: For a controlled village run, the trace should record observations, conversations, memory writes, retrievals, and belief updates where relevant. These records let the outside evaluator examine how information reached an agent and where it was altered or lost. Logging only final dialogue would omit the intermediate state transitions needed to distinguish a retrieval failure from a communication, belief-update, or planning failure.
qualification: The caption says memory rights; nearby context describes memory-writing behavior.
title: Log internal state changes needed to explain long-run behavior

explanation: Interesting village interactions are hard to compare if the environment has no controlled conditions or success criteria. Define scenarios that isolate a capability: a bakery closure tests fact diffusion and plan changes, a possible departure tests whether rumor uncertainty survives retelling, and a blocked route tests communication and replanning. The specific stories are examples; the reusable requirement is a scenario suite that makes improvement observable.
title: Replace unconstrained wandering with targeted behavioral scenarios

explanation: A single vague quality metric can hide important behavioral failures. The proposed scorecard measures diffusion reach after a fixed number of steps, source retention among informed agents, uncertainty preservation and false certainty for rumors, plus action consistency and time to replan. Keeping these dimensions visible makes it possible to tell whether a policy improves memory transmission, provenance, or planning rather than assuming they move together.
qualification: The talk proposes metric families but does not provide exact formulas, weights, or measured values.
title: Separate the dimensions hidden by an agent-quality scalar

explanation: Optimizing diffusion alone can reward agents for oversharing, while optimizing recall alone can encourage noisy or stale memories. Include privacy containment alongside information reach and measure whether remembered material remains appropriate to use. A change that spreads public facts faster is not unconditionally better if it also leaks private information, so evaluate the side effects of the same memory and communication policy.
title: Constrain information spread with privacy and stale-memory checks

explanation: The auto-research agent should not rewrite the application or its tests indiscriminately. Freeze the harness, scenarios, and metrics, then expose only intended policy choices such as memory writing, retrieval, communication prompts, trust rules, source attribution, or replanning triggers. This gives the search useful behavioral degrees of freedom while reducing the opportunity to raise scores by changing the measurement instead of improving the agent.
title: Freeze evaluation machinery and expose only a narrow policy surface

explanation: Retrieval-backed memory alone does not establish coherent long-term behavior. Preserve whether information was firsthand, secondhand, verified, or uncertain, and consider separating episodic memories from current beliefs. The speaker suggests recording sources in memory summaries and requiring hedging when retelling uncertain claims. These targeted policies address how an agent interprets retrieved information, not merely whether it can retrieve the right words.
title: Represent sources and epistemic status, not just recalled text

explanation: Each policy experiment should run the controlled scenario again, evaluate the complete scorecard, and revert if improvement or guardrail conditions are not met. Rollback is essential because changing social behavior can improve one dimension while harming another, such as faster public communication versus privacy or higher recall versus stale-memory use. The proposed loop is a conditional ratchet, not an assumption that every generated patch advances the system.
title: Accept changes only when the scorecard improves and guardrails hold

explanation: The speaker reports a mango-sale scenario that retains useful context after one auto-research loop, but explicitly declines to claim that the system generally improved without repeated loop results. Preserve that evidentiary boundary. A positive demonstration can motivate a policy-search method while still leaving open whether gains persist across scenarios, seeds, and repeated runs; the talk supplies no such broader measurement.
qualification: The mango result is reported qualitatively; no numerical before-and-after results or replication counts are supplied.
title: Do not generalize from one successful long-horizon rerun

explanation: Operational metrics can remain green while an agent performs a semantically disastrous action. In the stock example, the agent places the requested dollar amount into a share-quantity field, and the broker returns an ordinary success response. Evaluate whether tool arguments and resulting state changes match the user intent; HTTP status, latency, and absence of exceptions do not establish that the action was correct.
qualification: Illustrative transaction demo, not a reported production loss.
title: A successful API call can implement the wrong user action

explanation: Greedy decoding selects the highest-scoring token, but it does not ensure the underlying scores remain identical across executions. The presenters distinguish that limited sampling choice from system-level determinism and also note that a deterministic output could simply repeat a reasoning error. Do not treat temperature zero as either a repair for wrong tool use or a complete strategy for reproducing a production failure.
qualification: The talk attributes variation to numerical and serving effects but supplies no controlled reproducibility experiment.
title: Zero temperature does not guarantee correctness or identical system behavior

explanation: Replayability aims to reconstruct a past execution well enough to debug it, rather than to force a hosted model to generate identical text on demand. Captured decisions and state transitions let developers investigate a rare failure even when repeated fresh model calls behave correctly. This shifts the debugging target from the model distribution to the concrete run that actually caused the problem.
title: Record a failed run instead of requiring the model to regenerate it

explanation: Network logging misses local retrieval, in-process tools, memory operations, and other agent steps that never cross a network boundary. Instead, wrap semantic workflow nodes such as model calls, tool methods, and retrieval operations, recording what enters and leaves each one. The resulting trace corresponds to meaningful agent decisions, making it usable for both diagnosis and selective replay rather than only transport inspection.
title: Capture node inputs and outputs rather than only network traffic

explanation: A prompt alone is not a complete description of an agent execution. The Chronicle approach records node input-output pairs and permits metadata such as model version, sampling configuration, and code version; the closing guidance also calls out build identifiers and retrieved chunks. Preserve the variables that shaped the session so a later investigation can interpret the recorded behavior in its actual execution context.
qualification: The proof of concept allows recording metadata; the talk does not establish automatic complete capture of every variable.
title: Log version and retrieval context along with the prompt

explanation: Recording both sides of a tool call distinguishes an obedient tool from the model decision that supplied the wrong request. In the demo, the place-order tool receives a quantity of one thousand, and inspecting the previous node shows the planner generated that quantity. This localizes the semantic mistake upstream and identifies the exact payload a regression test must preserve, rather than blaming an otherwise successful API operation.
title: Trace backward from a bad tool action to the generated arguments

explanation: After identifying a wrong generated call, the presenters add a guardrail at the tool rather than depending on the model to stop making the mistake. This gives deterministic application code a chance to reject an unsafe action regardless of the exact generated wording. The recorded bad call then provides a concrete input for testing whether the new enforcement blocks the original failure.
qualification: The demo shows an order being blocked; the transcript does not provide the complete validation rule or establish comprehensive trading safety.
title: Enforce action constraints at tools even when model output varies

explanation: A captured failure becomes a focused regression test by stubbing unchanged nodes with their recorded outputs while running the modified component. In the stock example, replay the original planner output containing the bad quantity, execute the updated order tool, and assert that its result is blocked. This isolates a deterministic fix from fresh model variation instead of waiting for a rare bad generation to recur.
qualification: The actual demo stubs the first model node but leaves a later model live; fully model-free CI is a further available stubbing configuration.
title: Replay unchanged nodes and execute the changed component live

explanation: Deterministic tests target tool calls, guardrails, and other code whose expected behavior can be asserted under recorded inputs. Behavioral evaluation asks whether tone or the overall trajectory was appropriate and may use an LLM judge. The presenters describe both as necessary: removing model randomness from a guardrail regression does not evaluate whether future model behavior is helpful, and a subjective judgment does not replace an exact action-blocking assertion.
title: Keep exact component tests and behavioral judgments as complementary layers

explanation: When all relevant model nodes are replaced with captured outputs, the recorded context can drive repeatable tests of deterministic nodes without paying for another inference. This is a testing configuration, not a claim that all agent evaluation is free. It exercises how application code handles already-observed decisions, while new model behavior still requires separate live or behavioral evaluation.
qualification: The claim of free execution means no model calls, not zero infrastructure cost; the live demo itself leaves a later LLM active.
title: Remove fresh model calls from deterministic replay tests when appropriate

explanation: Identical model weights can yield different latency, throughput, reliability, and pricing depending on the serving provider. Evaluate the provider as a separate system variable rather than treating a model benchmark as sufficient evidence about production performance. The talk attributes these differences to the combined inference stack and illustrates the point with a coding-agent workflow that changes provider while retaining the model and application.
qualification: The provider comparison is vendor-reported and does not control or disclose all runtime conditions.
title: Hold model choice separate from inference-provider performance

explanation: The speaker compares two models generating a tower-defense game from one prompt and reports apparently similar working structures but a substantially lower task cost for one model. This illustrates why affordable iteration matters in agent workflows that call models repeatedly. The demonstrated game is not a general quality benchmark: assess actual task completion and expense together rather than inferring broad model equivalence from one attractive output.
qualification: The 5.6-times cost comparison is a vendor-reported single-task example; no detailed cost accounting or systematic quality assessment is supplied.
title: Compare the cost of completing a task alongside output quality

explanation: In the agent workloads described, prompts can exceed ten thousand tokens while outputs are shorter and large prefixes repeat across requests. Processing that input and constructing the attention cache can therefore dominate compute. Inspect input length and prefix overlap when diagnosing latency; a serving optimization aimed only at generating output tokens may miss the larger opportunity in processing the repeated prompt.
qualification: This workload characterization and overlap percentages are speaker-reported, not universal properties of all agents. The caption renders the cache name as KB.
title: Profile repeated input before optimizing only output generation

explanation: Prefix reuse can skip recomputation when a new request begins with text already processed, reducing time to first token. In a replicated service, however, cache state is local to individual replicas. Route a request toward a replica holding the relevant prefix; otherwise a cache-capable implementation may still recompute the prompt and fail to realize its potential latency or GPU savings.
title: Route shared-prefix requests to the replica that holds their cache

explanation: Long contexts and large models can make cache storage extremely memory intensive. The described hierarchy keeps hot blocks in GPU memory, warmer blocks in CPU RAM, and colder blocks on disk, moving less-used blocks out and fetching them when needed. This pairs capacity management with cache-aware routing: prefix reuse at scale depends on both finding the right cached state and maintaining it within scarce fast memory.
qualification: The mechanism is described architecturally; no isolated latency or capacity benchmark is supplied. Captions distort cold-cache and storage terminology.
title: Manage attention cache as a hierarchy rather than only GPU memory

explanation: Ordinary autoregressive decoding generates a token per forward pass and can leave the GPU underutilized. The described speculative method proposes several future tokens, then has the target model validate them together. Accepted drafts can reduce time per output token while retaining target-model validation. Distinguish this mechanism from simply trusting a smaller model to answer, and measure the realized gain under the serving workload.
qualification: The talk states that output quality is unchanged but supplies no detailed verification algorithm or comparative quality experiment.
title: Draft multiple tokens and verify them with the target model

explanation: Model-based speculation uses a small draft model and may achieve a higher acceptance rate, at the cost of extra compute. Model-free speculation reuses patterns from the prompt or prior output with lower overhead, but works best when the new output resembles that context. Evaluate both acceptance benefits and drafting cost instead of assuming that a more accurate draft mechanism always produces the fastest service.
title: Choose draft mechanisms according to overhead and output reuse

explanation: Speculation can improve an individual request while adding validation overhead to a batch. The speaker therefore describes a runtime that chooses between draft strategies according to request and workload characteristics rather than applying one static method everywhere. Adapting the draft model to real serving traffic is presented as an additional improvement path. Neither per-request latency nor draft acceptance alone captures the full batching tradeoff.
qualification: Hybrid and self-evolving speculation are vendor descriptions without separately reported ablation results.
title: Treat speculative decoding as a workload-sensitive serving decision

explanation: An API can have attractive average latency and still produce a poor user experience through timeouts, server errors, or rate limits. In a multi-call agent workflow, one intermediate failure can invalidate the task. Evaluate error rate and uptime alongside latency and throughput, and consider end-to-end task completion rather than treating the speed of successful calls as a complete account of performance.
qualification: No empirical workflow-failure model is supplied. The vendor uptime figure is reported, not independently verified.
title: Include API failures in the measure of agent performance

explanation: A provider can look fast under a particular benchmark while behaving differently for an application with other prompt lengths, repeated prefixes, traffic patterns, and latency requirements. Test the application workload across speed, reliability, cost, and quality before choosing a provider. This recommendation qualifies the talk's own promotional comparisons: aggregate rankings and a single game-generation example do not substitute for workload-matched measurement.
title: Benchmark providers on the actual prompt and traffic distribution

explanation: Treat an agentic application as a mixture of deterministic and nondeterministic components rather than replacing conventional quality assurance with model scoring. Trainline retains its ordinary software quality practices while adding offline and online evaluations for model behavior. This framing matters when a correct API implementation can still be composed into an unhelpful or policy-inappropriate customer interaction.
qualification: Trainline describes its operating practice, not a comparative experiment proving a particular testing mix.
title: Agent quality assurance combines software checks and model evaluations

explanation: Cost-driven model changes need a quality baseline, not just a lower token bill. Trainline first simulates the performance of a candidate replacement using offline evaluations and then checks live evaluations to determine whether the anticipated effect actually appears. The transferable rule is to test non-regression against the incumbent and verify that offline expectations survive deployment on real interactions.
qualification: No numerical cost savings, model comparison scores, or statistical acceptance thresholds are supplied.
title: Verify cheaper replacements offline, then confirm the effect online

explanation: A customer-facing agent should not be evaluated only for fluent tone. Trainline reports scoring its travel assistant from voice and helpfulness through complex ticket reasoning, where delay status and ticket type affect what a customer should receive. A useful evaluation therefore separates presentation quality from decisions governed by business rules, rather than allowing a pleasant answer to mask incorrect entitlement handling.
qualification: The talk does not expose the actual refund rubrics, labeled cases, or rates of entitlement error.
title: Score both conversational quality and domain-dependent entitlement reasoning

explanation: At organizational scale, product colleagues and other nontechnical specialists need to inspect behavior without asking engineers to export and explain logs for each request. Trainline presents self-service access to traces and insights as an operational benefit. This supports a workflow in which domain stakeholders can investigate evidence themselves while engineers retain responsibility for instrumentation and the surrounding production system.
qualification: This is an account of collaboration benefits, not a measured productivity study or an access-control design.
title: Shared trace access reduces engineering-mediated evaluation bottlenecks

explanation: Breaking a monolithic call into context collection, triage, policy review, reply writing, and finalization makes the location of a failure easier to inspect and repair. The workshop also acknowledges that sequential model calls take longer than its original single-shot implementation. Staging is therefore a debugging and responsibility-boundary technique with a latency cost, not an automatic improvement on every operational dimension.
qualification: Sequential slowdown is explicitly acknowledged at lines 1266-1272; no measured latency comparison or quality ablation is provided.
title: Use explicit stages to localize failures, accepting sequential latency

explanation: A trace should preserve the execution tree of a complete interaction, including nested model, function, and tool calls. Recording isolated calls without their parent conversation loses the relationships needed to identify where behavior went wrong. The workshop recommends getting this structure right during instrumentation, then using the tree to inspect stage inputs and outputs rather than treating the final answer as sufficient evidence.
qualification: The concrete example is a short staged support workflow; the talk does not demonstrate distributed or long-duration trace stitching.
title: Trace one interaction as a parent with nested calls

explanation: Trace collection should include latency, cost, token counts, inputs, outputs, and metadata, rather than simply recording whether an answer was produced. The workshop particularly highlights time to first token and uses a waterfall view to locate slow stages. These measurements allow teams to investigate operational regressions and behavioral failures together, especially when the application adds more tool calls and specialist stages.
qualification: The metrics are recommended and displayed in a vendor interface; no numerical performance target is established.
title: Record operational metrics alongside behavioral evidence

explanation: A new application can begin evaluation with concrete anticipated edge cases instead of waiting for production failures or relying on anecdotes. The workshop's golden support set captures nonnegotiables such as category correctness, severity for blocking issues, escalation policy, and output structure. This creates an initial basis for regression comparisons while remaining provisional: the speaker repeatedly says that real production data cannot be substituted away.
