qualification: The initial demonstration has ten handcrafted inputs; it is not evidence of comprehensive coverage or a representative production distribution.
title: Start from anticipated failure modes when production data is unavailable

explanation: Use deterministic scoring for requirements that can be expressed directly, such as category validity, schema shape, and the presence of required escalation reasons. Add a model judge for nuanced qualities such as branding or customer-facing style that the workshop cannot capture with ordinary checks. This separates cheap, reproducible checks from more interpretive scoring rather than using an expensive model for every requirement.
qualification: The talk recommends this division but does not calibrate its customer rubric against expert labels or quantify judge error.
title: Reserve model judges for judgments that cannot be codified cheaply

explanation: Centralizing prompts, parameters, tools, and scorers can let nontechnical specialists test changes without editing application code, while recording who changed what. The workshop explicitly warns that this shared interface is not a replacement for version control. Its recommended operating pattern keeps centralized source assets and automates synchronization into the managed runtime so collaboration does not erase change tracking and reproducibility.
qualification: The demonstration changes a model parameter through the UI; a complete promotion, approval, and rollback policy is not specified.
title: Managed prompt editing complements rather than replaces version-control rigor

explanation: The workshop recommends starting live model-based scoring at a higher sampling rate to understand baseline behavior, then reducing sampling once the output is understood. It suggests five to ten percent as a cost-management example while running cheap deterministic checks continuously. This is an economic operating heuristic; teams still need to consider what failures their chosen sample can and cannot reveal.
qualification: The suggested sampling rate is not justified by statistical power, rare-event coverage, or a demonstrated risk budget.
title: Use heavier judge sampling to establish a baseline, then reduce cost

explanation: Online evaluation rules can operate on an individual span or an entire trace, and metadata helps select the relevant execution paths. The workshop connects this to evaluating particular failures rather than indiscriminately treating every logged item alike. Instrumentation therefore needs to carry the identifying information that later automation will use; scoring selectivity is constrained by the structure and metadata captured upstream.
qualification: The transcript describes configurable targeting but does not present a validated metadata taxonomy or failure-detection recall.
title: Use trace metadata to target online scoring at relevant spans

explanation: Turn a discovered failure into a replayable evaluation, apply a targeted correction, and rerun both the failing case and the broader test set. The workshop uses a ticket that calls itself nonurgent despite blocking invoice export before a board meeting. Its business-impact interpretation overrides superficial wording, and the full-suite rerun checks whether a prompt change repairs that mistake without introducing other regressions.
qualification: This is a constructed workshop failure, not a documented live Trainline incident; displayed improvement is not numerically reported.
title: Replay a business failure and retest the full suite after remediation

explanation: An audience member challenges how online judging can work without ground truth. The speaker suggests capturing the edge case in a dataset and replaying it in a playground, but does not explain how reference labels or trustworthy reference-free judgments are obtained. Preserve this gap when applying the workflow: automation makes scoring operational, yet the meaning and correctness of its scores still require a separately justified evaluation design.
qualification: This is a limitation revealed by the exchange, not a claim that all online judges require a reference answer.
title: Online judge automation does not by itself resolve missing ground truth

explanation: Production traces reveal what an agent did and help identify failures, but comparing live configurations can mix different database states and tool versions. Reconstructing tasks in offline simulations lets teams rerun different configurations against the same conditions. The resulting comparison should include cost, latency, and retries alongside success, making the experiment about operational behavior rather than only retrospective trace inspection.
qualification: The talk motivates repeatability but does not quantify simulator fidelity or demonstrate that every production dependency can be reproduced.
title: Convert observational traces into repeatable counterfactual experiments

explanation: Public benchmarks provide a prior about model capabilities, but a release decision depends on the company's tasks, tools, policies, and environment. The speaker distinguishes broad orientation from production-specific evidence: a private benchmark should exercise the workflows actually being shipped. This avoids treating performance on coding, terminal, or computer-use benchmarks as direct proof of reliability in a different business domain.
qualification: This is a division of evaluation roles, not a claim that public benchmarks have no value or private benchmarks are automatically representative.
title: Use public benchmarks for orientation and private benchmarks for shipping

explanation: The experimental unit is the deployed agent system, not just its underlying language model. Simulations can compare prompts, reasoning settings, harness behavior, skills, and tools while keeping environments and evaluators unchanged. This helps determine whether an improvement comes from the system configuration that users experience, and prevents a model-only leaderboard from substituting for a controlled comparison of actual application behavior.
qualification: The nearby discussion lists stack-level variables; the talk supplies no factorial experiment or quantitative causal attribution among them.
title: Hold the environment fixed while varying the entire agent stack

explanation: A benchmark failure is not meaningful evidence against an agent if the task itself cannot be solved. The proposed task anatomy therefore includes a constructed oracle solution that traverses the same environment and verification sequence as the tested agent. Passing that solution provides a feasibility check before using the task to judge capabilities, although it does not prove the task matches production difficulty.
qualification: An oracle demonstrates a valid path under the constructed environment; it does not establish unique solutions or overall verifier correctness.
title: Require an oracle solution to establish that a benchmark task is solvable

explanation: The talk uses the Harbor-style task layout to distinguish instructions and an executable environment from the oracle solution and verifiers that the agent should not see. Metadata forms another task component. This packaging makes a simulation a versionable software artifact and preserves a boundary between solving the task and inspecting the answers or acceptance machinery used to score it.
qualification: The layout is described conceptually; hidden files alone do not constitute a demonstrated security boundary against an adversarial agent.
title: Separate agent-visible task material from hidden verification machinery

explanation: A useful simulator exposes realistic database, API, tool, and file behavior without launching the entire production system for every run. The suggested implementation uses snapshots, service sidecars, and mocks, with a separately prompted model standing in for a human user. The design tension is to preserve behavior relevant to the workflow while keeping the environment repeatable and economically runnable at scale.
qualification: No fidelity measurement or validation method for the simulated user is given; apparent realism should not be mistaken for established behavioral equivalence.
title: Build a miniature production environment rather than cloning all production

explanation: For workflows that span hours, the speaker proposes multi-step simulations with a separate prompt and verifier for each stage. The runner can stop early after a stage fails rather than spending the entire budget on an already failed trajectory. This offers both intermediate diagnostic points and an execution-control mechanism, provided the stage boundaries accurately represent the intended long-running task.
qualification: This is an architectural proposal; no hours-long run or empirical analysis of early termination bias is presented.
title: Give long-horizon simulations intermediate prompts and verifiers

explanation: An agent's outcome includes the modified environment, its trace, and produced artifacts. Verification can inspect database state, API interactions, user replies, and files instead of merely reading the final response. The speaker recommends choosing deterministic checks for clear outputs or calls and model-based judgments for qualities such as planning, with the mix determined by the task rather than one universal verifier type.
qualification: The talk lists possible verification surfaces but does not show a complete verifier implementation or validation results.
title: Verify changes to the world, not only the agent's final text

explanation: Simulation benchmarks can fail in several directions: an agent may recognize and exploit the simulator, broad verifiers may pass incorrect work, broken verifiers may reject everything, or agent outcomes may vary substantially across runs. These are defects or diagnostic warnings in benchmark construction, not necessarily agent capability differences. Evaluate the benchmark's behavior before trusting its score as a release signal.
qualification: These are failure modes the speaker warns about; no specific exploit or measured occurrence rate is shown.
title: Audit tasks for reward hacking and invalid pass-fail behavior

explanation: Treat a benchmark as software with its own continuous integration pipeline. Check pinned dependencies, base images, and fixtures, run the oracle, confirm checks reject a no-solution condition, and run agents repeatedly to estimate solvability and difficulty before approving a task. This makes benchmark acceptance a separate engineering process rather than assuming every generated task is immediately suitable for judging releases.
qualification: The negative-check wording in the captions is compressed; the surrounding sequence distinguishes oracle success, no-oracle failure, and repeated agent runs but supplies no thresholds.
title: Give benchmark tasks their own CI and acceptance process

explanation: A controlled full-stack simulation lets teams test remedies beyond adding prohibitions to the prompt. The speaker suggests changing the harness for context overload, putting a missing procedure into a skill, and enforcing an output schema through structured output. These examples frame error analysis as locating the appropriate engineering boundary rather than accumulating prompt instructions for every observed symptom.
qualification: The captions render harness inconsistently; the intended stack-level distinction is supported by the surrounding discussion, but no comparative remediation experiment is shown.
title: Fix failures in the system layer that owns them, not always in the prompt

explanation: Use observability failures to expand the private benchmark, then run experiments on that expanded set when the agent configuration changes. Results become a release gate before returning the revised agent to production. The benchmark is therefore a maintained asset that evolves with observed behavior, not a static launch checklist, and the observability and experiment systems need to preserve that connection.
qualification: The speaker presents an operating model, not a demonstrated production feedback-loop deployment with measured reliability improvement.
title: Connect benchmark expansion and agent release into two linked loops

explanation: Repeatedly improving an agent on the same benchmark creates a need for a standalone set that has not guided the experimentation process. In the Q&A, the speaker applies the familiar train-validation split idea and mentions eighty-twenty as a conventional starting point. The essential requirement is an unseen validation set for configuration assessment, not adherence to a universal numerical split.
qualification: The speaker explicitly says the split depends on the use case and does not answer the requested benchmark-size question with a sample-count rule.
title: Reserve tasks unseen during iterative agent configuration

explanation: The Q&A recommends a mix of bread-and-butter use cases and edge conditions such as tool failures or database problems. Thinking like an integration-test designer helps ensure the benchmark exercises happy paths and adverse conditions together. This is a coverage requirement rather than a claim that failure-mined examples alone reproduce the frequency distribution of production traffic.
qualification: No weighting scheme, distributional estimate, or coverage sufficiency criterion is specified.
title: Cover everyday workflows and dependency failures, not only curated successes

explanation: Subject-matter experts need not review every trajectory. The speaker recommends using them when agent outcomes and different verifiers disagree, for example when a supposedly solved task is marked unsuccessful or a trace is judged suboptimal unexpectedly. Those cases can reveal problems in the reviewing agent or rubric and provide targeted material for tuning the review process rather than indiscriminate manual inspection.
qualification: This is a resource-allocation recommendation; disagreement sampling alone is not shown to detect correlated errors shared by all verifiers.
title: Target expert review at disagreements between agents and verifiers

explanation: An agent can have permission and tools to manipulate a product while lacking the guidance needed to do so safely. In the reported comparison, a SQL view over an access-restricted table needed an explicit security-invoker setting; the MCP-only agent missed it while the skill-assisted agent included it. Evaluate correct product use and safety invariants, not merely whether the agent can call the integration.
qualification: This is one reported task with Sonnet 4.6; the transcript does not provide repeated-run error rates or independent security verification.
title: Tool access alone does not supply product-specific safety knowledge

explanation: A skill is described as a folder containing instructions and optional scripts or resources. Name and description in its front matter help the agent decide when to load the main instruction file, while additional references can stay unloaded until needed. This separates discovery from detailed context, but makes effectiveness dependent on both correct selection and actual retrieval of the necessary supplementary information.
qualification: The later experience report shows that agents may skip references; availability through progressive disclosure is not a guarantee of use.
title: Skill metadata and bundled references create staged context loading

explanation: The speaker advises treating a skill as guidance into the product's authoritative documentation rather than copying the documentation into another maintained artifact. Tell the agent where and how to find current information, and make the retrieval instruction explicit because agents may prefer stale training knowledge. This reduces duplicated information while preserving a route to product behavior that changed after model training.
qualification: The speaker separately keeps stable safety-critical guidance inline; the advice is not to externalize every instruction regardless of retrieval reliability.
title: Route agents to current documentation instead of duplicating volatile knowledge

explanation: Reference files may be available yet never read, especially when a task requires information spread across several files. Supabase initially put its security checklist in a reference and observed that agents often missed it, so moved it into the main skill. Stable guidance that must not be skipped belongs in the context guaranteed by loading the skill, not only behind optional discovery.
qualification: The observed skipping behavior is not quantified and may depend on agent implementation; the talk does not establish a universal reference-file limit.
title: Keep indispensable safety instructions in the main skill file

explanation: Product maintainers can guide agents toward the workflow they judge most effective. The concrete schema-editing sequence uses direct changes on a development or staging database, runs security and performance advisors, fixes identified issues, and only then creates a migration. The goal is to avoid generating a migration file for every exploratory change while ensuring checks happen before the final artifact is produced.
qualification: The sequence is specifically presented for development or staging, not permission to mutate a production schema freely.
title: Encode a product's preferred operational sequence, not just facts

explanation: A skill's text can be tested by running agents on representative product scenarios and inspecting task completion and tool behavior. Supabase used six scenarios, four agent-model combinations from two vendors, and three conditions: neither MCP nor skill, MCP alone, and MCP plus the skill. This tests the operational effect of documentation rather than assuming clear prose is sufficient evidence of useful guidance.
qualification: The talk names a completeness-based graded score but does not provide enough rubric, repetition, or sampling detail to reproduce the evaluation from captions alone.
title: Evaluate instruction documents through the agent behaviors they induce

explanation: The speaker reports that MCP plus the Supabase skill outperformed the other tested conditions for every model in the study: Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, GPT 5.4, and GPT 5.4 mini in their named agent interfaces. This supports guidance as an improvement lever when tools already exist, but only within the evaluated product scenarios and the study's completeness-based scoring.
qualification: The transcript supplies no numerical effect sizes, uncertainty, skill-only condition, or evidence for all products and agents.
title: A small product-specific study reports gains from adding skills to MCP

explanation: The closing recommendations combine three constraints: point to a single source of truth, be opinionated about how the product should be used, and start minimally before iterating. This frames skill development as an evolving engineering artifact rather than a one-time comprehensive manual. Expansion should preserve useful guidance and authoritative references instead of treating greater document length as evidence of quality.
qualification: The speaker recommends iteration but does not present a measured relationship between skill length, version changes, and performance.
title: Start a product skill minimally and expand through versions

explanation: Supabase is experimenting with serving documentation over SSH so agents can navigate it using familiar filesystem and Linux tooling. In the Q&A, the speaker suggests augmenting that interface with semantic search rather than limiting retrieval to naive file navigation. The reusable hypothesis is that existing agent tool fluency can reduce documentation-access friction without requiring an entirely new browsing interaction model.
qualification: The talk explicitly calls this an experiment still being worked out; it reports no retrieval-quality or efficiency comparison, and semantic augmentation is proposed rather than demonstrated.
title: Expose documentation through interfaces agents already know how to navigate

explanation: Although the talk calls skills agent-agnostic, its Q&A describes distribution as unresolved. Repository-packaged skills, a skills package, and plugins coexist, while some plugin formats are model-specific. Internally the speaker describes packaging skills in repositories so accessible projects can expose them for discovery. Distinguish reusable instruction content from the practical problem of installing, finding, and bundling it across different agent environments.
qualification: This is the ecosystem state reported in the talk, not a claim about current package-manager compatibility or a universally supported installation format.
title: Instruction portability does not imply a solved distribution ecosystem

explanation: The speaker reframes financial institutions' question about reasoning as whether an agent can operate within complex schemas and legacy APIs, sustain realistic workflows without compounding errors, and remain auditable. This motivates evaluating actual task and environment behavior instead of using model size as the sole proxy for competence. It also explains why specialization can be attractive for a bounded operational workflow.
qualification: This is the speaker's synthesis of enterprise needs; the subsequent experiment is a simulated financial question-answering setting, not a complete long-running production workflow.
title: Enterprise reasoning includes stack compatibility, error accumulation, and auditability

explanation: The dataset pipeline extracts tables from annual financial reports, generates question-answer pairs using a taxonomy developed with financial experts, and applies three verification layers. Programmatic checks use lineage, table, and column metadata; independent agents review the examples; experts assess realism and correctness. The transferable design is to combine structural validity with domain plausibility rather than treating generated question-answer pairs as self-validating training data.
qualification: The talk does not give rejection rates, reviewer agreement, or an independent audit of the final labels; roughly 6900 extracted tables are not all retained examples.
title: Validate synthetic financial tasks with structural checks, independent agents, and experts

explanation: The reported FinQA data contains roughly four thousand training examples, five hundred validation examples, and a held-out benchmark of two hundred ninety, with no company overlap between splits. Holding out the domain entity creates a stricter boundary than merely separating individual questions about the same companies. The key reusable idea is to choose split units that match the domain-level generalization claim being assessed.
qualification: Company-disjoint splitting is reported, but the transcript does not describe checks for other leakage channels or explain all filtering from the original table set.
title: Hold companies apart across financial training and evaluation splits

explanation: The finance experiments identify three recurring failures: inventing tables or columns, issuing poorly planned queries such as SELECT star that flood context, and repeating a failed strategy instead of using error messages to adapt. These failures concern disciplined interaction with tools and feedback, not only abstract reasoning. Keeping them distinct helps interpret why a targeted training intervention might improve a smaller model's task performance.
qualification: The speaker reports similar patterns in insurance work, but the transcript provides no frequency breakdown or detailed cross-domain evidence.
title: Diagnose schema invention, context flooding, and repeated failed strategies separately

explanation: The training agent interacts with generated SQL tables in a ReAct loop and receives a binary correctness reward from GPT 5 nano using reference-based evaluation. This ties the optimization signal to the question's final answer rather than requiring rewards for every intermediate action. It is applicable to the presented tasks because each has a single verifiable answer, not because all enterprise outputs admit binary correctness.
qualification: Reward correctness still depends on the reference and model judge; no judge-human calibration or false-positive analysis is reported.
title: A verifiable final answer can support a simple judge-based RL reward

explanation: The speaker reports almost sixty percent pass-at-one for the trained four-billion-parameter Qwen specialist versus fifty-one percent for its 235-billion-parameter variant. The specialist's accuracy more than doubles relative to its own base model, with results evaluated on the expert-curated held-out set of two hundred ninety examples. This is evidence for task-specific specialization, not proof that the small model is generally more capable.
qualification: Numbers are speaker-reported and rounded; uncertainty estimates, run variance, and full baseline configuration are absent from the captions.
title: A specialized four-billion-parameter agent reportedly exceeds its larger counterpart on FinQA

explanation: The talk attributes its under-five-hundred-dollar result to approximately four hundred twenty dollars in compute and forty dollars in judge API charges, using eight H100s and roughly a thousand concurrent environments. This establishes a reported bill for the described RL run. It should not be read as the total cost of extracting reports, building environments, developing the taxonomy, obtaining expert review, or operating the resulting agent.
qualification: The stated accounting covers compute and judge charges; it does not itemize data creation, expert labor, engineering effort, or deployment costs.
title: Separate a low RL training bill from the total cost of creating a specialist

explanation: To probe beyond its single-table training tasks, the study evaluates a variant requiring dependencies across two to five tables and sequential planning. The speaker reports improvement without explicit multi-table training. The interpretation is that learning reliable foundational tool use can transfer compositionally to a harder setting, but that interpretation remains bounded by the study's financial table environment and small held-out multi-table benchmark.
qualification: The multi-table benchmark is reported as eighty examples; exact lift, confidence intervals, and transfer to substantially different tools are not provided.
title: Test whether single-table tool discipline transfers to multi-table tasks

explanation: The study uses the BFCL benchmark to check whether finance-specific reinforcement learning damages general tool-calling capability. The speaker reports a slight overall improvement and minor gains in multi-turn and memory categories. This illustrates a useful validation pattern: evaluate the target domain and a broader capability check separately so a specialization gain is not silently purchased by an unmeasured regression elsewhere.
qualification: Only this named broader tool-use benchmark is discussed; it cannot establish preservation of every general capability, and exact scores are not narrated.
title: Check broader capabilities after domain specialization

explanation: The study compares training on the single-table set, mixing single- and multi-table data, and a curriculum progressing from simple to multi-table tasks. The simplest training set produces the largest reported improvement. The speaker attributes this to tool-use discipline being the actual bottleneck. This supports testing the hypothesized bottleneck directly rather than assuming a more complex training distribution is inherently more useful.
qualification: The result concerns this study's data mixtures and training setup; it does not establish that simple examples always dominate complex curricula.
title: Ablate simple data, mixed complexity, and curricula instead of assuming harder training wins

explanation: The study investigates richer rewards for intermediate behavior, including table access, query completeness, and an expert-designed weighted rubric. Despite that engineering, a single binary reward gives the largest improvement on the presented data. The reusable decision rule is to compare reward sophistication empirically with a simple correctness baseline, rather than inferring that a more detailed reward necessarily provides better learning guidance.
qualification: The speaker reports a local ablation outcome; the transcript lacks the exact rubric, weighting, training variance, and reward-model error analysis.
title: Validate reward shaping against a simple final-correctness baseline

explanation: The closing framework identifies environment complexity, autonomy horizon, and output complexity as distinct dimensions of agent evaluation. Ask whether environments are realistic and dynamic, whether task duration matches intended use, and whether outputs extend beyond the text artifacts benchmarks often emphasize. These axes expose gaps that a strong score on short, structured financial question answering would otherwise leave easy to overlook.
qualification: This is a proposed evaluation framework and research opportunity, not a set of axes fully exercised by the reported FinQA experiment.
title: Evaluate realism, autonomy horizon, and output complexity as separate axes

explanation: The speaker distinguishes valid, functionally correct code from code that violates the application's intended security or business rules. Pattern-based analysis is presented as insufficient for some logic-level issues because identifying the flaw requires understanding relationships and expectations. The reusable evaluation question is therefore not just whether code executes correctly, but whether the allowed behavior contradicts the intended authorization or business workflow.
qualification: The vendor's broad characterization of SAST is not independently evaluated in this source and should not be read as a formal limit of every static-analysis technique.
title: Functional correctness does not guarantee alignment with security intent

explanation: The described agent first constructs a global repository map and then launches specialists for classes of security issue. The intent is to analyze relationships between components and infer security expectations, rather than inspecting isolated snippets without application context. This architecture is particularly relevant to access-control and workflow flaws whose correctness depends on how several routes, data fields, and checks interact.
qualification: This is the product's described design; the transcript provides no ablation comparing global mapping with local-only analysis.
title: Map repository-wide relationships before delegating specialist security checks

explanation: Candidate security leads are not immediately equivalent to actionable vulnerabilities. The product description applies adversarial validation to check findings and noise gates to suppress low-validity or intentional behavior, then aggregates and deduplicates specialist outputs before exporting issues. This separates exploration from reporting and makes explicit that a multi-agent detector also needs a mechanism to control false positives and duplicated developer work.
qualification: No precision, recall, validation protocol, or independent ground-truth review is shown; calling findings validated is the vendor's characterization.
title: Separate candidate discovery from validation and deduplicated reporting

explanation: The speaker recommends using SAST and software-composition analysis alongside the contextual Hunter Agent rather than treating agent reasoning as a replacement for existing tools. The rationale is complementary coverage: established scanners handle their usual issue classes while the agent targets intent and logic gaps. This is a layered verification strategy, with separate mechanisms contributing different kinds of evidence about the codebase.
qualification: The presentation's stronger language about nothing slipping through is not supported by measured completeness; layering should not be interpreted as guaranteed vulnerability coverage.
title: Combine conventional security analysis with contextual agent review

explanation: The walkthrough gives two security-invariant failures. Any signed-in user can pass an admin check because users can write their own role field; separately, a password-only user can reach protected routes including admin functionality without completing multi-factor authentication. These examples show why evaluating the presence of an access check is weaker than checking whether untrusted state or incomplete authentication can satisfy it.
qualification: The second example appears at lines 291-302. The source shows issue explanations, not source code or executed exploit reproductions establishing either flaw independently.
title: Test authorization against mutable identity fields and incomplete authentication stages

explanation: The product's business-logic category includes skipping required workflow steps, abusing repeatable actions, and missing rate limits. These examples extend security review beyond malformed inputs or vulnerable library versions to sequences of individually valid operations. They provide useful scenario categories when testing whether an application enforces the intended process, especially where the exploit arises from repetition or bypassing a prerequisite rather than one obviously unsafe statement.
qualification: The categories are listed rather than demonstrated with concrete exploit traces, rate thresholds, or expected detection performance.
title: Include workflow skipping and repeatable-action abuse in security review

explanation: The issue workflow distinguishes an accepted finding that is considered valid but does not affect quality gates, a confirmed valid finding that does affect them, and a false-positive designation. This separates whether a report is true from the policy decision about whether it blocks shipping. Integrating these states with ordinary issue assignment lets humans make the remaining risk and remediation decisions after automated detection.
qualification: The meaning of these states is specific to the demonstrated product workflow, not a universal security-triage vocabulary.
title: Keep validity decisions distinct from release-blocking policy

explanation: The presenter says the demo project's deep scan took about an hour and notes that runtime depends on project size and complexity. Scans can be launched on demand or scheduled daily, weekly, or monthly for a chosen branch. This makes scan cadence and branch coverage explicit operational choices rather than assuming contextual security reasoning is an instantaneous check on every edit.
qualification: Only one precompleted small Python-project scan is described; no runtime scaling curve, monetary cost, or scheduling-effectiveness comparison is supplied.
title: Budget whole-repository reasoning scans separately from instant developer checks

explanation: The optimization loop asks a proposer agent for a new prompt, evaluates it against task cases, and reuses useful components of successful candidates. GEPA is described as combining candidates from its Pareto frontier rather than sampling indiscriminately. This turns prompt editing into a feedback-controlled search, but usefulness still depends on the evaluation signal and the available search budget.
qualification: The workshop demonstrates a single-prompt search, not a general guarantee of global optimization. The speaker is uncertain about adaptive batch sizing and more sophisticated stopping rules.
title: Use measured candidate performance to drive iterative prompt search

explanation: For structured extraction with known expected relations, custom evaluators can compare returned values against a golden dataset without asking another model to decide correctness. Colvin favors this over LLM judging when the task permits it. The deterministic computation removes one source of judge variability, but it does not make an incomplete or incorrect reference set trustworthy.
qualification: The custom metrics are explicitly presented as a useful starting point rather than a perfect evaluator suite.
title: Prefer deterministic comparison when a meaningful reference exists

explanation: The workshop's expected relations were generated by a similar extraction script using Opus 4.6 and then checked by the speaker. He repeatedly acknowledges that they may not be perfect. An optimizer can improve agreement with such a dataset while inheriting its labeling choices or errors, so reported accuracy must be interpreted as performance against this particular reference.
qualification: No exhaustive independent annotation or inter-annotator validation is provided in the transcript.
title: Treat model-generated gold as a checked hypothesis, not unquestionable truth

explanation: Aggregate comparison shows whether one prompt scores better, but individual cases reveal why. The workshop contrasts an erroneous spouse match with a correct exclusion and identifies a public figure incorrectly treated as a politician. Those cases supply actionable distinctions for the next prompt proposal, rather than merely inviting the instruction to improve accuracy in general.
qualification: Case names and some occupations are caption-rendered; the useful evidence is the visible distinction between relationship and political-role errors.
title: Inspect changed cases to identify the rule a prompt needs

explanation: Repeatedly generating a whole replacement prompt can accumulate edge-case instructions and make the agent slower. Colvin proposes splitting available instructions into components and selecting a bounded subset, such as twenty sentences from two hundred. The bound limits verbosity by construction, trading the flexibility to invent detailed new wording for control over prompt size and latency.
qualification: The workshop actually generates full prompts; bounded component selection is suggested, not compared experimentally here.
title: Bound prompt growth by optimizing a fixed-size subset of components

explanation: An attendee obtains high aggregate accuracy from a prompt that explicitly excludes aunts and uncles even though the reference includes them. Colvin suspects the optimizer did not encounter those relationships in its exposed subset. Training and evaluation splits both need coverage of important categories; otherwise an apparently simpler rule can fit common cases while systematically deleting valid rare outputs.
qualification: Overfitting is the speaker's diagnosis of an audience-reported run, not a fully investigated causal result. His data-volume suggestion is not a universal sample-size rule.
title: Cover rare distinctions in both optimization and held-out data

explanation: Different workshop participants obtain different results, prompting discussion of variance. Colvin recommends running each evaluation case repeatedly and notes that the adapter can return custom numerical scores, allowing objectives beyond mean accuracy. Repetition improves the estimate of typical behavior at additional compute cost; it does not prove that the underlying model has become intrinsically less variable.
qualification: No repeat count, confidence interval, or variance-aware objective is actually demonstrated. The speaker separately says arbitrary floats can be returned as scores.
title: Repeat stochastic cases before trusting small score differences

explanation: Prompt optimization may need repeating when the target model changes, so a better model arriving soon can erase the value of bespoke tuning. Colvin contrasts this with large, repeated extraction workloads where a cheaper specialized model can save enough to justify weeks of analyst effort. The decision depends on workload scale and savings, not on optimization being universally worthwhile.
qualification: The invoice volume and monetary comparisons are illustrative business reasoning, not measured outcomes from the demonstrated system.
title: Pay for model-specific optimization when repeated workload savings justify it

explanation: A narrow extractor has a comparatively enumerable set of distinctions, while a general coding agent can face a huge variety of trajectories. Colvin warns that thousands of tests may still represent only a small part of that space. Optimizing aggressively against them can improve the suite while over-specializing the agent, making broad-task coverage a separate constraint on optimization usefulness.
qualification: This is a qualitative warning, not evidence that five thousand tests are always insufficient or that general coding agents cannot be evaluated.
title: Optimization becomes harder as the task distribution broadens

explanation: A model may answer public-data questions from its existing knowledge rather than using the supplied source or search tool. Colvin observes this in the political example and argues that selecting context matters more when handling private domain rules absent from training. Newly published public material is proposed as a shareable approximation, but the workshop does not establish that it faithfully reproduces private workloads.
qualification: The speaker explicitly treats the private-data prevalence statistic as uncertain; no such statistic is needed for this claim.
title: Public known-answer demos can understate the need for domain context

explanation: When no reference answer exists, evaluations may use human annotation, code execution, or feedback from the originating system. These signals answer narrower questions than overall success. Colvin illustrates the gap with a smoking-cessation agent: a decades-long health outcome is impractical to observe during development, so lexical safety checks become proxies whose limitations must remain explicit.
qualification: The smoking example is hypothetical; successful code execution and forbidden-word checks are presented as starting signals, not complete correctness criteria.
title: Without gold answers, distinguish useful proxies from the real outcome

explanation: Managed variables extend prompt management to a typed object containing instructions, model selection, and generation settings. Values can be updated remotely and targeted to a percentage of calls, separating behavioral experiments from a full application deployment. The demo changes response language and model selection, while the configuration mechanism provides a way to apply later optimized prompts to running agents.
qualification: This is a vendor demonstration. A later wiring error requires a code edit and restart; autonomous optimization of managed values is described as work in progress.
title: Manage typed agent configurations with percentage-based rollout

explanation: Applying the optimized prompt to a selected live failure still misclassifies a sports-commentator father as a political relation. A configuration change and an improved aggregate optimization result therefore do not establish that a particular error has disappeared. A release decision needs to recheck the relevant case rather than treating the optimized prompt label as evidence of correction.
qualification: The numerical gain is speaker-reported during the demo; the transcript does not establish independent held-out testing, statistical significance, or a production rollout.
title: Reported optimization gains do not guarantee that a selected failure disappears

explanation: Colvin says explicit feedback buttons receive little engagement and suggests keeping them simple when used. Corrections in the user's next message can provide a stronger practical signal of dissatisfaction and can seed annotated examples. Positive replies or disappearance are interpreted as success only heuristically; absence of a complaint is not independently verified correctness.
qualification: The sparse-ratings observation is personal experience. The speaker explicitly says departure is assumed to mean success, leaving ambiguity about abandonment.
title: Use next-turn behavior as a feedback signal when explicit ratings are sparse

explanation: For regulated workflows, the speaker describes recording categorical performance while withholding raw inputs and outputs from the observability platform. This retains aggregate evaluation signals without exporting generated text that could contain private client information. It sacrifices diagnostic detail; self-hosting within a private environment is presented as another option when richer inspection is needed and permitted.
qualification: The transcript describes this pattern and vendor deployment options, not a formal privacy guarantee for arbitrary categories or metadata.
title: Export evaluation categories instead of sensitive prompt and response content

explanation: Prompt wording is only one part of an agent configuration. Colvin names model choice, compaction, tool registration, and code mode as additional dimensions, and final Q&A contrasts full-website context with selective queries suitable for a smaller model. Optimizing the surrounding information workflow may therefore matter as much as editing instructions, especially when moving a task onto cheaper models.
qualification: The workshop directly optimizes a prompt only. Broader configuration search is a future direction; the website example is a secondhand account, not reproduced evidence.
title: Treat context strategy and tool registration as optimization dimensions too

explanation: A harness that eagerly loads every tool description and repeatedly appends complete results can consume context before useful work starts. Čurn argues that this is not required by MCP, which does not prescribe the agent's context architecture. Interface evaluation should therefore distinguish protocol constraints from client behavior before treating a costly implementation as evidence against the entire protocol.
qualification: The talk critiques a particular eager-loading pattern; it does not establish that protocol design never affects cost or ergonomics.
title: Attribute context overhead to harness choices before rejecting a protocol

explanation: Progressive discovery exposes a search mechanism first and introduces only the tools relevant to the current task. This avoids paying context costs for a large catalog that is rarely used in full. The speaker contrasts the approach with eager registration and notes that CLI users already discover commands incrementally through help rather than loading every command into the prompt.
qualification: No quantitative context-saving measurement is supplied, and discovery quality itself is not evaluated in the talk.
title: Load tool definitions when needed rather than registering the whole catalog

explanation: Delegating a task to a fresh subagent can keep the parent context smaller, but the delegated tokens still cost money. If a tool returns credentials into that context, sensitive values remain accessible to subsequent model-mediated activity there. The speaker therefore treats context splitting as partial isolation, not a solution for carrying secrets or large data safely through an agent workflow.
qualification: This is an architectural warning, not a demonstrated exploit or an evaluation of every subagent isolation implementation.
title: Subagents relocate context pressure without eliminating token cost or secret exposure

explanation: Code mode lets the agent discover definitions using familiar code-navigation techniques and combine tool calls as an executable program. MCPC's JSON output can be piped through shell utilities such as jq, allowing orchestration without narrating every intermediate result back through the model. This requires an execution environment and a usable interface; it is not merely a different spelling of eager tool registration.
qualification: The broad claim that models are better at code than native tool calling is the speaker's rationale, not established by an isolated controlled comparison here.
title: Represent tools as navigable code and compose results outside model context

explanation: Čurn presents CLI and MCP as different layers rather than mutually exclusive connector choices. A CLI is a familiar local entry point for agents but can hide transport and authentication details; MCP supplies a standard remote interaction surface. A CLI wrapper can preserve those protocol features while letting the agent use shell commands and existing command-discovery habits.
qualification: This is the design argument behind the speaker's own client, not proof that every remote integration requires MCP or that all CLIs lack observability.
title: Combine a standard remote protocol with a shell-friendly local interface

explanation: The demo authenticates a remote MCP connection through the browser, stores credentials in the local OS keychain, and keeps sessions alive between invocations. Different coding agents can then reuse one configured client instead of each maintaining a separate connector setup. This separates connection lifecycle from an individual model conversation and reduces repeated configuration work across agents.
qualification: The transcript describes storage and reuse but does not test credential isolation, revocation, or multi-user access controls.
title: Keep connector authentication and sessions outside individual agent setup

explanation: The client demo starts a remote task asynchronously, checks its progress, and can detach before collecting results later. This avoids forcing a long-running operation into one continuously blocking interaction and leaves room for local work. The mechanism is useful only when both the server and the client expose the protocol feature; a capable protocol alone does not ensure harness support.
qualification: Task submission and detachment are shown; the transcript does not capture a complete failure-recovery or cancellation test.
title: Use protocol-supported asynchronous tasks for long-running tools

explanation: The connector-evals framework reverses the usual agent leaderboard question: instead of asking which agent is best, it compares how one agent performs with different connector forms such as native CLI, MCP, and MCPC. Holding the agent configuration fixed makes interface cost and latency differences more interpretable, rather than confounding them with a simultaneous model or harness change.
qualification: The reported charts use a named agent/model configuration, but the captioned model name is unreliable and task details and scoring criteria are not provided.
title: Hold the agent fixed when comparing connector interfaces

explanation: The speaker reports early charts where MCPC and native CLI are similar in token cost and elapsed time, while raw MCP sometimes finishes sooner but consumes more tokens. This is a tradeoff rather than a single universal ranking: lower token spend and lower wall-clock time need not coincide. Connector selection should preserve both dimensions instead of collapsing them into a slogan.
qualification: The tests are explicitly early; no chart values, sample size, variance, success-rate controls, or causal explanation appear in the transcript.
title: Evaluate connector token cost separately from completion time

explanation: A discovery listing is not the final payment request: a seller can advertise one price and return a higher amount in the 402 response. Kaur's unguarded buyer pays the changed amount, while a deterministic comparison blocks it. The same boundary must include recipient wallet and network, because validating price alone still permits paying an unintended destination or chain.
qualification: The price-change experiment uses controlled test infrastructure; wallet and network changes are additional attack conditions discussed, not exhaustively enumerated production findings.
title: Compare final payment requirements with approved purchase terms before signing

explanation: Signature verification can accept several requests bearing the same payment number even though only one will settle on-chain. A seller that releases a distinct valuable response for each request loses data despite valid-looking verification. Kaur recommends shared state recording pending and completed IDs, with repeated requests receiving the saved result instead of triggering additional independent fulfillment.
qualification: The transcript does not specify transactional locking or atomicity of the shared-state implementation, which would affect concurrent requests.
title: Track in-progress and completed payment IDs before releasing repeated deliveries

explanation: A buyer may retry after a timeout without knowing whether the previous payment succeeded. If each retry uses a new payment number, the chain can treat them as independent valid charges for one desired result. Keeping the same payment number across retries makes the attempt a retry of the original purchase rather than permission to create additional purchases.
qualification: This advice addresses the described x402 payment-number flow, not arbitrary payment API retry semantics or all timeout recovery requirements.
title: Reuse the purchase payment ID across timeout retries

explanation: A facilitator's valid signature signal does not guarantee eventual settlement: insufficient funds or inconsistent state can still cause payment failure. Waiting for settlement before releasing a valuable result reduces unpaid fulfillment but adds latency. The speaker particularly favors waiting for expensive, confidential, per-request generated, licensing, activation, or provisioning outputs, leaving cheaper performance-sensitive delivery as a business risk decision.
qualification: The alternative low-value delivery example at lines 220–222 has unclear captions, so no numeric risk threshold is extracted.
title: Choose delivery timing based on settlement risk and value at stake

explanation: Payment enforcement fails if the same report is reachable through another endpoint that lacks the paywall. A buyer who discovers the unprotected route can bypass the purchase flow without breaking payment cryptography. Kaur proposes a direct boundary test: request every endpoint intended to be paid and check that it returns payment-required behavior before releasing the content.
qualification: This is a route-coverage recommendation; the talk does not provide an exhaustive endpoint inventory or automated test implementation.
title: Test every protected endpoint rather than only the advertised paid route

explanation: A response cache keyed on a public URL can turn one authorized purchase into free delivery for later buyers. The speaker recommends placing cached content behind the seller's paywall so payment checks happen before serving it. For confidential, expensive, or per-request generated data, she additionally proposes disabling storage with cache-control no-store rather than exposing a reusable cached response.
qualification: The public-cache default describes the scenario under attack, not a universal HTTP or x402 default. Header compliance across intermediaries is not tested.
title: Keep paid caches behind authorization and avoid storing sensitive generated results

explanation: Separate paid pages may each accept the same verified payment ID if they do not share fulfillment state, while only one settlement succeeds. Kaur extends the shared payment-ID ledger with a mapping to the delivered page. A subsequent request using that ID for a different resource should conflict rather than buy two outputs with one payment.
qualification: The recommendation is presented as a 409-conflict defense. The talk does not detail concurrent claim acquisition or the exact resource identity schema.
title: Bind each payment ID to the specific resource it purchased

explanation: A service directory can establish that a service responds without establishing who operates it or owns its payment wallet. A look-alike seller with a familiar name and lower price can therefore attract an agent's purchase. Kaur recommends enterprise approval policy over seller identity, not merely choosing the cheapest discovered name or assuming directory presence supplies organizational trust.
qualification: The trust limitation is the speaker's characterization of the discovery system in the tested setup, not an independently audited claim about every version or directory.
title: Treat discovered services as untrusted identities until separately approved

explanation: Strict allowlisting is suitable for conservative enterprises but restricts agents that need to explore new sellers. The proposed compromise separates approved, blocked, and probationary sellers, with later human review of newly discovered identities and their interactions. Approval lists also need active maintenance because legitimate sellers can rotate domains, wallets, networks, coins, and prices rather than remaining static forever.
qualification: The suggested review windows are examples, not experimentally validated thresholds; the transcript does not fully specify what probation permits a seller to do.
title: Balance seller exploration with allowlists, blocklists, and human-reviewed probation

explanation: In the experiment, seller text suggests that a fuller summary exists elsewhere, and Llama 3.2 chooses to fetch it and pay again. Keyword checks miss indirect suggestions, while a model attack classifier can also miss cases. Because the authorized plan needed only one purchase in that turn, a deterministic execution guard blocks the second payment despite the agent's continued desire to make it.
qualification: The zero-attack outcome refers to this constrained one-call experiment, not general prompt-injection immunity. Legitimate multi-purchase tasks need a different scoped plan.
title: Enforce the approved purchase plan even when the model follows an upsell hint

explanation: A valid-looking payment can still produce the wrong economic outcome, so payment observability must include more than the final transaction status. Kaur recommends following one ID across the whole sequence and checking that the trace explains buyer intent, the seller called, and the response received. Missing answers indicate missing instrumentation before attempting more elaborate rollout decisions.
qualification: This is a recommended debugging and rollout method; no complete machine-readable trace schema is supplied.
title: Trace one payment ID through intent, seller response, and fulfillment

explanation: After instrumenting a payment path, Kaur proposes shadow operation with roughly twenty to twenty-five success and failure cases, followed by error analysis. Those findings decide where to place guards, alerts, or blocking behavior. Replaying the same cases after enforcement changes supports decisions about tightening or relaxing policy in the context of the specific business workflow.
qualification: The case count is a practical starting suggestion, not demonstrated statistical sufficiency or comprehensive security coverage.
title: Turn traced successes and failures into a replayable enforcement rollout set

explanation: Sending a confident acknowledgement does not establish that a fact was durably stored for later use. The talk distinguishes byte storage from ownership: the owner is the system whose persistent state can reconstruct what happened. For each future-relevant fact, identify that owner and how to replay it, whether the fact belongs to a calendar, ticket, repository, transcript, or memory store.
qualification: The motivating Telegram/state-hole incident is summarized by the speaker without an issue identifier or reproduced persistence trace.
title: A remembered fact needs a named system of record and a replay path

explanation: The model does not directly inherit every durable fact; the harness assembles a working set from transcript, memory, session state, policy, and tool definitions each turn. A missing or stale input can yield a fluent answer over incomplete reality. Evaluation of an agent failure should therefore record which context and versions the run actually inherited, not infer completeness from confident language.
qualification: This explains a failure mechanism; it does not establish that every incorrect answer is caused by missing context or that model faults are absent.
title: Inspect assembled context before attributing coherent mistakes to reasoning

explanation: Two callers can load the same old state, edit different records, and each produce a locally valid save while the later save erases the earlier mutation. The proposed invariant is one ordered commit path for each mutable state boundary, implemented with an appropriate queue, mutex, transaction, or lock. Parallel retrieval, independent sessions, and subagent work can remain concurrent outside that boundary.
qualification: The talk offers architecture choices, not a tested concurrency implementation or a recommendation to use one particular lock granularity everywhere.
title: Serialize commits to shared state without serializing all agent work

explanation: A tool call with no recorded result can leave a session waiting for an event that will never arrive, causing new messages to queue behind it. Runs need deadlines, cancellation, watchdog visibility, tool timeouts, and explicit error results. Recovery commands must bypass the blocked lane they are meant to repair, and the receipt must record the final outcome so later work does not guess.
qualification: The incident's exact triggering cause is not established; the proposal addresses the shared production failure of indefinite waiting.
title: Every external operation needs a terminal outcome and a recovery path

explanation: A past click is not durable permission for whatever a later retry attempts. The harness should represent approval as scoped execution state carrying the approving actor, session, run, tool, arguments, expiry, outcome, and receipt linkage. These bindings must survive retries and callbacks; an expired approval should terminate rather than remain retriable and block unrelated channel work.
qualification: The approval-drift incident is a speaker-described example; no concrete approval-object schema or authorization implementation is supplied.
title: Bind approval to the exact action, identity, run, arguments, and lifetime

explanation: An internal message tool can report success because it accepted a request even when the user-facing interface never renders the result. Conversely, a user may receive a reply that the system fails to persist. Success criteria must therefore distinguish component acknowledgement from the desired external effect, such as a rendered message, updated ticket, existing calendar event, or changed file.
qualification: The transcript supplies an incident sketch, not an independently inspected UI trace. Different workflows require different final boundaries.
title: Verify success at the boundary the user actually cares about

explanation: The proposed receipt links what the model proposed, what policy allowed or denied, what execution attempted, and what the user-visible boundary confirmed. A transcript captures speech, while a tool result captures a component's claim; neither alone proves the complete action. Keeping the chain allows later turns and operators to distinguish intent, authorization, attempted execution, and verified outcome.
qualification: Receipt is an architectural contract in this talk, not a specified standard format or cryptographic proof mechanism.
title: Preserve an action receipt, not just the agent transcript

explanation: Agent runs can begin from user messages, webhooks, timers, tool results, subagents, or replayed events. Recording only the conversational request loses the distinctions needed to understand repeated or unexpected work. The audit begins by naming the triggering event and its identity, making deduplication, event ordering, and authority analysis possible before interpreting downstream model and tool behavior.
qualification: The captions misspell deduplication; the surrounding passage clearly identifies the operational purpose. No event identity format is prescribed.
title: Record the trigger identity before reasoning about order and authorization

explanation: Rather than attempting an abstract audit of every agent at once, the speaker recommends selecting one real production path and asking five concrete questions. Identify its trigger, inherited state, authority, actual execution, and surviving evidence. The execution record should include arguments, attempts, idempotency information, and external results so the audit evaluates side effects rather than a model's summary of intended work.
qualification: This is an inspectable starting audit, not a comprehensive coverage or reliability benchmark for the full deployment.
title: Audit one real path through trigger, state, authority, execution, and evidence

explanation: Humans forget and leave teams, while model context is compacted or discarded. The speaker argues that architecture decisions should record rationale alongside the chosen rule and how it is enforced, with supporting examples or code references. This creates recoverable context for later maintainers and agents who need to understand why an apparently arbitrary restriction should remain in place.
qualification: No single ADR format is required; this is documentation guidance rather than evidence that recording rationale alone enforces compliance.
title: Preserve why a rule exists, not only the rule itself

explanation: A product requirements document need not be exhaustive to be useful. Cichra recommends preserving why a feature exists, the problem it solves, the intended goal, and the user's journey through the application. This keeps product intent available after the immediate implementation context is lost and gives later executable scenarios a reason to exist beyond mirroring generated code.
qualification: The talk presents a minimal useful structure, not a complete specification standard for every regulated or complex product.
title: Keep requirements lightweight but preserve the problem-to-journey connection

explanation: A markdown specification describes desired behavior but does not establish that the product implements it. The speaker proposes BDD/Cucumber scenarios as a human-readable intermediate layer whose steps execute as code. Connecting scenarios to product documents and critical journeys lets reviewers inspect behavior directly, rather than relying only on the readability of generated implementation tests.
qualification: The talk does not provide actual feature files, step definitions, or passing runs; readability and coverage still depend on scenario quality and implementation.
title: Bridge prose intent and generated tests with readable executable scenarios

explanation: Agent-generated interfaces become more consistent when a design system defines component vocabulary, visual properties, usage rules, and previews. Cichra illustrates this with a primary-button definition and a one-visible-primary-button rule. Small components and patterns can then be reviewed, composed, and reused, giving both humans and agents concrete references instead of asking for consistency as an abstract aesthetic instruction.
qualification: The button constraint is an example design rule, not a universal UI requirement; no visual-regression accuracy or measured consistency improvement is reported.
title: Make visual consistency reviewable through vocabulary, rules, and previews

explanation: The workflow makes a pull request the agent's deliverable and uses git hooks as an unavoidable local feedback point during normal development. The same tasks run in CI to catch skipped local execution. Formatting, typing, duplication, architecture, and documentation checks become automated rules, leaving human review focused on higher-level product and design decisions rather than repeated mechanical debates.
qualification: The speaker acknowledges that agents can skip checks, which is why CI remains necessary. No bypass-proof guarantee or concrete hook configuration is supplied.
title: Run the same mechanical checks locally and in CI

explanation: A test that bypasses the application through direct database access can cease to exercise the user-visible path it claims to cover. The team's BDD suite forbids imports of modules that can reach the database, forcing interaction through browser features. This uses architectural restrictions to preserve the intended test boundary instead of depending on agents to remember that boundary while generating tests.
qualification: The claim describes this team's end-to-end test policy; it does not prohibit database access in every kind of test or prove complete browser coverage.
title: Enforce end-to-end test realism by forbidding database access

explanation: The speaker describes splitting code into layers, linting imports, returning plain shapes rather than ORM objects, and disallowing database access from rendering templates. These constraints aim to prevent accidental query behavior such as N+1 access at known architecture boundaries. The reusable principle is to encode a recurring failure's structural precondition as a check rather than relying exclusively on repeated review of individual symptoms.
qualification: The speaker's assertion of no N+1 queries is not independently demonstrated; the extracted claim is prevention within the specified layers, not proof against every query antipattern.
title: Prevent a failure class structurally instead of repeatedly finding instances

explanation: Text documents do not enforce themselves, while a bare linter error may state a prohibition without explaining it. Cichra connects them: checks reject an invalid commit and link the agent to the decision record explaining the rule and the intended fix. The resulting edit-check-read-repair loop keeps the rationale usable at the moment of violation rather than depending on continuous prompt retention.
qualification: The workflow is described from experience; no compliance-rate comparison or concrete diagnostic message format is given.
title: Make failed checks point back to rationale and repair guidance

explanation: Different activities need different immediate feedback even when all use the same work-check-repair structure. The speaker describes faster browser iteration for UI work, ADR lookup for architecture work, and test selection based on changed files and coverage. Specialized skills focus the agent's attention and shorten local feedback rather than requiring every iteration to run the full suite indiscriminately.
qualification: This concerns focused local iteration; the talk separately retains CI enforcement. It does not establish that skipped checks are unnecessary for final acceptance.
title: Keep the repair loop stable while adapting its checks to the current work

explanation: The approach consumes substantial context during research, but the speaker reports that repeated context compaction is tolerable when important product decisions survive in external records and are rediscoverable. The goal is not to preserve every conversational detail forever. It is to leave durable reasons, rules, and goals that an autonomous agent can recover while continuing a multi-hour task.
qualification: The number of compactions and successful continuity are personal reports, not a controlled memory-retention study or a guarantee that any compaction policy is safe.
title: Support long sessions with decisions that can be looked up after compaction

explanation: Long-running agent failures are not one problem. Finite or degraded context can erase progress, weak planning can leave partial features, and generous self-judgment can label an interface complete without its backend. Diagnose which failure occurred before choosing memory, decomposition, or independent verification; extending runtime alone does not establish completion.
qualification: A practical failure taxonomy, not measured prevalence or a formal causal study.
title: Separate context, planning, and self-judgment failures

explanation: An initializer can turn a vague application request into a feature list, progress file, repository, and startup script. Each fresh worker first orients itself, smoke-tests the environment, implements one failing feature, verifies it, commits, and updates status. Persisting these artifacts prevents each session from rediscovering startup procedures or trusting conversational memory alone.
qualification: Describes their earlier harness; later models allowed less rigid decomposition and fewer resets. JSON was reportedly overwritten less often than Markdown, not guaranteed safe.
title: Initialize persistent artifacts before repeated feature work

explanation: Split construction and criticism into separate contexts with different system prompts. The critic judges the actual output and returns defects; the generator determines fixes. In Q&A the speakers warn that sharing the generator's reasoning can contaminate the evaluator with the same mistaken belief that something works. Independence is an operational design choice, not proof that an LLM critic is unbiased.
qualification: The speakers still acknowledge evaluator preference for LLM-style output and substantial critic prompt tuning.
title: Give the critic a separate job and context, not the builder's reasoning

explanation: A browser-equipped evaluator opens the running app, clicks controls, and attempts the promised workflow. This tests whether features actually connect end to end. The game-maker example rendered a plausible editor but ignored movement keys; the critic-equipped version exercised play mode and caught route-ordering and deletion bugs that reportedly escaped unit tests.
qualification: Selected app demonstrations, not evidence that browser testing catches every defect or replaces unit tests.
title: Exercise user behavior rather than infer functionality from appearance or unit tests

explanation: Subjective quality becomes evaluable when an owner states a sufficiently specific preference. Their design critic scores design, originality, craft, and functionality, weights weaknesses more heavily, and uses reference-site few-shot examples to align its judgments with human taste. This creates a usable optimization target without pretending that one team's preferred aesthetic is universally correct.
qualification: Rubric weights varied with model capability; the stated target was their taste, including avoiding stereotyped AI aesthetics.
title: Make taste explicit with weighted criteria and reference examples

explanation: Repeated criticism can expose that an entire approach is trapped below a rubric threshold. In their separate generator–evaluator loop, persistent low originality sometimes caused the builder to discard the design and restart, whereas solo loops kept patching it. Make replacement an allowed action when local edits do not improve the target criterion, rather than equating iteration with preserving sunk work.
qualification: Observed behavior in their examples, not a guarantee that a critic prevents stagnation or that restarts are cost-optimal.
title: Allow the critic to trigger replacement, not endless local patching

explanation: The planner defines product direction and workflows rather than prescribing every technical detail before execution. A wrong early implementation decision can otherwise be inherited by every sprint and magnified over hours. Let the builder and evaluator negotiate concrete features and tests nearer to implementation while retaining the high-level spec as a recurring reference point.
qualification: Their newer pattern contrasts with the comprehensive feature lists needed by earlier models; not an argument against all detailed planning.
title: Keep the initial plan high-level to avoid cascading technical mistakes

explanation: Before coding, the generator proposes a feature and verification method; the evaluator can reject oversized scope, weak tests, or missed edge cases. They exchange files until agreeing on a contract, then the evaluator grades against that contract rather than only the original vague specification. This converts user-story intent into observable assertions without requiring an omniscient planner.
qualification: Agreement between agents is not independent evidence that the contract fully captures a user's needs.
title: Negotiate testable completion before implementation begins

explanation: A critic's usefulness depends on whether its findings identify concrete repairs. The game-maker agents negotiated 27 contract criteria; the speakers contrast this with vague criteria that yield vague feedback and unfocused edits. Split broad expectations into sufficiently granular assertions so the generator can locate and repair the defect, while avoiding treating that example's criterion count as a universal target.
qualification: The 27 criteria are specific to the illustrated application; no comparison isolates an optimal granularity.
title: Use granular criteria to make critiques executable

explanation: Their initial QA critic noticed bugs but excused them instead of demanding repairs. The main improvement loop was to read complete traces, find judgment mismatches with human expectations, and adjust prompts for layout defects and edge cases. Automated trace scanning provided a first pass, but the speakers emphasize line-by-line human reading to understand the model's limited observations and mistaken decisions.
qualification: Qualitative calibration experience rather than a quantified agreement study; trace-based understanding was preferred over merely increasing experiment volume.
title: Debug critics by reading where their judgments diverge from humans

explanation: A harness should compensate for observed model weaknesses, not preserve every historical workaround. Their newer model supported longer coherent builds, less sprint decomposition, and evaluation after a larger generation instead of every sprint. They retained planner, generator, and evaluator roles while removing complexity. Evaluate each model–prompt–task combination before assuming that either a maximal harness or no harness is best.
qualification: Co-evolving model and harness observations do not isolate causal contributions of individual components.
title: Re-test scaffolding when model behavior changes

explanation: Fresh contexts and structured handoffs can reduce drift, but they are not mandatory for every capable model. The speakers moved their newer generator–evaluator workflow to a continuous session with compaction after context-anxiety behavior improved. Q&A explicitly makes this a use-case and evaluation decision, preserving the warning that lossy summaries can still drift rather than equating context length with coherence.
qualification: The audience's proposed numerical smart-zone thresholds are not validated by the speakers.
title: Choose fresh sessions or continuous compaction using task-specific evidence

explanation: Use filesystem state to preserve what was attempted, how it was evaluated, which defect was found, what fix was applied, and whether it worked. Their suggested timestamped JSON log plus high-level file-structure documentation lets another agent or human resume work without reconstructing the entire conversation. Explicitly prompt these updates throughout the loop instead of hoping compaction retains every important decision.
