Watershed reports internal success rising from roughly 43% to 92% while improving prompts, skills, few-shot SDK examples, tool ergonomics, plan-execute decomposition, and elicitation of expert judgment. The process remains inspectable when the agent fails or the chosen ground truth is only one defensible expert answer; higher task scores and process validity are distinct achievements.
qualification: Dataset size, grading rubric, model changes, uncertainty, and component ablations are not supplied, so gains cannot be assigned to the harness alone.
title: Keep task-success optimization separate from process guarantees

explanation: A long task-duration capability claim can look much weaker at an enterprise-relevant reliability threshold. The speaker contrasts reported horizons around 16–18 hours at 50% success with roughly three and a half hours at 80%. Benchmark progress should therefore state the probability attached to the horizon, and readers should not interpret a 50% horizon as dependable autonomous completion of equally long production work.
qualification: These are the speaker's interpretation of an external benchmark, with approximate figures and uncertain captioned model names; 80% is also not asserted to be enterprise sufficient.
title: Report task horizon together with its success probability

explanation: Code can satisfy the immediate function while introducing maintainability and security problems. Sonar describes testing models on more than 4,000 problems, first assessing functional correctness and then inspecting complexity, bugs, and security. The claimed finding is that strong functional scores coexist with these residual issues. Agent evaluations intended for production should preserve those dimensions instead of collapsing them into a single task-pass result.
qualification: The vendor's benchmark protocol, task distribution, numerical scores, and security ground truth are not supplied.
title: Evaluate complexity, bugs, and security separately from functional success

explanation: The talk warns that faster generation may create security, maintainability, reliability, and complexity work that erodes the initial velocity gain. It cites a study in which an early three-to-fivefold boost reportedly dissipated over three months. A productivity assessment should therefore follow the lifecycle of generated changes and their cleanup costs, not treat the immediate volume or speed of code production as durable value.
qualification: The cited university study is not reproduced or independently inspected, and the presentation does not establish that all teams follow this trajectory.
title: Track downstream technical debt when measuring coding-agent productivity

explanation: The speaker accepts the value of formal methods for provable code while warning that a large existing codebase includes dependencies, technical debt, and messy interactions. Verification of an isolated component does not automatically settle system behavior. This motivates embedding checks into development workflows and using multiple perspectives rather than treating one proof or one final review as complete assurance of enterprise software.
qualification: The categorical phrasing is the speaker's framing, not a formal impossibility theorem about verifying software.
title: Distinguish local code proofs from verification of a large software system

explanation: Context explains the existing codebase through architectural awareness and semantic navigation. Constraints express permitted dependencies, coding standards, guardrails, and the architecture the organization wants, which may differ from current structure. The talk separates these deliberately: supplying only more repository context omits normative rules. It reports over 30% fewer tokens in testing when context and constraints help agents navigate and solve tasks more directly.
qualification: The token-reduction result has no task list, baseline, sample size, or ablation protocol; it is not a guaranteed saving.
title: Give agents both architectural navigation and intended constraints

explanation: The proposed zero-trust approach avoids relying on a single model or verification technique. Algorithmic methods inspect data flow, control flow, known patterns, and secrets, while agentic review examines intent, business logic, and less predefined concerns. These layers address different failure surfaces in complex software. The speaker attributes lower reported production outage frequency to customers using layered verification, without presenting a controlled causal comparison.
qualification: Customers reportedly have 44% fewer AI-derived outages, but sample selection, controls, event definitions, and confidence intervals are absent.
title: Combine algorithmic checks with agentic intent and business-logic review

explanation: Agents must understand the code they modify, so cleaner code can reduce reasoning and navigation effort just as it helps humans. The speaker describes running the same tasks on typical and cleaned codebases and observing lower token, reasoning, and energy requirements on the cleaned versions. This makes maintenance part of the agent operating environment rather than a purely human aesthetic concern.
qualification: No measurement amounts, cleaning procedure, task suite, or controls are provided; compounding future benefits are argued rather than established by the one-shot view.
title: Maintain code quality as an input to future agent efficiency

explanation: Verification is organized as three linked loops. During generation, agents receive context, constraints, verification feedback, and repair opportunities. CI combines algorithmic and agentic review with evaluations and quality gates. A maintenance loop keeps the codebase understandable and addresses accumulated problems. The speaker argues that these loops reinforce one another positively when designed together and negatively when quality is neglected during rapid adoption.
qualification: This is an operating framework, not evidence that merely installing three categories of tools yields the reported improvements.
title: Coordinate agent-inner-loop checks, CI gates, and code maintenance

explanation: The talk contrasts verification added after generation with checks inside the agent's active problem-solving loop. Context and constraints guide the initial work; verification feedback then lets the agent repair issues before handing off the result. This is a process placement decision, not merely another reviewer tool. Its intended benefit is to reduce the defects and uncertainty that later CI review must absorb.
qualification: The speech does not isolate the effect of feedback timing from context improvements, verifier choice, or subsequent remediation.
title: Return verification feedback while the agent is still working

explanation: A bank test reportedly achieved a 92% issue reduction using guide-verify-solve within agentic coding loops. The speaker explicitly says this is not a 92% improvement on every loop; it is a cumulative result as the agent works over minutes and hours. Preserve the unit and time span of such results, and avoid converting an end-to-end remediation outcome into a universal per-step multiplier.
qualification: One reported bank test lacks issue definitions, baseline counts, setup, and uncertainty; broad enterprise efficacy is not established.
title: Distinguish cumulative issue reduction from per-iteration improvement

explanation: Containment measures conversations handled without a human, but avoiding handoff can violate the business goal. In the banking example, an agent should answer an early mortgage-payoff question and forward context to a senior banker because it signals a refinancing opportunity. The lower-containment agent can therefore perform better. Evaluate escalation against the intended workflow rather than assuming every human transfer is a failure.
qualification: The intern comparison is an explanatory scenario grounded in reported aggregate banking containment, not a documented matched-worker experiment.
title: Treat designed handoffs as successful work when the business mandate requires them

explanation: The framework separates what exists before execution from what the agent actually does at runtime. Configured capabilities describe the agent's mandate and platform, while runtime evidence covers tasks, execution, and outputs. Governance spans both groups and includes business boundaries, risk, compliance, observability, and behavioral quality. This broadens evaluation beyond one conversational metric, though a readiness score should not be confused with measured outcome accuracy.
qualification: The speech describes 26 components but does not enumerate all of them consistently; six pillars plus governance are later called seven pillars.
title: Assess configured readiness and runtime execution under shared governance

explanation: Each component receives zero if absent, one if observable and measurable, and two if tracked and analyzed over time. Manual measurement qualifies for the middle level, so automation is not a prerequisite for starting. The important distinction is between a one-time observable property and an ongoing management practice that can react to change. This is a maturity rubric, not a direct probability of task success.
qualification: No empirical validation is given for the numerical spacing between maturity levels or their relationship to business outcomes.
title: Distinguish having a component, measuring it, and managing it over time

explanation: Druid weights governance and mandate more heavily than technical capability because the stated goal is business effectiveness. The reported design assigns governance 39%, mandate 26%, platform 12%, and outputs 9%, with other components completing the score. This makes priorities visible and can reverse a containment-only ranking. The weights encode the framework authors' judgment rather than a statistically established universal recipe.
qualification: The complete weighting table and its calibration are absent; these percentages should not be generalized across organizations without justification.
title: Make business priorities explicit in evaluation weights

explanation: The speaker differentiates autonomous execution from human-AI collaboration. An autonomous agent needs stricter success or cancellation boundaries because no human reviews the final decision; a content-producing assistant may tolerate more imperfect drafts when a human decides what to use. Define that division of responsibility and its risk boundaries before deployment rather than selecting a target accuracy independently of the workflow.
qualification: The surrounding percentage examples are loosely phrased and are not validated or suitable as recommended numerical tolerances.
title: Set error tolerance according to who makes the final consequential decision

explanation: A system prompt is only part of an agent's mandate. The talk includes the desired business outcome, policy boundaries, permitted facts and documents, allowed connected systems, who may invoke the agent, and spending limits. A contract-renewal target illustrates why the mandate should name a measurable objective. This contract supplies the context needed to judge whether later tasks and outputs serve the intended business purpose.
qualification: The 70% contract-renewal target is illustrative, not a reported causal outcome or recommended benchmark.
title: Define the mandate as outcomes, evidence scope, permissions, and budget

explanation: Broad tool access is not inherently a sign of a better agent. The speaker contrasts a small allowed endpoint set with an MCP server exposing thousands of tools, and later states that tool effectiveness matters more than tool count. Assess discoverability, skill granularity, orchestration, and prompt burden within the business boundary. Extra capabilities can make behavior harder to understand without improving the required outcome.
qualification: The talk offers a design principle, not an experimental relation between tool count and failure rate.
title: Scope tools to the mandate and evaluate their effective use, not their number

explanation: Druid recommends platform-level support for memory, skills, orchestration, and human handoff rather than letting each agent reinvent them. In particular, a central action center gives people one place to engage with agents across the organization. The evaluation question becomes whether an individual agent integrates correctly with that service, not merely whether it implements some local escalation behavior.
qualification: No comparative deployment evidence or required implementation pattern for the shared service is given.
title: Evaluate whether agents use a shared handoff and orchestration layer

explanation: A global business target is insufficient to judge a specific execution. Log the input, confirm required context, and associate success criteria with the individual task before judging the output. The contract-renewal example makes the issue concrete: observing that a contract was renewed does not establish whether that particular renewal met its intended conditions. Task-linked criteria make runtime outcomes auditable rather than inferred from a coarse activity label.
qualification: The talk does not provide a complete task schema or criteria for deciding whether a contract renewal is successful.
title: Attach success criteria and required context to each individual task

explanation: The employment analogy changes after deployment: an agent's evaluation should continue. The proposed cadence reruns evaluation weekly on live traffic against a human baseline, then improves and retests. A slide contrasts a flat green containment line with a falling broader score, illustrating how one vanity metric can conceal drift. The framework emphasizes ongoing management, though it does not specify the human-baseline matching method.
qualification: The 83-to-60 broader-score decline versus flat 92% containment is a presentation illustration, not a documented longitudinal experiment.
title: Reevaluate live behavior regularly instead of treating deployment as the end of assessment

explanation: The speaker reports aggregate containment near 80% in financial services, 87% in healthcare, 93% in HR and IT, and 99% in higher education from 15 months of production data. These are not presented as a ranking of agent quality: banking deliberately includes more handoffs. Compare containment with the mandate and escalation design of the domain rather than imposing one universal target across unlike workflows.
qualification: The vendor provides no sample sizes, cohort definitions, traffic weighting, dispersion, or methodology for the aggregate figures.
title: Interpret industry containment differences through designed workflows

explanation: The ROI discussion should include the alternative use of human capacity, not only which job or routine task is displaced. Ask what work moved off a person's desk and what the released time let the business accomplish. In the mortgage example, automated routine balance work enables a banker to spend time on a customer reconsidering financing. This extends the scorecard from automation volume to human capability enabled.
qualification: This is an ROI framing and scenario, not a measured revenue uplift or controlled estimate of reclaimed hours.
title: Measure what higher-value human work the agent enables

explanation: An agent score belongs to a dataset, model service, agent harness, sandbox and settings together, not to a model name alone. Silent inference or sandbox updates can change behavior even when the visible model identifier stays fixed. With routing providers, explicitly select the backend rather than allowing tasks within one run to reach different providers. Report the configuration so comparisons have an interpretable object.
qualification: Endpoint changes may remain unobservable; configuration reporting reduces ambiguity but cannot eliminate hidden service drift.
title: Benchmark the complete configuration, including the endpoint route

explanation: Changing a dataset version changes the experiment, even when the update fixes existing tasks rather than adding new ones. The speaker keeps Terminal Bench 2.0 to preserve comparison with earlier runs and recommends pinning the evaluation harness. When compatibility forces upgrades, maintaining a fork and selectively backporting needed changes is proposed as a way to reduce unrelated experimental changes.
qualification: The speaker explicitly acknowledges the tension between keeping a shared bug and upgrading for new agent/provider support.
title: Preserve comparability by pinning benchmark and harness versions

explanation: Sequential agents on one mutable local system do not encounter equivalent starting conditions: earlier tasks can modify the environment for later ones. Use an isolated sandbox per task, install and execute the selected agent there, and retrieve results and trajectories before destruction. This separates task execution from the evaluator’s own machine and preserves the behavioral record needed for later analysis.
qualification: The workshop demonstrates this workflow for a small Git task, not every supported agent or sandbox backend.
title: Run tasks in fresh sandboxes and collect evidence before teardown

explanation: Repeated trials support several distinct views: average run score, best and worst run scores, the fraction of tasks solved in every trial, and the fraction solved at least once. The intersection describes observed consistency, while the union describes an observed capability ceiling. Similar averages can hide different reliable task sets; the speaker prefers the stronger consistency base when averages are close.
qualification: These are empirical summaries of five trials, not statistical guarantees or estimates of all real-world task distributions.
title: Separate consistently solved tasks from ever-solved tasks

explanation: Sampling controls reduce one source of randomness but leave hardware, floating-point behavior, inference optimizations and other system effects. The speaker reports changed results after a driver update despite an apparently deterministic setup. Temperature should also respect model recommendations, and a single chosen seed may favor some models. Repeated runs remain necessary rather than treating a seed as reproducibility proof.
qualification: The driver-update example is anecdotal and the caption is imprecise; no controlled decomposition of nondeterminism is provided.
title: Temperature zero and a seed do not make agent benchmarks deterministic

explanation: An unattended benchmark can penalize an agent that tries to ask a nonexistent user; changing its role instructions would change the experiment. Similarly, web access may let an agent retrieve public benchmark solutions. That behavior is not automatically undesirable for a useful agent, but it changes whether the evaluator measures independent problem solving or successful completion using available information. Inspect traces and declare the intended construct.
qualification: The speaker describes observed lookup and a proposed prompt change, not a controlled estimate of either effect.
title: Prompt and tool access determine what a benchmark measures

explanation: CPU and memory limits can slow tasks, cause crashes or prevent completion independently of model reasoning. Increasing concurrency also competes for provider throughput and aggregate sandbox allocations; running every task at once can trigger rate limits or exhausted resources. Choose parallelism together with endpoint capacity and per-sandbox requirements, and do not interpret resource-induced failures as straightforward evidence of a weaker model.
qualification: No universal safe concurrency value is given; it depends on provider quotas and workload resource requirements.
title: Treat resources and concurrency as potential score confounders

explanation: A fixed generous deadline can reduce disadvantages from slower inference endpoints, but extra time can also fund repeated unsuccessful loops. The speaker initially used two hours per task to avoid handicapping open-weight deployments, then moved toward one hour after observing expensive unproductive retries. Timeout policy therefore shapes both measured ability and evaluation expense and should be an explicit experimental choice.
qualification: One hour is the speaker’s practical choice for this benchmark, not a generally validated optimum.
title: Set time budgets with both endpoint fairness and wasted search in mind

explanation: A crashed sandbox can create a low score that does not reflect task-solving ability, so retry decisions should distinguish infrastructure failure from agent behavior. If the model itself causes the crash through its actions, that failure is part of what the benchmark should measure. A retry policy that treats both categories alike either unfairly penalizes the model or conceals meaningful failures.
qualification: The distinction requires diagnostic judgment; the talk does not supply a formal classifier or exhaustive retry taxonomy.
title: Retry infrastructure errors without erasing model-caused failures

explanation: A requested reasoning level is not necessarily the level used during execution. Agents may rename parameters, lack support for certain modes or otherwise alter configuration. The speaker checks and corrects result labels so they reflect the effective setting rather than the submitted one. This is especially important when comparing reasoning modes, because a mislabeled run can falsely suggest a model-level effect.
qualification: The transcript illustrates label inspection but does not establish automatic verification for every agent implementation.
title: Record the settings actually honored by the agent harness

explanation: The speaker reports that raising Opus 4.6 to maximum thinking lowered benchmark scores in two harnesses. Trace inspection suggested that long reasoning pauses consumed the one-hour task budget before enough environment interactions occurred. A less deliberative agent could try commands, observe missing dependencies and repair them across more turns. Reasoning effort should be evaluated jointly with available action time rather than assumed to improve success monotonically.
qualification: This is the speaker’s trace-based explanation of configuration-bound results, not a controlled causal ablation; GPT comparisons reportedly behaved differently.
title: More reasoning can reduce task completion under a wall-clock limit

explanation: A model with a lower advertised unit price can consume enough additional tokens and time to cost more overall. The workshop compares near-leading benchmark scores against token use and total charges, and also shows the same model costing differently across agent harnesses. Model selection should consider achieved quality, reliability and complete execution expense together rather than assuming a fast or cheap model name means cheap task completion.
qualification: Prices and comparisons are speaker-reported for the displayed configuration; captions inconsistently render the GPT name.
title: Compare total task cost rather than nominal model cheapness

explanation: A score claims success or failure; task traces show requests, reasoning, commands and outcomes that make the claim inspectable. The speaker uses traces to investigate refusals, excessive thinking, instruction deviations and inference problems. After each run, repeated characters or leaked prompt-template tokens can suggest serving or tokenizer issues rather than task incompetence. Published bars should link back to their component runs and task records.
qualification: These symptoms are diagnostic guidance, not proof of a unique root cause. Automated trace analysis still needs links back to inspectable evidence.
title: Use trajectory evidence to explain surprising benchmark results

explanation: The dashboard admits scored runs only when all benchmark tasks have executed and rejects incomplete test runs from default comparison. The live Git restoration succeeds with a score of one, but is not shown as a complete run because it contains just one task. This preserves the difference between proving that an evaluation pipeline works and producing a comparable full-dataset result.
qualification: The speaker mentions filters for excessive errors and timeouts without specifying reproducible thresholds in the transcript.
title: Keep demonstration task success separate from a valid benchmark run

explanation: A shopping user may arrive with an aesthetic feeling rather than a finished query or the right vocabulary. A search-wrapper agent assumes away that articulation gap. The proposed system instead helps form the intent through discovery, preference elicitation and exploration before recommendation. Tests should include incomplete and ambiguous goals so success is not restricted to users who already know exactly how to ask.
qualification: The motivation is grounded in commerce; applicability to finance or education is suggested rather than demonstrated.
title: Evaluate collaborative discovery, not only retrieval from clean queries

explanation: The discovery state combines session history, personal context and explicit constraints with softer preferences inferred from reference images. Those inferred signals carry confidence rather than being treated as equally certain facts. Evaluating the state includes checking that supplied information is retained and represented correctly. The distinction matters because subsequent questions and recommendations depend on both what the agent knows and how uncertain that knowledge remains.
qualification: The talk mentions confidence within an error bound but does not define the bound, label source or calibration method.
title: Represent hard constraints, inferred preferences and uncertainty separately

explanation: Not every useful state variable can be extracted once and retained indefinitely. Inventory is the speaker’s example of information that must be retrieved or refreshed in real time because unavailable products make recommendations ineffective. Working-state design should identify such volatile fields separately from stable preferences and conversation facts, then refresh them before presenting options that depend on their current values.
qualification: No freshness window, retrieval implementation or stale-inventory error rate is provided.
title: Refresh state variables whose staleness invalidates recommendations

explanation: A state extractor should respond to meaningful input changes without gratuitously rewriting unrelated constraints. The described counterfactual test flips part of a user query, checks that the corresponding extracted constraints change and verifies that irrelevant fields remain the same. This complements fact-retention checks: a state can contain the original facts yet still fail to update selectively when the user revises a requirement.
qualification: The transcript gives the testing logic but no counterfactual dataset construction or pass threshold.
title: Test that changed input constraints change state while unrelated fields remain stable

explanation: Discover the blockers to a useful answer, compare possible elicitation moves and prioritize the unknown with the greatest immediate information value. In the living-room example, room width may matter more than refining style confidence because furniture that cannot fit is unusable. The associated graders look for blocker identification, question utility and over-asking, so gathering more preferences is not automatically considered better collaboration.
qualification: Information gain is described as a planning objective, not a supplied numerical estimator or proven optimal policy.
title: Ask the most consequential next question rather than resolve every unknown

explanation: A user’s constraint needs a mapping into the product ontology before it can reliably guide retrieval. The proposed agent forms that bridge as it explores the constraint, using known preferences and conversation context to select candidate products or styles. Q&A adds that merchant domain expertise should inform how a constraint maps to merchant metadata rather than expecting a generic agent to infer every catalog-specific distinction alone.
qualification: No ontology schema, mapping accuracy result or fairness metric is specified.
title: Bridge user preference language to retrievable catalog metadata

explanation: Text works when a preference is easy to state; subjective style may instead require shared visual anchors. The agent can show nearby styles on a preference board, then use reactions such as hovers or clicks to update confidence. Format-selection evaluation asks whether the chosen modality fits the question and user’s articulation gap, rather than rewarding visual output regardless of whether it helps uncover the preference.
qualification: Hover and click signals are proposed evidence of preference, but the talk does not quantify their reliability or distinguish attention from liking.
title: Choose text or visual elicitation according to the articulation problem

explanation: The described user simulator is seeded with constraints that the shopping agent initially does not know. Evaluation observes how efficiently the agent uncovers those preferences and how many turns the process takes. This provides a more targeted elicitation test than grading only the final recommendation. The speaker also flags repeated questions and questions that fail to supply useful next-step information as inefficient behavior.
qualification: There is no simulator validation against real shoppers, disclosure of hidden-preference coverage or reported recovery rate.
title: Use hidden-constraint simulators to evaluate elicitation and turn efficiency

explanation: The same factual content can be more or less usable depending on its presentation. Policy or review queries may call for a summary, product comparison for a table across relevant axes, and style inspiration for images. The proposed response-format grader checks whether important information is easy to find rather than buried in text. Presentation is treated as part of the agent’s task-solving intelligence, not optional decoration.
qualification: These are example format choices, not a fixed rule that all comparison queries require tables.
title: Grade the answer’s presentation against the user’s decision task

explanation: An attractive response can still fail if it hallucinates product information or leaves the user unable to act. The speaker therefore separates response-format accuracy from data fidelity and user actionability. The first checks presentation fit, the second checks accurate capture of information, and the third asks whether the presentation supports a confident next action. These dimensions target different failure modes within the same final answer.
qualification: Actionability is framed as moving toward purchase in this commerce system; no causal purchase-conversion evaluation is presented.
title: Assess factual fidelity and actionability alongside format

explanation: Q&A separates two kinds of authority: merchants contribute domain knowledge for mapping constraints to catalog metadata, while the agent decides the response format. The stated reason is to maintain a common horizontal layer and a seamless user experience across merchants. This boundary prevents catalog expertise from automatically becoming control over how the user sees and compares options across the whole shopping system.
qualification: This describes the team’s current product choice, not a demonstrated fairness guarantee or a general commerce standard.
title: Use merchant ontology expertise without delegating cross-merchant presentation policy

explanation: In Q&A, the speaker reports that users prefer direct involvement when exploring styles and possibilities, while price comparison or negotiation is a more plausible role for a user’s agent. This limits the assumption that higher automation is always the desired experience. The same answer explicitly says agent-to-agent interaction has not yet been built; an MCP interface is an expectation, not evidence of a deployed collaborative system.
qualification: User-study size, protocol and representativeness are not disclosed, and the speaker describes an early product stage.
title: Distinguish discovery involvement from downstream delegation

explanation: The speaker recommends placing auto-raters at every step of the discovery, research and response loop rather than assessing only the final recommendation. Raters can start simply and expand as the system develops. This keeps state fidelity, question selection, preference discovery and response presentation visible as separate improvement targets instead of letting a good final-looking answer hide failures earlier in the collaboration.
qualification: The transcript gives stage-specific targets but no rater prompts, human-calibration procedure or longitudinal evidence that expanding raters improves outcomes.
title: Grade each stage of the collaboration loop and evolve the raters

explanation: Taking on technical debt can be reasonable when it produces customers or features, but added complexity can eventually consume more value than the shortcut generated. The speaker frames this as an ROI question rather than a universal prohibition on messy code. Refactoring decisions should therefore compare the continuing cost of complexity with current business benefits instead of treating all debt as equally urgent or harmless.
qualification: The talk supplies a conceptual framing, not a quantified financial model of technical debt.
title: Evaluate technical debt as a business investment with compounding costs

explanation: The team compared five open-source orchestrators against seventeen criteria and built proofs of concept after gathering requirements. The speaker proposes accelerating this with deep research and per-criterion agents, but warns that a polished report can assert product features that do not exist. Preserve the acceptance criteria and executable checks even when research becomes faster, including checking whether a claimed capability is only available in beta.
qualification: The original manual evaluation and POCs happened; the 90%-faster agentic replacement is the speaker’s estimate, not a measured comparison.
title: Validate research findings with requirements and working proofs of concept

explanation: An earlier orchestration refactor took three hours of interactive work and contained ten major mistakes. Re-running the task with newer model-and-harness combinations reportedly reduced the needed iterations, with one solving after an additional iteration and another essentially one-shotting it. Historical tasks can expose changed operational capability, but the unit being compared includes the evolving harness and interaction pattern, not only the underlying model.
qualification: These are selected task replays without disclosed sample size, repeated trials or fully frozen harness conditions.
title: Replay historical tasks to reassess agent usefulness as systems improve

explanation: Later runs used more planning, subagents, shell commands and verification, and were somewhat more expensive in model execution. The speaker still considered them more productive because they required less manual work. Evaluate agent-assisted development using the human correction and supervision burden alongside compute expense; a cheaper model run is not necessarily the cheaper engineering process when it leaves extensive editing and guidance to developers.
qualification: The estimated one-fifth completion time is not supported by a detailed time-and-motion study.
title: Include manual intervention when assessing coding-agent cost

explanation: The speaker highlights a recurring failure pattern: developers launch an agent before leaving, then discover a critical omission in the prompt, plan or requirements. Better execution ability does not compensate for an incomplete task definition. Before treating a long run as autonomous delegated work, check whether the specification contains the necessary constraints and acceptance expectations rather than assuming the model will reconstruct missing intent.
qualification: This is guidance supported by audience recognition and experience, not a measured omission rate or formal preflight checklist.
title: Check the prompt, plan and requirements before unattended execution

explanation: A task-duration claim at fifty-percent success is different from a duration at which one can confidently leave an agent unattended. The speaker prefers eighty percent or higher and argues for ninety or ninety-nine percent when forming a delegation mental model. Long runs that are coin flips can waste both elapsed time and attention; choose task scope using the reliability required by the workflow, not the longest advertised horizon.
qualification: These are desired operating thresholds; the talk does not establish that current agents attain them on arbitrary tasks.
title: Interpret autonomous task horizons at a useful success probability

explanation: The talk contrasts faster shipping with degraded maintainability and reliability, then treats code volume and commits as incomplete evidence of refactoring benefit. Wider developer participation and sustained feature delivery are additional observations, but they still require business interpretation. Assessing a coding-agent or architecture change should distinguish visible production activity from usable, reliable product improvement rather than declaring success because generated code or commit frequency increased.
qualification: The reliability charts are unnamed examples; the company contribution graphs are observational and not controlled productivity measures.
title: Do not equate code or commit velocity with product quality

explanation: Asked to refactor the legacy pipeline, a modern model announced completion after roughly ten minutes and produced about two thousand lines. Inspection showed mostly scaffolding and missing model implementations, including deployment/bootstrap work. Verify that required behavior exists and runs before accepting a large autonomous change. A fast response or plausible project structure is weaker evidence than an implementation that reaches the intended functional parity.
qualification: This is one broad-goal experiment, not a general estimate of model failure probability. Predicted future improvement is speculation.
title: A completion message and substantial scaffolding do not prove a refactor is implemented

explanation: Waiting could make refactoring cheaper as models, tools and monitoring improve, but current complexity can already constrain customers, costs and feature work. The speaker judges the rebuild worthwhile because it reportedly reduced pipeline time and cost, supported larger files and shortened feature delivery. The decision should compare those available gains against waiting; it need not assume either a full rewrite now or indefinite postponement is universally correct.
qualification: These are speaker-reported business outcomes without isolated causal attribution or detailed baseline metrics.
title: Choose refactor timing using current business constraints, not only future model progress

explanation: Models may navigate several repositories successfully when placed under a common parent folder, yet end-to-end tests, deployment and sandbox provisioning remain harder across repository boundaries. In Q&A, the speaker says cloning and setting up multiple repositories also slows an automated development environment. Repository structure should therefore be judged by integration and verification work, not only by whether the agent can find files in each repository.
qualification: The team chose a monorepo, but the talk also allows isolating parts of a system instead of undertaking a full refactor.
title: Separate repository navigation ability from cross-repository verification overhead

explanation: All PR reviews during the described refactor were human, while local AI review checks were supplementary. Besides catching errors, reviews helped the small group working on the new repository transfer context and understand what had been introduced. This makes review a knowledge-sharing mechanism as well as a quality gate, especially when generated code and concentrated implementation work would otherwise outpace the rest of the team’s understanding.
qualification: This describes the historical workflow; the speaker notes reviews are becoming more autonomous over time, without comparing their effectiveness.
title: Use human PR review to preserve understanding during a rebuild

explanation: The team reportedly got fifteen of seventeen requirements right initially and evolved its engineering verification processes during the refactor. Planning modes were adopted as tools began supporting them, rather than assuming the first workflow would remain sufficient. Reassess both requirements and guardrails when capabilities change, and check hidden library assumptions such as whether a required feature is actually released instead of merely promised or in beta.
qualification: No full guardrail framework, requirement list or failure taxonomy appears in the transcript.
title: Revisit requirements and verification practices as the development system changes

explanation: An agent can execute each individual action yet fail where work crosses application boundaries. The onboarding example spans accounts, Slack, meetings and hardware procurement, often without one human owner for the whole process. Evaluation should therefore distinguish success at tool primitives from completion of the actual multi-system job. The speaker frames catastrophic failures as incompatible with trust even when average completion looks superficially acceptable.
qualification: The sixty/eighty-percent discussion and database-deletion scenario are rhetorical examples, not measured failure statistics.
title: Tool competence does not establish end-to-end workflow reliability

explanation: The speaker attributes coding-agent progress partly to the ability to run code and test outputs. Many knowledge-work goals instead involve questions such as whether a report lands or a design fits the brand, which are not answered by a simple unit test. This motivates additional verification signals for the intended outcome rather than assuming successful tool execution or syntactically valid artifacts establish that the work met its purpose.
qualification: The contrast is a motivating argument, not a claim that all code correctness is decidable or all knowledge work is untestable.
title: Recognize where executable correctness checks stop answering the real question

explanation: Humans often resolve ambiguous work by looking at the same screen and discussing it together. The proposed agent interaction borrows this shared context so the user does not need to reconstruct every detail in prose. The claimed benefit is less explanation and less lost intent, not necessarily a larger model. This is especially relevant to spatial design tasks where the visible target carries information a textual description may omit.
qualification: The transcript motivates the interaction pattern but does not measure explanation savings or prove that shared context resolves every ambiguity.
title: Shared screen context can reduce the burden of explaining intended changes

explanation: The proposed loop adapts robotics-style perception, planning and action to screen work. Agents should inspect what changed after acting and recover when a step fails, rather than immediately moving to the next action. Observing the rendered result supplies feedback about whether the action actually achieved the intended state. This separates an agent that can issue interface commands from one that can monitor its progress through a workflow.
qualification: The feedback loop is the design proposal; the talk does not benchmark recovery behavior across arbitrary applications.
title: Observe action consequences and recover instead of firing and forgetting

explanation: The agent is asked to perceive rendered layout, current state and visible changes, not just scrape page code. The speaker argues that operating from the same pixels and structure as the user can also support software without a dedicated API. This creates an observation channel for output verification, while requiring an agent to interpret what is visible rather than equating backend or markup success with a correct user-facing result.
qualification: The API-independence claim is presented as a design advantage; broad application coverage and robustness are not measured.
title: Check the interface users actually see rather than only the page’s underlying representation

explanation: The talk contrasts chatbot-style turns with an agent that reacts while the user is still working and can offer suggestions without waiting for a completed prompt cycle. Shared perception is the proposed enabling context. This is a different interaction objective from autonomous batch task completion: evaluation would need to preserve the speaker’s ambition for timely assistance without mistaking the demonstrated annotation workflow for a finished continuous collaborator.
qualification: This is an aspiration in the talk, not a demonstrated latency result or implemented end-to-end real-time system.
title: Distinguish continuous collaboration from repeated prompt-and-wait cycles

explanation: The demonstrated Chrome extension lets users draw around a region or select an element and attach an instruction such as changing a heading’s color or doubling its font size. It captures feedback together with location and style information into a summary for the implementation agent. The reusable mechanism is to anchor the requested change to a concrete visible target instead of relying solely on an ungrounded description.
qualification: The speaker says this eliminates back-and-forth in the example; no measured general reduction in misunderstandings is supplied.
title: Package visual targets, feedback and style details together for implementation

explanation: The verification demonstration uses a design.md file to describe design rules, including colors, components and layout. The agent checks the rendered work against those expectations and can turn supplied design information into rules when it is not already written. This operationalizes part of an otherwise subjective question such as brand fit by creating an explicit reference, while leaving the validity of that reference itself open to review.
qualification: No rule schema, visual grader calibration or false-positive/negative rate is provided.
title: Make visual design expectations explicit enough for repeatable checks

explanation: The demonstrated verifier does more than assess a static page’s appearance. It traverses application behavior like a user, for example adding or deleting a task where those operations are available. It then writes a report naming passed checks and anything that failed. Visual compliance and functional flow checks are complementary evidence because a page can look correct while an interaction path does not work.
qualification: The transcript describes a small demonstration, not coverage of every user path or evidence that automated reports are always correct.
title: Combine visual inspection with walking real user flows

explanation: A conference experiment records a design meeting with wearable devices, imports the transcript and summary, and sends the extracted insights to an agent through an Apply action. The agent changes website colors and an emoji, then starts verification. This illustrates audio as another source of shared task context, with the same downstream check loop rather than treating a meeting summary as proof that the requested edits were correctly implemented.
qualification: This is a narrated one-off experiment with simple edits; transcription fidelity, consent/privacy and complex requirements are not evaluated.
title: Route captured design discussions into edits and immediate verification

explanation: A failed design check can mean the implementation violated the intended policy, or that the human actually wants a new design policy. In the color-change example, the speaker keeps that judgment with the user: update the design specification to allow the desired change, or require the agent to fix the violation. Verification therefore needs an adjudication step rather than automatically treating existing rules as permanently correct.
qualification: The example happens to pass the current rules; the revise-versus-fix path is explained rather than demonstrated as a failed-check recovery.
title: When a verifier flags a design conflict, distinguish rule changes from implementation fixes

explanation: To emulate agent customers, the team wrapped its cloud sandbox service in an MCP server that coding agents could operate directly. It first selected accessible tools and smoke-tested simple programs and language conversion before expanding to a broad suite. Testing through the customer-facing agent interface includes its encoding and tool behavior, instead of assuming direct service tests cover the entire path the agent actually experiences.
qualification: This harness is described for the team’s own platform; MCP familiarity is a motivation, not evidence that every model will use the tools correctly.
title: Expose infrastructure through the same interface an agent customer uses

explanation: The team asked an agent to write a thousand tests across ten domains to cast a wide net, not because that number supplied a statistical guarantee. Preparatory work included credentials and deciding how failures should be investigated. The reusable method is exploratory workflow generation to discover unexpected service interactions; the resulting test count should not be confused with representativeness or verified coverage of all customer behavior.
qualification: No complete suite, sampling rationale, validated oracle or measured detection rate is provided.
title: Use broad generated workflows for discovery without treating an arbitrary count as coverage proof

explanation: The experiment stores findings in SQLite rather than accumulating independent Markdown files. The speaker says this makes a thousand-test effort manageable and supports multiple local subagents executing workflows and writing their results. Structured result storage becomes part of the evaluation harness when concurrency and volume make document-style reporting hard to aggregate, while leaving the specific schema and concurrency safeguards as implementation details not supplied here.
qualification: The transcript does not disclose a schema, transaction strategy, measured throughput or guarantee of safe concurrent writes.
title: Store many concurrent agent test results in a queryable database

explanation: A code interpreter and a cloud browser stress different aspects of the same sandbox platform. The suite includes package development, training programs and PDF generation for code-oriented work, while browser scenarios open tabs, scrape pages, download screenshots and exercise forms or logins. The evaluation unit should reflect the application’s actual workflow demands rather than assuming one generic sandbox smoke test says enough about every hosted agent workload.
qualification: The described examples establish workload diversity but not representative workload frequencies or a universal test taxonomy.
title: Shape infrastructure tests around the hosted application’s workflows

explanation: The team uploaded an image and downloaded it expecting the same artifact back. The mismatch was traced to an incorrect encoding layer in the MCP wrapper. Round-trip tests can therefore expose failures in the interface even when the underlying sandbox appears to accept the operation. For binary artifacts, completing an upload/download call is weaker evidence than checking that the returned object preserves what was supplied.
qualification: The exact comparison method, affected encoding and repair are not given, so this is a failure pattern rather than a reproducible implementation recipe.
title: Test uploaded and downloaded artifacts for preservation across interface layers

explanation: After observing failures, the team grouped them into interface-layer and sandbox-layer problems. An image round trip failed through the MCP encoding layer, while files written to a sandbox directory could not later be retrieved. This classification matters because a hosted agent traverses a gateway, tools and a computing environment; a failed customer workflow does not by itself identify the model or the backend sandbox as the root cause.
qualification: The file-retrieval failure’s precise root cause is not supplied; the talk does not offer a complete attribution algorithm.
title: Separate interface defects from sandbox execution defects before assigning failure

explanation: The cloud-browser tests opened enough tabs to exhaust session and sandbox memory, producing failures not seen in the same way in the code-interpreter environment. The speaker highlights that workload-specific resource demand can dominate task completion. Memory exhaustion should be recognized as an environmental failure mode during browser evaluation rather than interpreted only as inability of the model to carry out the requested workflow.
qualification: No tab counts, memory allocations, failure rates or controlled resource ablation are supplied.
title: Browser concurrency can turn memory limits into complete workflow failure

explanation: Failures clustered around filesystem primitives such as read, write and execute permissions, mounted filesystems and whether storage persists or disappears. These constraints affect whether an arbitrary agent-generated workflow can create artifacts, retrieve them later or run produced programs. Evaluate those semantics explicitly rather than testing only that a file API returns a successful response or assuming local storage behavior matches the hosted environment.
qualification: The talk names relevant primitives but does not provide an exhaustive matrix of expected filesystem behavior.
title: Include permissions, mounts and persistence in sandbox workflow tests

explanation: A machine-learning package may need to spawn a process, a code interpreter may need packages installed where its kernel can discover them, and a coding workflow may depend on binaries being in executable locations. Small environment restrictions accumulate into business-task failure. Tests should therefore exercise these runtime prerequisites, including relevant access controls, rather than assuming that an agent’s valid program can execute in every sandbox configuration.
qualification: Low-level kernel and security captions nearby are unclear; this claim preserves concrete examples without endorsing those garbled definitions.
title: Check process and dependency prerequisites required by real agent workloads

explanation: The speaker moves from familiar LLM-generated unit and integration tests to broader sandbox workflows because low-level environmental controls can block goals in ways developers may overlook. Asking an agent to attempt many varied complete tasks surfaces interactions between its chosen methods and infrastructure primitives. This is presented as a discovery technique, not as a replacement for deterministic tests, validated oracles or careful diagnosis of any failures found.
qualification: The transcript calls this fuzzy testing and illustrates exploratory benefits; it does not establish formal fuzzing coverage or compare detection rates.
title: Complement unit and integration tests with end-to-end generated agent workflows

explanation: Moving coding agents from laptops into remote sandboxes enables scale but changes the available MCP tools, applications and environment. A task that works on a rich local workstation may fail under different remote packages, permissions or resources. The closing recommendation is to test locally and then exercise a broad set of domain workflows remotely, making the actual deployment environment part of the evaluation rather than an assumed equivalent.
qualification: The talk does not prescribe complete environment replication or prove all local/remote differences can be eliminated.
title: Re-test broad workloads remotely instead of extrapolating from local success

explanation: The speaker describes adding SSH access so customers, or their coding agents, can enter a sandbox and inspect why an application does not run smoothly. This complements top-level workflow results: direct environment access can reveal missing tools, dependency placement and other conditions that are difficult to infer from a failed task alone. Inspection is an operational debugging affordance, not evidence that the agent will automatically identify or repair every fault.
qualification: This is a vendor feature description without an evaluated debugging success rate or security model.
title: Provide an inspection path into remote environments for diagnosing agent failures

explanation: A contract names the goal and desired end state instead of prescribing every action. The presenters argue that more capable models can select their own execution strategy, so unnecessary procedural constraints leave intelligence and potential cost improvements unused. This is an abstraction for expressing intent, not evidence that prompts, context engineering or harness design are universally solved.
title: Specify the outcome while leaving execution strategy to the harness

explanation: A complex workflow can be expressed as several contracts whose intermediate results unlock later obligations. This preserves flexibility within a step while constraining the overall path toward the final state. The presenters distinguish composition from inheritance and explain that multiple contracts can also constrain the same run; composition therefore supplies structure without specifying every tool call.
title: Compose intermediate obligations rather than only one final instruction

explanation: A workflow can bind particular subagents to specified skills, tools and input/output obligations. When a required dependency is unavailable, the program should not run rather than silently substituting another method. The concrete search example requires a preferred search CLI and skill. This turns organizational tool choices into executable constraints, although the enforcement described here is mediated by model instructions.
qualification: The transcript describes an instruction-level dependency check, not an independently proven security boundary.
title: Make required skills and tools prerequisites for execution

explanation: Instead of repeatedly chatting with an agent, bind an executable contract to an event. The hosted implementation supports schedules and webhooks, including GitHub issues and pull requests. Each trigger starts a workflow responsible for delivering the stated output, such as an issue-to-commit transformation. The reusable unit is therefore an ongoing operational obligation rather than a single conversational exchange.
title: Define a standing agent job as a contract plus a trigger

explanation: Start with a loosely specified outcome and allow a strong model to discover a workable approach. Once a successful trace exists, codify its execution details into a more specific workflow. The presenters describe this as moving along a spectrum from what to how, potentially lowering cost and variability; they do not provide a comparative experiment measuring the savings.
qualification: Successful-session reuse is described; neither determinism nor a quantified cost reduction is demonstrated.
title: Use expensive discovery runs to derive cheaper pinned procedures

explanation: The presented coding workflow launches reviewer agents when pull requests arrive and requires developer agents to incorporate feedback before considering work complete. Fresh sessions compare outputs with a declared contract instead of relying solely on the producer to approve itself. The speaker reports some changes passing immediately and others taking fourteen review rounds, but provides no accuracy study of the reviewers.
qualification: Fresh contexts address the described self-confidence loop; they do not establish reviewer independence in a statistical sense.
title: Apply fresh-session contract review as backpressure on development

explanation: OpenProse deliberately leaves execution in a model-interpreted, comparatively fuzzy layer instead of isolating each call behind deterministic typed code. The speaker identifies the corresponding weakness: the model may assert that it met the contract, and different model strengths can yield very different results. Declaring an outcome therefore does not itself supply a trustworthy completion check.
title: A declarative executor can still incorrectly declare its own completion

explanation: The presenters propose using a fast decision model after a job to compare messy real-world state against the ideal contract state. A related proposed use is routing incoming events to the appropriate issue or pull-request job. These are opportunities to make verification or scheduling cheaper, not reported completed capabilities of the demonstrated system.
qualification: The speakers explicitly say the decision-model integrations are still being built; no verifier calibration or error rates are given.
title: Separate generative execution from proposed cheap decision checks

explanation: The hosted interface asks for confirmation before an operation that costs money and again before deploying a job that will spend on future events. The distinction matters because an apparently small configuration change can authorize an unbounded series of later runs. The demonstration makes that financial side effect visible through a user click rather than treating deployment as a harmless edit.
qualification: The transcript demonstrates confirmation prompts, not spending limits or protection against every possible financial side effect.
title: Require explicit confirmation when creating spend-bearing automation

explanation: The presenters explicitly recommend ordinary chat for one-off or exploratory tasks where the user does not yet know what they want. Their contract approach is aimed at frequent work requiring reliability, repeatability and auditability. The boundary is intent maturity: an agent may help draft the contract, but reliable recurring execution assumes the desired obligation can eventually be articulated.
title: Use contracts for known recurring work, not undirected exploration

explanation: Textual workflows encode organizational operating procedures as well as task data. The speakers argue that an on-premises stack using approved models and an existing harness can keep both inside the organization. This is a deployment option enabled by the described portable application layer, not a claim that using markdown automatically satisfies procurement, privacy, compliance or security requirements.
title: Treat workflow definitions as institutional knowledge worth retaining privately

explanation: For financial-model documentation, the presenters propose comparing generated material with historical outputs, timing the manual process, and obtaining ratings from working quants. The example includes model purpose, tested conditions and upstream model references. The demonstrated document concerns a public interest-rate model, while actual acceptance by compliance staff, auditors and regulators remains a separate part of the deployment problem.
qualification: No benchmark protocol, expert rating distribution, acceptance rate or realized savings is supplied.
title: Evaluate generated model documentation against historical work and expert ratings

explanation: The presenters say they internally benchmark their runtime instructions and use an evolutionary process to reduce the kernel while checking whether runs continue to conform. This frames instruction compression as a constrained optimization problem rather than merely deleting text that looks redundant. The transcript does not describe the conformance dataset, search procedure, evaluation budget or measured compression-quality tradeoff.
qualification: This is an internal-method report without reproducible implementation details or numerical results.
title: Shrink agent instruction kernels against conformance checks

explanation: OpenProse is presented as text interpreted by an existing coding-agent harness rather than a replacement harness. The framework avoids prescribing a particular provider-specific subagent implementation, allowing contracts to move across tools. That portability still has capability prerequisites: the speakers say more complex multi-agent workflow shapes require a harness with subagents, so plain text alone cannot supply missing execution facilities.
qualification: Harness independence is an architectural aim; compatibility is not exhaustively tested in the transcript.
title: Separate a portable contract layer from harness-specific agent mechanics

explanation: The speaker warns that evals asserting a specific tool call can become invalid when a model or harness changes, even when the application still works differently. Spending months building such checks may slow useful upgrades without adding proportional safety. The caution concerns brittle implementation assumptions and evaluation theater, not an argument to eliminate regression tests or deploy changes without verification.
qualification: The talk gives no measured rate of obsolete tests; the later recommendation is still to run local coded evals.
title: Avoid tying long-lived evals unnecessarily to a particular tool path

explanation: Model labs aim to improve general-purpose capability, whereas downstream application teams need to supply company-specific data meanings, access patterns and domain knowledge. Borrowing lab vocabulary or benchmark designs can conceal this difference in responsibility. Evaluation should therefore ask whether the assembled product works in its setting, not simply whether the underlying model displays an impressive generic capability.
title: Choose eval objectives for the application rather than copying model-lab benchmarks

explanation: An expert using autocomplete can often delete a wrong suggestion, while an autonomous product or medical application assigns users a very different burden. The speaker asks whether the product augments a domain expert or replaces one. This distinction affects how much responsibility can reasonably be left to users and therefore which failures must be prevented or verified by the application itself.
qualification: The talk contrasts product categories, not a validated risk-assessment framework.
title: Account for whether users can recognize and repair agent errors

explanation: The ceiling is the most impressive capability an agent can exhibit; the floor is the worst behavior it can produce. Examples of floor failures include deleting data, recommending competitors and sending unwanted customer emails because tools were accessible. The speaker argues that these failures undermine trust even when capabilities are impressive, making floor improvement a distinct objective for deployed application teams.
title: Raise the failure floor that determines user trust

explanation: For modern agents, behavior comes from the code, tools, connections and harness rather than a single managed prompt string. The speaker therefore recommends local evals that resemble ordinary unit or end-to-end tests, maintained as code. A prompt playground alone can miss the system that actually determines outcomes; this is an argument about evaluation scope, not a claim that every case requires a full end-to-end run.
title: Keep offline agent evals as executable tests of the assembled system

explanation: Finding a strange trace is insufficient for prioritizing agent improvements. Date the onset so engineers can investigate recent model or dependency changes, and estimate affected-user share to distinguish isolated events from broad failures. The speaker treats these two dimensions as essential because agents can exhibit effectively endless edge cases; temporal and population context make an issue actionable rather than merely interesting.
title: Track when each issue began and what share of users it affects

explanation: Very high-volume applications can learn from experiments on a small fraction of traffic, including a free-tier slice. With only five or ten users, the speaker would not recommend ordinary A/B experimentation. Small user count does not imply low stakes: an internal enterprise tool can provide critical information. Evaluation strategy therefore depends on both available observations and the importance of being correct.
qualification: The talk does not specify power calculations, randomization design or experiment-safety criteria.
title: Choose experiments according to traffic volume and consequence

explanation: Clustering traces can help one-off exploration, but cluster membership and boundaries can move, making onset and growth hard to track reliably over time. Similar-looking outputs may also have different root causes that need separate fixes. The speaker gives wrong quoted prices versus wrong refund calculations as an example of failures that a generic price-issues cluster could misleadingly merge.
qualification: This is a warning about naive operational clustering, not proof that all temporal clustering methods fail.
title: Do not mistake semantic trace clusters for operational issues

explanation: The speaker recommends applying code mode to trace analysis: write classifiers, execute them in a sandbox, and run the computation at production scale. This offers a programmable route beyond manually inspecting logs or repeatedly prompting over raw traces. The talk supplies the operational pattern but not classifier code, accuracy results, cost measurements or the conditions under which this outperforms alternative analysis methods.
qualification: Scalability is asserted from practitioner experience; no load test is included.
title: Use code-executed classifiers to analyze traces at production scale

explanation: Rather than asking an agent to discover arbitrary anomalies, extract deterministic signals such as keyword frequencies and look for changes. A keyword spike does not itself prove an issue, but it supplies a concrete candidate for agent investigation. This separates anomaly detection from interpretation and gives the agent a bounded question instead of an open-ended search over everything that might be wrong.
qualification: The assertion that agents are bad at anomaly detection is not supported by a benchmark in this talk.
title: Detect tangible anomalies first and delegate their investigation

explanation: The initial question is how to make the agent better, not simply how many issues can be found. Some failures may not be solvable with present tools or worth solving locally, and a forthcoming model may address them more cheaply than building equivalent capability internally. This creates a prioritization boundary around production improvement rather than an obligation to repair every strange behavior immediately.
qualification: Waiting for improved models is presented as an example of judgment, not a universal reason to postpone product fixes.
title: Optimize for worthwhile improvements rather than every detectable error

explanation: The proposed loop traces production use, builds datasets, experiments with changes, evaluates offline, deploys a candidate and then learns from new usage. Keeping online and offline systems separate risks benchmarking stale or inaccurate data, or monitoring failures without testing improvements. The transferable mechanism is a feedback connection between observed application behavior and repeatable offline comparisons, not merely collecting more logs.
title: Connect real usage traces with offline evaluation and redeployment

explanation: Humans should review additions to datasets, evaluation criteria and proposed application changes because these define the boundary for subsequent automated optimization. Otherwise agents may optimize toward incidental production quirks or irrelevant failure definitions. The speaker advocates removing people from tedious lower-level work while retaining involvement in direction setting, rather than fully automating the choice of what success should mean.
qualification: The talk does not offer a formal governance protocol or quantify overfitting risk.
title: Keep humans responsible for the target that agents optimize

explanation: Once traces, evaluation criteria and datasets reproduce a production issue, agents can propose changes and hill-climb against that defined target. Candidate interventions include changing the model or how context is aggregated. The useful division of labor is to let automated exploration test many implementation options while preserving a reviewed optimization boundary, rather than accepting arbitrary changes simply because an agent generated them.
qualification: The caption says evil criteria; surrounding context concerns evaluation criteria, but the quote is preserved unchanged.
title: Let agents search implementation alternatives against reproducible failures

explanation: A customer-support dataset should represent common support requests, yet real users do unexpected things with the application. The speaker describes agents proposing dataset updates from observed usage so offline examples stay connected to production. This is not indiscriminate copying of every trace: dataset changes still require review because they change what later optimization rewards and which user behaviors the application is expected to support.
title: Continuously align evaluation examples with actual user behavior

explanation: Observed error patterns can reveal requirements missing from the original specification. In the customer-support example, proposed criteria include not naming competitors, being concise and answering in the requested language. Agents may reproduce these failures and suggest new evaluators, but the resulting criteria are proposals for the application objective rather than automatically valid definitions of quality.
qualification: No judge prompts, human-agreement checks or evaluator error rates are provided.
title: Turn recurring errors into explicit candidate evaluation criteria

explanation: Useful supervision need not come only from explicit ratings or developer annotation. Customers saying the support answer was incorrect, expressing frustration, or internal staff editing a suggested reply can all feed the improvement loop. These behavioral signals make data collection less manually intensive, but the talk presents them as interesting inputs to analyze rather than authoritative labels of the precise error or its correct fix.
title: Harvest corrective behavior as improvement-loop signal

explanation: The demo changelog writer responds to a merged product PR by proposing documentation changes through another GitHub PR. A reviewer can approve or request changes; the writer revises until release. Both approval and corrective requests are then connected to traces and evaluation, turning an existing review workflow into data for improving the writer rather than requiring a separate labeling ritual.
title: Reuse approval and revision requests as structured agent feedback

explanation: The changelog writer is described as factually accurate yet unclear because it leaks internal implementation jargon. Reviewer edits expose the difference between code-level descriptions and how customers understand features. The proposed fix changes context or the writer skill and adds evaluators for jargon and user-facing clarity. Accuracy alone therefore misses a practically important failure mode in release communication.
qualification: The transcript narrates a demo diagnosis without showing the underlying annotation rubric or example outputs in full.
title: Evaluate communication in the customer domain, not only factual correctness

explanation: The demo first reproduces poor user-facing language with the existing implementation, then evaluates a candidate on the updated dataset. It checks that format compliance and accuracy remain comparable while user-facing language improves. This is a multidimensional regression check: an improvement on a newly discovered criterion should not be considered in isolation from previously important requirements.
qualification: The transcript reports qualitative deltas, not numerical scores, confidence intervals or an independent held-out evaluation.
title: Reproduce a failure on the baseline before comparing a candidate

explanation: The internal demo accepts a relatively permissive automatic improvement flow because the changelog writer never directly publishes to production; it only raises pull requests. Reviewers can provide feedback on the next increment. This ties acceptable autonomy to action scope and reversibility, rather than treating a favorable offline comparison as sufficient justification for unrestricted deployment to customer-visible systems.
qualification: This is explicitly an internal, lower-exposure example, not a general deployment-safety guarantee.
title: Permit more self-improvement when outputs remain behind review

explanation: The speaker describes teams pairing production signals with detailed traces and running improvement agents on recurring jobs, daily, weekly or when an interesting batch arrives. Inputs can include user feedback, internal labels and annotations. This makes the cadence data-driven and operationally repeatable, while the talk leaves selection thresholds, batch sizing, review staffing and failure-handling policy unspecified.
qualification: Cadences are reported practitioner patterns, not benchmarked optimal schedules.
title: Run improvement loops when enough fresh signal has accumulated

explanation: Automated analysis changes observability infrastructure from mostly ingesting traces to repeatedly reading large volumes of historical data. The speaker argues that old traces become useful context, so cheap retention, data ownership and limited sampling are valuable. These are workload and architecture considerations for improvement loops, not evidence that every system must retain every trace indefinitely regardless of cost or privacy constraints.
qualification: The storage recommendation is vendor-framed; no quantitative workload, privacy or retention analysis is provided.
title: Design trace storage for repeated agent queries and long retention

explanation: Static handcrafted questions exercise known requirements but do not explore all the ways an agent can behave unexpectedly. The speaker draws an analogy with chaos engineering: deliberately stretch and break the system to learn its boundaries. This expands evaluation beyond cycling familiar offline cases; the talk does not specify a perturbation generator, adversarial coverage metric or procedure for safely applying this exploration in production.
title: Complement known regression cases with exploratory stress testing
