This separates structural processing from language generation so the resulting procedure can remain linked to source components rather than being an unconstrained narrative summary of memory.
qualification: The full seven-stage pipeline is referenced visually and not enumerated; determinism and reliability are assertions, not independently tested guarantees.
title: Limit generation to synthesis within a mostly deterministic transformation

explanation: The speaker says grounding alone is not enough and asks whether steps and descriptions throughout the skill are covered by underlying memory evidence. A demonstrated patient-intake skill links steps to actual tool calls and entities from an earlier conversation. The reusable check is granular provenance across the procedure, so packaging a grounded topic does not excuse unsupported individual instructions.
qualification: The demo inspects a previously generated skill; the transcript does not show executing it successfully or clinical validation of its instructions.
title: Check that grounding covers the procedure, not merely its overall topic

explanation: Coherence is proposed as a quality check on the subgraph selected for distillation. If it spans multiple topics, the system can suggest splitting the result into several skills. The speaker specifically describes community detection as a signal: mixing information from multiple graph communities may indicate that the skill should be decomposed, rather than accepting a broad but poorly focused procedure.
qualification: Community boundaries are a heuristic signal; no threshold, algorithm choice or coherence-to-task-success validation is supplied.
title: Use graph structure to identify skills that mix unrelated subjects

explanation: A generated skill should retain links from its components to supporting memory. If that data changes, is removed, or becomes contradictory, background curation can detect possible staleness and a governed registry can serve an updated version. This treats skills as maintained artifacts with dependencies, not permanently valid text produced once from an earlier successful run.
qualification: The source describes detecting and surfacing drift; it does not establish an automatic repair policy, update correctness, or governance success rate.
title: Track source changes so a packaged skill can be flagged as stale

explanation: Evaluation serves as the specification for an enterprise AI system, not a report added after a model is selected. Define numerical business outcomes, acceptable error behavior, and operational targets before implementation. For a support agent this includes which simple queries should be deflected from humans, not merely a generic accuracy score. Build a repeatable measurement system around those targets so later model and feature choices become testable decisions.
title: Specify business success before choosing models

explanation: Collect examples of how domain experts actually respond to customers, including gray areas and confusing questions. Use these examples as an initial evaluation dataset and automate the comparison between generated and expected responses. The important unit is a representative business interaction, rather than a conveniently predictable demo prompt. The resulting pipeline should continue measuring live responses against the business goals after deployment, not stop at a one-time launch assessment.
title: Seed evaluation with expert responses and ambiguous cases

explanation: Use different evaluation layers for different failure types. Deterministic format checks and established classifiers can handle routine validity or PII concerns; a separate judging model can assess semantic properties such as groundedness and relevance; behavioral evaluation checks tool selection, loops, and repeated actions. Correct text is not sufficient evidence of correct execution. Separating these layers makes their responsibilities explicit and avoids relying on an expensive semantic judge for every check.
title: Separate cheap validity checks, semantic judgments, and agent behavior

explanation: An account-balance answer can pass format and semantic checks while the agent unnecessarily queries the database three times. Evaluate duplicate calls and retries as behavior because costs that look harmless in a demo accumulate across thousands of production requests. The final answer and the execution trace therefore need separate assessment. This example motivates tool-use efficiency checks; it does not establish that every repeated call is avoidable or incorrect.
qualification: Illustrative account-balance example; no measured cost reduction is supplied.
title: Detect wasteful trajectories even when the final answer is right

explanation: Collect and visualize the sequence of classification, account access, retrieval, reasoning, and guardrail operations so disputed outcomes can be investigated. The same traces can support online intervention when calls fail or duplicate. Define a bounded retry policy and then report or hand off to a human rather than allowing indefinite retries. The speaker gives three retries as an example policy, not a universal optimal threshold for every tool or failure mode.
qualification: The banking trace is simplified for a presentation slide; the retry count is illustrative.
title: Use observable traces to bound recovery attempts

explanation: Enterprise data strategy must cover both the information agents answer from and the tracking data used to inspect them. Plan collection and trace schemas around audit access, operational monitoring, and judging requirements. When teams use different frameworks and clouds, consolidate tracing into a common layer that can serve multiple consumers. A trace dashboard alone does not replace this underlying data-management work, particularly when many agents produce data across organizational boundaries.
qualification: Databricks products illustrate the architecture; the general principle is not evidence that one vendor stack is required.
title: Plan trace schemas and shared access as a data foundation

explanation: A central orchestrator distributes work to specialists and provides a common control and investigation point. Event-driven choreography instead lets independent agents consume relevant events from a message bus and execute in parallel, reducing coordination round trips when tasks do not depend on one another. Choose the pattern according to control needs and actual dependencies rather than assuming more agents automatically improve the workflow. Low-confidence work can additionally be routed to humans.
qualification: The latency benefit is architectural guidance, not a benchmarked comparison in the transcript.
title: Choose central orchestration or event choreography by dependencies

explanation: Treat prompt modifications as enterprise change management rather than informal text edits. Versioning is necessary but insufficient: record the failure that caused the change, the intended correction, and why the new version should address it. This preserves an investigation trail when later behavior changes or regressions occur. The speaker specifically warns that terse source-control commit messages can leave versions available while making their purpose impossible to reconstruct.
title: Version prompts with failure-linked change rationale

explanation: Provider leaderboard results do not determine whether an upgraded model will work for a particular enterprise use case. Run candidate models against the organization’s own evaluation dataset and compare performance in that context. Maintain the ability to switch models rather than creating an untested dependency on one provider or version. This turns model choice and upgrades into governed empirical decisions, although the talk does not prescribe a statistical selection method.
title: Validate model changes against enterprise-specific evaluations

explanation: Start with a feasible set of real cases, score responses automatically, and send below-threshold cases for human inspection. After repairing the prompt or tool behavior, add the failure as a regression case. Assign dataset ownership and categorize failures so later changes can be checked against relevant problems, such as authentication mistakes. The library grows through operational learning; the reported starting set of 200 banking cases is not a universal dataset-size requirement.
qualification: The speaker reports an eight-week banking project and targets, but does not verbally provide the full post-launch metric table.
title: Turn reviewed low-scoring responses into owned regression cases

explanation: After a bank changed interest-rate policies, users received notifications but the chatbot kept giving answers based on old documents. Negative customer feedback signaled a problem; inspecting traces showed the updated policy had not reached the vector database through embeddings. The corrective action was to repair data freshness rather than assume the model needed replacement. This illustrates how outcome monitoring and source-level traces jointly isolate a production failure.
qualification: Speaker-reported customer incident; no raw logs, timing distribution, or independently audited results are supplied.
title: Connect user dissatisfaction to stale retrieval inputs

explanation: Prepare a production playbook that detects degradation through evaluations, diagnoses it through traces, contains it through prompt rollback or human routing, fixes the fault, and adds regression tests. Connect this workflow to existing IT service-management alerting so the responsible person is reached when failures occur. Evaluation infrastructure therefore supports incident handling as well as development. Recovery patterns mentioned elsewhere are references, not fully specified procedures in this transcript.
title: Integrate an AI incident playbook with operational ownership

explanation: Behavioral evaluations can become expensive when every prompt or tool fix reruns hundreds of cases repeatedly. Govern evaluation execution as the dataset grows: use a small relevant subset for intermediate continuous-integration checks and reserve the full evaluation for integration to the main branch. This trades some early detection breadth for faster, cheaper feedback while retaining a broader gate. Dataset categorization helps make these subset choices more meaningful than arbitrary sampling.
qualification: Proposed cost-control workflow; no measured speedup or missed-regression rate is given.
title: Run targeted subsets during iteration and full suites at mainline integration

explanation: Tokens are a useful internal consumption measure but do not directly express customer value. Trace spending to completed outcomes, such as bugs fixed or support requests closed, and connect those outcomes to organizational objectives. Lower token cost or higher usage alone cannot establish return on investment. This distinction matters when incentives reward consumption and teams oscillate between indiscriminate parallel usage and budget-driven withdrawal instead of learning which tasks merit agents.
title: Measure what token spending accomplishes rather than token volume

explanation: A new technology becomes easier to try when its gains are framed relative to work the customer already understands. The speaker uses horsepower as an analogy: a familiar baseline can make efficiency and return on investment legible even before a prospective user has internalized the technology. For agents, discover customers’ mental models rather than assume token counts or technical benchmarks answer their purchasing and task-selection questions.
qualification: The historical narrative is an analogy, not independent evidence validating an agent metric.
title: Express value in a baseline customers already understand

explanation: Agent developers and early adopters can enjoy experimentation and parallel execution in ways that do not represent prospective users. Their willingness to spend tokens, familiarity with tooling, or excitement is not evidence that a novice can identify valuable use cases. Customer-facing measurement should therefore be grounded in the user’s decision context, including people who still use basic chat workflows, rather than the habits of a technically enthusiastic conference audience.
title: Do not infer ordinary customer value from enthusiastic builders

explanation: Generating more code can move the limiting step to human review instead of improving end-to-end delivery. When pull requests accumulate faster than people can assess them, apparent execution gains do not establish value or justify the spend. Assess quality at a pace compatible with generation and account for verification workload. The speaker explicitly declines to solve code review; the reusable observation is that automation changes where the bottleneck resides.
qualification: Industry anecdotes and attributed claims are discussed without a controlled productivity study.
title: Measure throughput after verification, not just generation

explanation: Scalable verification depends on convergence about what counts as good work. Code review is offered as a domain with relatively developed shared assumptions, even if those assumptions need revision for agent-generated work. Build or adapt a clear rubric that fits customer expectations so measurement can potentially scale with execution. The existence of agents that produce outputs is insufficient if their buyers must invent acceptance criteria and return-on-investment logic on their own.
qualification: The talk proposes this direction but supplies no validated rubric or code-review framework.
title: Create shared assumptions before automating evaluation

explanation: Mousepower is a proposed way to think about communicating agent value, not a literal universal unit. Measuring cursor movement or screen traversal does not capture high-dimensional information work or establish a clean human-agent efficiency ratio. The speaker jokingly describes a measurement device before rejecting that approach. The useful artifact is a task-appropriate rubric that verifies valuable work and allows customers to assess whether their token expenditure was worthwhile.
title: Do not mistake interface movement for useful work

explanation: Select agent tasks using two different uncertainties: how predictable the steps are and how clear the acceptance criteria are. A flight purchase has required facts and actions even if some choices vary; painting a masterpiece lacks an equally predictable route and judgment standard. Separating these axes prevents a valuable-sounding task from being mistaken for an economically automatable one when either execution or verification remains poorly specified.
qualification: This is a thought-starter matrix, not an empirically validated entropy measure.
title: Evaluate uncertainty in both execution and acceptance

explanation: When a task has a predictable pathway with low uncertainty in its steps, a conventional script can be a better fit than spending tokens on an agent. The decision rule is not that valuable tasks require AI, but that agent flexibility should solve a real variability problem. This criterion addresses execution structure; it still needs to be combined with an assessment of whether the output can be verified economically.
title: Use scripts when execution has little uncertainty

explanation: High uncertainty in acceptance criteria can make verification indistinguishable from execution. If a person must essentially redo the work to decide whether the agent helped, the token spending may not create an economic advantage. Before deploying an agent, inspect the practical checking burden rather than assume output volume equals saved labor. This warning targets hard-to-judge tasks; it does not establish that every subjective task is impossible to assist.
title: Avoid workflows where checking requires redoing the task

explanation: The proposed sweet spot combines enough execution uncertainty to benefit from an agent with sufficiently clear acceptance criteria that checking is easier than doing. A repeatable checking pattern may itself be implemented by another agent, allowing execution and verification to scale together. The speaker calls this an NP-style shape as an analogy, not a complexity-theoretic classification. Task selection and verifier design should therefore be considered together rather than in separate product stages.
qualification: The speaker explicitly describes the proposal as still in the works; no experimental validation or universal framework is provided.
title: Prefer nontrivial tasks with repeatable, cheap checking

explanation: Knowledge work processes ambiguous, diffuse information into an actionable judgment, decision, or finding rather than transforming physical material. Coding is one instance of that broader class, alongside legal, medical, actuarial, and research work. This framing matters because an architecture effective for programming should not automatically become the template for every information task. Evaluate the information-seeking and judgment workflow appropriate to the domain rather than treating noncoding work as code search with different documents.
title: Define knowledge work by information inputs and actionable outputs

explanation: Code often has persistent identifiers, paths, method definitions, and narrowly specified tickets. Noncode knowledge can have implicit meanings and context-dependent rules that require discovering what to search for. A phrase such as thirty days might denote a deadline, grace period, or retention policy, so lexical matching alone can retrieve the wrong concept. Design retrieval and task decomposition for the ambiguity of the actual domain instead of assuming grep-like workflows are generally sufficient.
qualification: The contrast is the speaker’s generalization; it does not establish that all coding work is narrow or all noncode work requires semantic retrieval.
title: Do not transfer durable code identifiers to ambiguous knowledge search

explanation: Knowledge tools and organizational structure form a reinforcing loop: better ways to find and store information create new workflows and specialized roles; trained workers use them to produce more knowledge, which creates demand for further tools. An agent workflow should likewise change with its tools instead of treating retrieval improvements as isolated add-ons. Specialization only helps when workers or agents know how to use the available primitives and exchange useful intermediate results.
title: Improve tools and work organization together

explanation: A retrieval tool can determine whether a knowledge task is cheap enough to be routinely performed, not simply whether it is theoretically possible. The speaker compares searching uncataloged manuscripts with using a library catalog and extends that argument to large PDF archives. Better retrieval may unlock previously uneconomic workflows through fewer searches and less context expenditure. This is an argument for measuring operational effort alongside accuracy, rather than celebrating any benchmark increase without considering its resource requirements.
title: Judge retrieval improvements by workflow feasibility, not only accuracy

explanation: A weak BM25 result is not sufficient evidence against lexical search in general because many implementations and configurations exist. Optimize the baseline before comparing it with a new retrieval tool or architecture. The talk contrasts unoptimized and optimized versions and describes substantial accuracy differences, making baseline quality part of the causal explanation. This does not establish which parameters are universally best; the transferable requirement is a credible, task-appropriate baseline.
qualification: Results are speaker-reported leaderboard comparisons; configuration details are not provided in the transcript.
title: Treat BM25 as an implementation family that needs tuning

explanation: Once accuracy appears to plateau, tool-use efficiency can still materially improve the economics of a search workflow. The speaker treats a small accuracy difference as run variance while emphasizing a reported twenty percent reduction in tool calls at roughly ninety percent accuracy. Evaluate the number of calls and resources needed to achieve an outcome alongside answer quality. Do not infer exact token or cash savings solely from fewer calls without measuring call sizes and pricing.
qualification: The speaker equates call reductions with token/resource savings; underlying runs, variance estimates, and a cost accounting are absent.
title: Track tool calls when accuracy differences are within run variance

explanation: If a capable model and a human both stall when restricted to the same search primitive, the bottleneck may be access to relevant information rather than reasoning ability. The speaker uses an enterprise PDF benchmark to argue that even unlimited lexical searches cannot always recover the needed material. Improve the retrieval representation and tools before assuming the model must become smarter. Equal scores under restricted tools do not prove equal underlying intelligence.
qualification: The benchmark name and model names are imperfectly captioned; no full experimental protocol is spoken.
title: A shared human-model ceiling can indicate a tool bottleneck

explanation: PDF-based knowledge tasks may require more than OCR text and lexical matching. The speaker describes using vision-capable, multimodal retrieval to access document structure and tables, producing a reported accuracy jump on an enterprise benchmark. A retrieval evaluation should therefore reflect the actual document modalities rather than only text exports. This improvement still leaves a gap to the reported human result, so stronger input representations alone are not presented as a complete solution.
qualification: Vendor-affiliated benchmark account; visual leaderboard details and multimodal retrieval implementation are not available.
title: Preserve tables and visual evidence in document search

explanation: Have the main agent identify important aspects of an open-ended question and issue separate search queries rather than personally conducting every search. Searcher agents investigate those aspects independently and return compact memos; the main agent synthesizes an answer from their findings. The speaker reports a 3.5-point improvement and a roughly forty percent reduction in the remaining gap to an oracle or human reference. The example transfers the partner-and-assistants organization of legal research into agent design.
qualification: The transcript alternates between an oracle perfect-document gap and a human gap; treat the percentage as a speaker-reported relative-gap interpretation, not independent error-rate verification.
title: Separate problem decomposition, specialist search, and answer synthesis

explanation: Introduce better tools to overcome an observed performance ceiling and ensure the harness or model knows how to use them. Grep-like queries, BM25, and semantic search are different primitives, not interchangeable names for search. Decompose work and organize returned knowledge instead of relying on ever-larger context windows: the speaker argues that context remains costly and tiny compared with large legal corpora. Tools and orchestration must be co-designed for the information problem.
qualification: The scale comparison is rhetorical guidance; no measured context-cost curve or training recipe is given.
title: Teach retrieval primitives and organize around finite context

explanation: When experts cannot cheaply grade arbitrary generated answers, start with a known source page and ask an LLM to generate a question about it. Run the retrieval agent on that question and check whether it finds the source page using code. This reverses the normal question-answer-grading workflow and avoids repeated expert lookup. It evaluates a retrieval target rather than guaranteeing that every final answer to the question is correct or complete.
qualification: Speaker-reported telecom case; synthetic questions may not represent the full real-user distribution.
title: Generate queries from known pages to obtain code-checkable retrieval labels

explanation: In the telecom project, adding published techniques increased complexity and broke previously working behavior. Replacing weekly expert comparisons with automated tests reportedly allowed dozens of evaluations per day. The team then removed unnecessary complexity and focused on embedding choice, chunking, and the lexical-search mixture. The reusable mechanism is faster regression feedback for simpler targeted tuning, not a guarantee that these particular parameter choices or synthetic tests explain every difference between competing teams.
qualification: The speaker explicitly says he does not know why his team succeeded and only suspects other teams lacked tests; no controlled comparison is established.
title: Increase feedback frequency before adding retrieval complexity

explanation: Break contract review into spotting clauses or defects, retrieving supporting documents, drafting amendments, and deciding whether to keep an amendment. Existing answer-first retrieval tests cover one stage but not the entire agent. Different components need different known-answer constructions, so do not mistake a successful retrieval benchmark for complete validation of contract analysis. The decomposition also exposes which parts of the business workflow remain hard to grade with limited expert access.
title: Decompose contract review into separately testable stages

explanation: Past expert edits can supply expected review flags by comparing an original contract with its signed or revised version. Before adopting this strategy, verify that both versions and usable decision history are actually retained. In the presented project only final contracts were available, and negotiation complicated the record, so the proposed diff-based route could not be used. Historical supervision is a data-availability-dependent technique, not free ground truth simply because documents exist.
title: Use historical contract changes only when paired versions exist

explanation: Start with a known rule, construct a clause and surrounding contract with a targeted compliance condition, and ask the agent to recover the expected flag. This creates test inputs whose labels are known in advance rather than requiring experts to grade every output. The team reports 275 such tests. Coverage remains limited by the rules experts or documentation can provide, and the transcript’s clause-generation wording is internally inconsistent about whether the initial clause violates the rule.
qualification: The cap-above-$1-million example is speaker wording, not a verified statement of airline policy; the captions say both without breaking and breaking the rule.
title: Build synthetic contracts around known compliance rules

explanation: Take a signed contract, remove a clause, and test whether the agent notices that something required is missing. Mix these mutations with intact contracts that should produce no flag so the test also discourages indiscriminate flagging. The team found its agents missed most removed clauses, making the task diagnostically useful. Expected content depends on supplier type and template, so absence detection requires more domain reasoning than locating a suspicious phrase already present.
qualification: The reported failure is qualitative; no denominator, omission taxonomy, or final recovered performance is supplied.
title: Delete expected clauses and include unchanged valid contracts

explanation: When full answer labels are expensive, test relations that should hold across equivalent inputs. Changing supplier names or addresses, reordering clauses, or rerunning the same contract should not arbitrarily change the number of review flags under the stated assumptions. These consistency checks can be implemented in code without an LLM judge. They test robustness and invariance, not whether every flag is legally correct; apparently irrelevant fields must truly be irrelevant for the chosen rule.
title: Test irrelevant edits, clause order, and repeated execution

explanation: Use contract templates already maintained by experts and supply arrays of possible values for each blank. Generate combinations whose rule compliance is known so each resulting contract has expected flags that code can check. This turns a small number of expert artifacts into many tests, including both compliant and violating cases. The benefit depends on meaningful template coverage and reliable labels for combinations; the technique does not prove that arbitrary negotiated contracts are covered.
qualification: The team reports replacing a roughly four-week feedback cycle with a script returning evaluation in five minutes; end-to-end production readiness is not established.
title: Expand expert templates with rule-aware value combinations

explanation: Choose exact matches or code checks when known answers or invariant relations make them available. In this contract project, the team found LLM-judge noise large relative to the behavior it was trying to improve, and finding a suitable judge prompt or harness became almost as hard as the original problem. This is contextual advice to reduce evaluator uncertainty, not a claim that all semantic judging is useless or that legal meaning can always be reduced to code.
qualification: No judge-calibration dataset or quantitative noise estimate is provided; the team reports not finding a suitable judge for this project.
title: Avoid introducing a second hard problem when code can grade the task

explanation: Answer-first testing generalizes by choosing an expected result, generating an input that should elicit it, and checking recovery of that result. The speaker gives tool trajectories with expected endpoint order as another application. Some projects required changing the original solution design slightly to become evaluatable. This makes evaluability an architectural constraint, but the speaker explicitly says the paradigm does not apply to everything and does not provide a universal transformation recipe.
title: Change the solution design when it makes evaluation possible

explanation: After synthetic tests help improve an agent, gather real expert feedback and use it to generate better tests rather than only patch the observed output. Adjust generation prompts, mutation ideas, or clause-removal strategies so later iterations capture the newly discovered failure class. This leverages limited expert access across future experiments. The mechanism emphasizes correcting the evaluation process; it does not eliminate the need for real feedback after optimization on synthetic examples.
title: Use scarce expert feedback to improve the test-generation loop

explanation: Knowing labels for generated tests makes development faster, but passing those tests is insufficient evidence to ship the product. The final caveat separates an iteration tool from a go/no-go release assessment. Synthetic constructions and invariance checks cover chosen rules and transformations, while real-world contracts may expose unmodeled cases. Preserve this boundary when using the reported evaluation speedups so an efficient test harness is not mistaken for complete production assurance.
title: Use answer-first tests for iteration, not a standalone shipping decision

explanation: A system-level risk review separates where the system can technically break, whether deployment controls contain the error, and what business harm follows if it reaches users. The proposed framework expands these into thirteen dimensions covering data, design, validity, fairness, failure modes, explainability, authority, human mediation, exposure, monitoring, financial impact, legal impact, and scale. This structure makes model capability only one component of assurance rather than a substitute for reviewing the deployed workflow.
title: Evaluate technical failures, deployment controls, and business consequences together

explanation: The retrospective analysis reportedly associated almost ninety-eight percent of examined incidents with the proposed thirteen dimensions and found an average of six dimensions per incident. Use this as a reminder to investigate combinations of technical and organizational weaknesses rather than stop at the first plausible model error. These statistics describe how the researchers categorized recorded incidents; they do not establish predictive coverage of future failures or an independently validated causal decomposition.
qualification: The title references 1,368 failures, but the spoken transcript does not give a detailed sampling, coding, reliability, or denominator protocol.
title: Treat incidents as interacting failures rather than single model defects

explanation: A common failure category is not necessarily the category most strongly associated with harm. The reported plot places human mediation and harm detection among particularly consequential dimensions, while frequent categories such as scale and system design are described as less strongly associated. Prioritize investigation and resources according to potential harm rather than treating every dimension equally. The analysis is associative, so these observations should not be converted into causal effect estimates or universal rankings.
qualification: The transcript provides a qualitative plot interpretation without effect sizes, confounder controls, or raw incident data.
title: Allocate evaluation effort by harm association rather than frequency alone

explanation: Even a system with technical defects may avoid harmful outcomes if deployment controls contain errors before they affect decisions. The speakers report that deployment-control dimensions are more strongly associated with harm than technical failures in their analysis. Evaluate authority, effective human review, external exposure, and monitoring rather than assume a strong model makes deployment safe. The claim supports layered containment, not an excuse to ignore model quality or evidence that any nominal human-in-the-loop arrangement is effective.
qualification: Retrospective association, not a randomized comparison proving control interventions reduce harm by a measured amount.
title: Assess control effectiveness separately from technical model strength

explanation: Decompose risk into how often the model fails, whether failures reach real decisions, whether they go uncaught, and the severity of consequences. The same model can therefore create different risk under different authority, review, and monitoring setups. Evaluate those pathways explicitly instead of reporting error rate as a complete risk measure. This is a conceptual decomposition of the deployment chain, not a fully specified probabilistic formula or calibrated quantitative risk model.
title: Distinguish failures from consequential uncaught failures

explanation: Keep the traditional discipline of testing assumptions, inputs, and behavior under stress, but enlarge the test boundary to the entire agentic deployment. Check whether retrieval returns appropriate information, tools can fail safely, human review catches mistakes, permission boundaries hold, and the system recovers. A held-out model metric alone cannot answer these questions. This procedure targets the interactions that determine whether technical failures become harmful actions rather than merely assessing response text.
title: Extend stress testing to retrieval, tools, permissions, review, and recovery

explanation: Agent evaluations inspect selected scenarios from a large space of inputs, tool responses, and action sequences. An AI that generates tests or judges outcomes can itself be wrong, while its scenarios can miss important failures. Govern the evaluator as part of the system: determine whether it is reliable, what the evidence actually covers, and whether the evaluated configuration matches deployment. A passing score is only meaningful within those limits.
title: Check evaluator reliability, coverage, and deployment applicability

explanation: Start with a claim about what the system should do and deliberately try to break it. Identify where the claim fails, add supporting controls or exclude that territory, then repeat the challenge until confidence is appropriate. The speakers invoke confirmation bias to motivate this failure-driven loop. The transferable procedure is adversarially testing requirements rather than assembling only confirming demonstrations; the talk does not supply a validated stopping criterion or formal confidence calculation.
qualification: The historical number-series experiment is a speaker-retold analogy with imprecise wording, not new empirical evidence about the proposed evaluation loop.
title: Challenge explicit claims instead of confirming attractive examples

explanation: Use repeated build-break-fix testing to map where outcomes are sufficiently reliable and where uncertainty or risk remains high. Route deployment according to both reliability and materiality, limiting high-risk use to regions supported by evidence and using containment or alternative workflows elsewhere. This makes the evaluation output an operational boundary rather than just one aggregate score. The map remains conditional on tested scenarios and must not be read as proof about every untested input.
title: Map trusted, uncertain, and high-risk regions before routing work

explanation: The airline example follows incorrect advice through customer reliance to organizational legal consequences. A chatbot said a bereavement discount could be claimed after purchase within ninety days, conflicting with policy. The proposed evaluation would state an approved-policy consistency requirement, challenge post-travel refund advice, add policy checks or human escalation, and retest whether those controls stop errors before reaching customers. This is a counterfactual application of the framework, not a reported predeployment experiment that actually prevented the incident.
qualification: The incident is retold by the speakers; no legal source is supplied or independently checked in this extraction.
title: Test the entire policy-advice failure chain and retest controls

explanation: Rank use cases by materiality so scarce review and testing resources concentrate on consequential deployments rather than treating every application equally. The speakers propose company-specific scales incorporating business context and note that risk can change. Combine that prioritization with system-level stress testing and make deployment decisions only in regions where evidence supports confidence. The talk describes the purpose of a materiality scale, but not enough scoring details to reproduce or calibrate one.
qualification: No scale weights, thresholds, validation protocol, or risk-update cadence are specified.
title: Scale evaluation effort to changing business materiality

explanation: The opening design discussion describes compartmentalizing storage so new event types can be added without tightly coupling persistence to session execution. The reusable architectural move is to define interfaces at the event layer, not merely between services. This keeps changes in what is recorded from automatically becoming changes in how a running session works.
qualification: Architectural explanation of a revision; no comparative reliability or migration measurements.
title: Virtualize event storage independently of session execution

explanation: Provision the environment separately from the agent, including reachable domains and installed packages. The workshop initially uses unrestricted access for a joke agent, but explicitly says production access should be narrowed to required domains or MCP servers. The SEC research example then provisions relevant websites and Python packages, illustrating task-specific environment configuration rather than unrestricted execution as a default.
qualification: Dependency installation is described in ending Q&A as occurring at environment creation and being cached, not automatically on every turn.
title: Treat the environment as a permissioned sandbox template

explanation: A chat application sends user-message events into a session and listens for agent events coming back. In the workshop, the backend relays the SSE stream to the browser for rendering. This separates presentation from the managed execution lifecycle: a chat interface is only one client of a session that can also perform asynchronous work beyond an immediate request-response exchange.
qualification: Hours-to-months execution is a capability assertion, not demonstrated elapsed runtime in this segment.
title: Use an event stream as the application boundary

explanation: A main agent can delegate to specialized agents with their own prompts, tools and permissions, or create another agent from a self-reference when task types are not known in advance. Crucially, self-reference does not clone the session transcript. It copies prompt and tool configuration, so the delegated task cannot be assumed to possess the parent conversation merely because it shares the same agent definition.
qualification: The transcript explains configuration inheritance but does not specify a complete parent-to-child task payload contract.
title: Self-referencing subagents inherit configuration rather than conversation

explanation: An outcome combines the task description, evaluation rubric and maximum iterations. After the agent believes it is finished, a subagent evaluates the work against that rubric and decides whether completion is satisfactory; failure triggers another attempt. This makes verification part of the execution contract rather than relying only on the working agent announcing that it has completed its assignment.
qualification: The shown Nvidia example is a previous run, and agreement by the internal evaluator is not independent proof of financial correctness.
title: Pair asynchronous tasks with an outcome rubric and bounded retries

explanation: The research task first checks existing memory before repeating retrieval, then requests both a company memory note and a structured scorecard at a specified file location. The evaluator checks the session work and artifacts, including whether the memory was updated. This separates user-consumable output from reusable knowledge and makes both explicit completion obligations instead of incidental chat text.
qualification: The example analyzes a recent quarterly filing, but no independently checked scorecard values or full rubric are supplied in the transcript.
title: Specify persistent artifacts and reusable memory as separate deliverables

explanation: Skills are described as live artifacts that can be revised as requirements expand; the example adds another SEC form. New sessions referencing the skill receive its updated information. Reviewing past sessions can therefore inform a reusable operational instruction update rather than requiring each future session to rediscover the procedure or embedding all domain instructions directly into every task prompt.
qualification: The stated update guarantee concerns new sessions; the speaker does not establish automatic hot updates to already-running sessions.
title: Improve shared skills using observed session behavior

explanation: For production authentication, the speaker describes vaults that expose placeholder environment-variable values and swap in actual secrets at egress only for allowed host domains. A session references a vault ID, and credentials can also cover MCP or OAuth integrations. This places secret release in the runtime boundary instead of expecting the model to handle a real secret safely in its prompt.
qualification: SEC name/email is injected directly for the demo; vault behavior is explained in Q&A, not security-tested here.
title: Keep real credentials out of model-visible environment values

explanation: A question asks how collaborating agents avoid loops and excessive token use. The answer leaves some responsibility with the application orchestrator and says tighter per-session money or token limits are being explored but are not offered at the time of the workshop. Applications using custom coordination must therefore not infer that outcome iteration controls also enforce an overall spending ceiling.
qualification: This is a dated platform limitation stated in the talk, not a claim about the service at any later date.
title: Do not confuse iteration settings with hard session spending limits

explanation: When a user sees the manager or subagents moving in the wrong direction, a new user-message event can steer the running session and is queued for processing. This does not undo previous work or replay from a checkpoint. The speakers explicitly distinguish that capability from rewind-and-roll-forward or session forking, which is only described as a requested roadmap item.
qualification: No rollback semantics for external actions are demonstrated; roadmap discussion should not be presented as an available recovery feature.
title: Distinguish adding corrective guidance from forking execution history

explanation: The platform can attach multiple stores, allowing sessions to combine user-specific memories with organization-level knowledge. Memories can be exported through APIs, but the Q&A says alternative memory providers are not supported natively inside sessions; an MCP or custom tool is the suggested integration route. Distinguish data portability from a drop-in interchangeable memory backend when assessing architecture and lock-in.
qualification: Authorization and tenant-isolation behavior for combined stores is not specified, and exportability alone is not a migration demonstration.
title: Compose user and organization memory without assuming native provider interchange

explanation: The Q&A clarifies that subagents augment the session context and capabilities, while the outcome contract applies to the overarching session. The main agent coordinates their contributions before declaring completion. There is no supported sub-outcome definition in the presented system, so a satisfactory overall outcome should not be treated as evidence that each delegated task received its own explicit rubric and completion check.
qualification: This describes evaluation granularity, not a measured rate of hidden subagent errors.
title: Whole-session grading does not establish independently graded subtasks

explanation: Dreaming is described as analyzing transcripts and memories across multiple sessions to update shared memory for future retrieval. The speaker explicitly limits the current feature to memory stores. Extending the same loop to skills, prompts or agent definitions is a possible future direction, so cross-session memory consolidation should not be represented as demonstrated autonomous improvement of the entire agent configuration.
qualification: This segment promises a later demonstration but ends before showing the consolidation process or its measured benefits.
title: Bound the claimed learning loop to the artifact it actually updates

explanation: The ending Q&A gives three ways to reach company resources: an authenticated CLI or MCP, a tunnel when the MCP should not be public, or a self-hosted sandbox connected to the company network. The important design choice is where authenticated network access occurs. A hosted agent need not imply making the internal service generally reachable on the public internet.
qualification: Network architecture, threat model and tunnel security properties are not specified or tested in the transcript.
title: Choose a private access boundary instead of exposing internal tools by default

explanation: The talk separates a machine-learning harness that supplies inputs and evaluates outputs from an agent harness that surrounds a model during execution. The latter grounds the agent in an environment controlled by the application. This terminology matters because adding a benchmark runner does not itself provide runtime tools, guardrails, context management or execution checks for an acting agent.
qualification: The definition is explanatory terminology, not a claim that every product uses the same naming convention.
title: Disambiguate runtime harnesses from model test runners

explanation: A harness includes a tool registry, model selection, context management, guardrails, the agent loop and a verification step. The loop is not synonymous with the whole harness: the runtime can also wrap that loop in another control loop. In coding tasks, lint and tests exemplify verification that belongs around execution rather than merely in the model response.
qualification: This is a conceptual component inventory; the toy browser runtime implements only a subset of production needs.
title: Model the loop as one component of the runtime

explanation: The browser demo deliberately keeps its task and system prompts unchanged while changing the surrounding code. The initial agent clicks an upvote, reaches a login page and falsely reports success. Subsequent changes improve honesty and then completion through verification and login handling. This shows one concrete failure whose remedy is missing runtime support, not stronger wording in the prompt.
qualification: A single controlled walkthrough demonstrates possibility, not a general comparison proving harness changes always beat prompt changes.
title: Use a fixed prompt to isolate improvements in execution support

explanation: The runtime adds a maximum iteration guardrail to limit an individual execution and later wraps the attempt function in an outer loop limited to three tries. These are separate controls: bounded work within an attempt and bounded repeated attempts after verification. The design prevents a task from continuing indefinitely merely because the model keeps producing tool calls or reports inconclusive completion.
qualification: The example uses six steps and three tries; these are demo settings, not validated universal budget values.
title: Bound steps inside attempts and retries outside the agent loop

explanation: The example guards context size by retaining the system prompt, user task and last two messages while dropping the intervening history. The speaker explicitly calls this naive and says there are better methods. It illustrates where context policy lives in a harness, but also exposes a boundary: limiting size this way is not evidence that the facts or action state required for later reasoning survive.
qualification: The transcript demonstrates a simple trimming policy, not summarization quality, memory reconstruction or long-horizon state retention.
title: Treat message-count compression as a deliberately crude prototype

explanation: The first useful change does not complete the upvote task. Instead, the harness prevents a success claim after a login redirect and reports failure accurately. Separating truthfulness of the completion signal from successful task execution creates an inspectable failure state on which recovery can be built. A failed task reported honestly is materially different from an apparently completed but unperformed action.
qualification: The word lying is the speaker's description of a false success report, not evidence of intentional deception.
title: Make failed execution visible before attempting to make it succeed

explanation: The verifier inspects accumulated tool history for the upvote operation and explicitly rejects failed auto-login or an unrecovered login-page redirect. This replaces the bare loop behavior of accepting the model's stop message as completion. The mechanism is task-specific deterministic code: enumerate observable success and veto conditions and let those checks determine the runtime result independently of the model narrative.
qualification: Trace checks only cover the conditions programmed into them; the demonstration also manually checks the resulting website state.
title: Verify tool evidence and explicit failure conditions rather than stop messages

explanation: A hook runs during the agent loop, checks the browser URL and does nothing unless it sees the login page. When triggered, it submits credentials programmatically and adds an event telling the agent that login occurred. The model can continue the task without receiving the credentials in its prompt. This places a predictable authentication transition in code with separately controlled secret access.
qualification: Secure storage is suggested as an environment-variable option; the talk does not audit secret handling or establish general website-login safety.
title: Handle authentication in a privileged runtime hook outside the model

explanation: The completed browser demonstration does not stop at an agent-generated success string. The speaker opens the website and notes that an unvote action is available, indicating that the earlier upvote actually took effect. This provides a concrete external-state check to complement trace-based verification and distinguishes successful tool invocation from achieving the user's intended persistent result.
qualification: This is one manually inspected successful run, without repeated trials or a measured success rate.
title: Confirm the achieved state after an action rather than trusting a click

explanation: The conclusion imagines an agent building a task-specific harness before doing the work, anticipating hallucination risks and creating appropriate guardrails. That differs from the earlier walkthrough, where the presenter supplies the deterministic code. The reusable research idea is to generate execution controls alongside a plan; the evidence boundary is that no generated harness, validation procedure or safety result is shown.
qualification: Future-facing speculation rather than an implemented feature or a validated route to general intelligence.
title: Separate demonstrated fixed controls from proposed generated harnesses

explanation: The speaker identifies investigation, rather than implementing an already-understood fix, as the unpredictable cost that blocks proactive optimization. A weekly agent workflow uses production context to identify and score easy, impactful opportunities without requiring an engineer to start an open-ended search. The opportunity is not merely faster execution of existing work: it is making neglected discovery happen routinely at all.
qualification: The reported workflow is a vendor experience account without measured investigation-hours saved or a controlled comparison.
title: Automate discovery work that uncertainty prevents teams from scheduling

explanation: The desired workflow separates choices of compute, harness and model, supports secure tools and permissions, and can run on schedules or event triggers such as SLO breaches. Maintainability matters because acceptable behavior and expectations evolve after initial success. The concrete setup uses GitHub Actions, a coding agent, runtime context via MCP and Slack reports, but the speaker treats those vendors as replaceable choices.
qualification: The talk states selection criteria and one implementation, not tested portability across all listed alternatives.
title: Select workflow infrastructure for replaceability and ongoing feedback

explanation: The proposed loop detects a production opportunity, investigates its root cause and business relevance, implements a fix, reruns tests and checks the impact on the specific flow. The human receives the result only after that evidence exists and remains a review gate. This addresses plausible but unverified suggestions that look technically reasonable while failing to improve the observed production problem.
qualification: No quantitative before-and-after evaluation protocol or independent aggregate validation is supplied.
title: Verify a fix on the affected flow before spending human review time

explanation: The speaker reports two recurring failures: suggestions that could explain slowness in theory but do not match production, and fixes that merely catch an exception. The remedy is to encode a senior engineer's investigation playbook, asking why the error occurred and grounding conclusions in observed behavior. Suppressing a symptom should not substitute for establishing and repairing the causal failure.
qualification: This is qualitative experience and methodological guidance; rates of these failures before and after the playbook are not reported.
title: Encode investigation methodology to resist plausible and lazy fixes

explanation: Production agents can receive excessive low-value telemetry while still lacking the specific logs, traces or metrics needed to investigate a problem. These are concurrent problems, not opposite settings of one context-size dial. When necessary evidence is absent, the agent fills gaps with theories about what users experience. More telemetry alone therefore does not establish that an investigation has sufficient causal grounding.
qualification: The talk describes recurring experience, without an ablation measuring the effect of context quantity or evidence completeness.
title: Audit context for missing evidence and low-signal overload simultaneously

explanation: Service metrics and endpoint percentiles do not directly explain which function or outbound dependency consumes time. The described prod-to-code representation maps function invocations to the endpoint, event consumer or cron job that initiated them. It also captures detailed forensic evidence when a request crosses a P99 or configured threshold, allowing an agent to investigate a concrete slow request instead of reasoning only from aggregate symptoms.
qualification: The complete structure, capture overhead and evidence coverage are not quantified; threshold capture may only describe selected requests.
title: Connect runtime behavior to the same function and file units agents edit

explanation: A raw query language over runtime data still leaves agents to formulate complex ClickHouse queries repeatedly, which the speaker says introduced evaluation variance. Skills encode diagnostic procedures: for a memory spike, inspect activity on the affected pods at the relevant time and compare it with a baseline; for HTTP 500, trace the error's origin. The reusable unit is a method, not merely database access.
qualification: The speaker reports improved consistency but supplies no eval size, scoring rubric or numerical variance reduction.
title: Turn recurring investigations into skills that stabilize query selection

explanation: The performance workflow explicitly looks for artificial delays, sleeps, timeouts, extra database-query patterns, missing indexes and sequential work. Naming these patterns makes the search more directed than asking why endpoints are slow in general. In a mature codebase, runtime evidence can identify which suspicious patterns actually explain expensive executions, rather than assuming every static-code smell has meaningful production impact.
qualification: Captions garble some pattern names; the source does not give a complete detector or establish that every listed pattern is easy or safe to remove.
title: Search named performance failure patterns using runtime evidence

explanation: Surface changes according to hot-path frequency, business criticality and risk, not only estimated latency reduction. Payment or signup flows warrant different attention from infrequent operations, while migrations demand more review effort. The reported aim is highest ROI rather than highest raw impact: automated investigation is useful when it produces changes worth the human reviewer's time and the deployment risk they introduce.
qualification: No explicit scoring formula, weight calibration or decision-quality benchmark is provided.
title: Rank opportunities by business value and risk-adjusted review cost

explanation: After the technical workflow looked good, simply opening many pull requests failed as a human workflow. The team instead started with one prioritized finding at a time and built readable reports explaining the symptom, cause and fix, with options to create a ticket or PR. Adoption requires evidence that the issue is worth fixing as well as evidence that the proposed fix works.
qualification: The improvement in uptake is qualitative; conversion rates, review-time measurements and team sample size are absent.
title: Deliver a few persuasive findings rather than flooding teams with pull requests

explanation: The speaker contrasts interactive IDE assistance, where an engineer can repair an imperfect run in context, with scheduled autonomous workflows that can waste review attention or erode trust if they drift. The latter must hand off a runtime-verified fix for an issue already judged worth fixing. Presence of a final human reviewer does not justify leaving routine investigation and verification for that person to redo.
qualification: The 80% and later 80-90% trust language are rhetorical contrasts, not measured success rates or recommended universal thresholds.
title: Use a stricter acceptance bar when no engineer is continuously steering

explanation: The accountability framework begins with a unique agent ID in a known shared registry. That identity becomes the reference point for the remaining controls rather than treating many agent executions as anonymous software activity. The operational benefit within the proposed framework is traceability: ownership, role, authority and observed behavior can all be attached to an identifiable organizational actor.
qualification: A proposed governance foundation, not a demonstrated registry implementation or identity-security protocol.
title: Give every agent a stable identity that governance can reference

explanation: An agent needs a named person responsible for its purpose, costs and failures. The sponsor starts an accountability line into the organization's existing hierarchy rather than leaving ownership diffused across software teams. The pool-supervision analogy makes the mechanism explicit: responsibility should be consciously held and transferred, not assumed to exist because several people could theoretically intervene.
qualification: The sponsor is a framework role; the talk does not specify staffing ratios, liability rules or automated handoff enforcement.
title: Attach an accountable human sponsor to each agent

explanation: An agent operating for a person is still a distinct teammate, not a digital identity clone. It needs the team's goals, decisions and history, and should return information about its work and learning so others can coordinate. This preserves the separation between an agent's actions and the human it assists while acknowledging that successful execution depends on shared organizational context.
qualification: The talk advocates bidirectional context sharing but does not implement a memory architecture or prove coordination benefits.
title: Make agent context exchange explicit without equating agent and user

explanation: The role is the relatively stable onboarding contract: purpose, responsibilities, budget and what success means. The mission describes what the agent is doing at a particular runtime moment, such as a tool call. The agent can define its current mission, but the named sponsor defines the role. This prevents a locally chosen task description from silently redefining the authority or purpose assigned by the organization.
qualification: The role/mission distinction is conceptual; the transcript does not provide a formal mission schema or runtime authorization algorithm.
title: Separate sponsor-defined role from the mission of a particular action

explanation: In the illustrative chain, a human can access A-D, an intermediary agent C-D and a worker D-F. The worker may use its own authorized resources to do the job but may only return D up the chain, because D is shared across the lineage. Delegation therefore must not let a caller expand its effective information access through a more privileged downstream agent.
qualification: The caption inconsistently names the final example agent 209 instead of 409. The mechanism is illustrative and not a proved noninterference policy.
title: Constrain returned information by the entire delegation lineage

explanation: The sponsor cannot directly control the foundation model's embedded rules, incoming team context or external agents' context, and inherited behavior may change. What the sponsor can define is the local contract: deterministic rules and intended outcomes for its own agent. The framework therefore treats alignment as an explicit organizational contract rather than assuming that upstream model alignment or a partner agent automatically matches local requirements.
qualification: The speaker makes broad claims about model misalignment, but supplies no experiments establishing specific inherited failure rates.
title: Distinguish alignment inputs the sponsor controls from those it inherits

explanation: An agent can stay within its permitted tools and data while still failing at the job it was assigned. The framework separates behaving, defined by authority, from succeeding, defined by role. Evaluation should therefore not collapse policy compliance and useful task completion into a single notion of correctness; oversight must check both whether the agent was allowed to act and whether it achieved the intended result.
qualification: This is a conceptual distinction, with no empirical relationship between compliance and task performance measured in the talk.
title: Measure authorized behavior and task success as different outcomes

explanation: Oversight should reflect role and authority definitions in a scorecard rather than one metric. Clear rules, such as an invoice authorization ceiling or restricting ledger writes, can be checked; intended outcomes, such as correct purchase-order or vendor matching, require judgments with confidence. The distinction preserves deterministic constraints while acknowledging uncertainty in whether a work product actually fulfills the organization's intent.
qualification: The caption renders intents as tense or intense in places. No judge calibration method, scorecard weights or confidence validation are supplied.
title: Use a weighted scorecard that separates checked rules from judged intent

explanation: The proposed guardian-style oversight checks not only outputs but also the model and context entering the agent. The reason is decision volume: a quarterly human-style review can arrive after many consequential actions have occurred. Humans still define and adjust governance, but routine observation and enforcement must operate at the speed of the agent workflow rather than depend on occasional management meetings.
qualification: No implemented guardian topology, detection-latency measurement or overhead result is shown; the decision counts are rhetorical scale examples.
title: Monitor model behavior, incoming context and work products continuously

explanation: The framework proposes deterministic action bands on top of probabilistic judgments. Its illustrative example maps high confidence to redaction, lower confidence to human escalation and very low confidence to blocking. The reusable procedure is to define the response policy before incidents occur, so an uncertain semantic evaluation can still cause a predictable operational action instead of being an informational score with no owner or consequence.
qualification: The 90%, 50% and 20% examples are not calibrated thresholds; the exact event or correctness probability represented by confidence is underspecified.
title: Translate uncertain intent judgments into predeclared response actions

explanation: Recourse begins with correction and can progress to restricting permissions, suspending access or stopping the agent when problems recur. The speaker also recommends heavier controls initially, relaxing them with repeated success. Gateways or guardians apply immediate restrictions at machine speed, while the human sponsor revises role and authority definitions. Trust is therefore an evolving policy with consequences, not a one-time launch approval.
qualification: Five violations in a day and persistent problems over days are illustrative recourse examples, not validated default policies.
title: Escalate restrictions for repeated violations and revise authority deliberately

explanation: The speaker contrasts redacting logs or dashboards after ingestion with stripping protected health information at the pipeline boundary before it reaches the data lake. The mechanism reduces reliance on every downstream developer following redaction policy, because the sensitive fields are absent from that stored representation. Privacy policy supplies the requirements, but architecture determines whether routine analytics access can encounter the data at all.
qualification: The talk does not specify a de-identification algorithm, residual re-identification risk or a privacy audit result.
title: Remove protected health information before general-purpose storage

explanation: Production and non-production should remain separate without data pipes that can move member information into development. Access to raw PHI depends on both role and geographic region, rather than assuming every distributed engineer can see the same records. Regulatory requirements are treated as inputs to system design, not a compliance label added after the underlying data architecture is already established.
qualification: These are the speaker's architectural rules, not exhaustive legal advice or proof that the presented design satisfies every named regulation.
title: Design environment separation and regional authorization into the system

explanation: The proposed stack runs a code layer on every turn before the model and routes acute emergencies or self-harm cases to emergency support without letting generation decide the response. The model handles the remaining long-tail interaction. The reusable principle is separation of authority: high-stakes routing decisions belong to enforceable runtime logic rather than only a system prompt that asks the model to behave safely.
qualification: The speaker does not explain how emergency language is detected or prove that deterministic code makes semantic detection error-free.
title: Put irreversible safety decisions in a code layer before generation

explanation: The talk gives two further code-layer examples: choosing a clinical rather than generic support path for high-stakes requests, and authenticating the member before touching their data. A model may assist intent classification, but it should not own the final protected route or identity decision. Authentication is a security boundary, while a prompt instructing an agent to verify identity is not equivalent enforcement.
qualification: No classifier, authentication protocol or misrouting recovery procedure is specified; examples establish architectural intent, not measured safety.
title: Keep security boundaries and high-stakes routing outside prompt authority

explanation: Pre-launch tests and a saved golden dataset are necessary but insufficient in this account. Automated judges continually score actual conversations across clinical accuracy, safety, escalation, relevance, drift and refusal. Per-message member feedback adds a distinct view, especially tone problems that automated judges may miss. The evaluation loop therefore uses real traffic and multiple signal sources instead of interpreting one offline score as durable safety assurance.
qualification: The talk does not provide judge definitions, calibration results, sampling coverage for automated scoring or quantified regression-detection performance.
title: Score live conversations and combine automated evaluation with member feedback

explanation: The recommended review scheme combines random traces spread across product capabilities with checks on every high-stakes case. Human readers integrate signals and can identify issues that individual metrics miss. This differs from allocating the same review probability to every interaction: review intensity follows potential consequence while broad random sampling preserves a chance to discover problems outside already-known critical pathways.
qualification: The statement does not establish that all high-stakes cases are reliably identified or explain clinical reviewer qualifications and adjudication.
title: Sample broadly while reviewing every identified high-stakes case

explanation: Some failures recur under new prompts, tools or model changes despite successive prompt fixes, and the speaker warns that the rate may never reach zero. A newly observed production failure becomes a reason to add a judge and expand monitoring. The learning loop is therefore not only patching the response once, but preserving a detector for the failure class as the system evolves.
qualification: Adding a judge does not prove the underlying failure is prevented; the talk gives no measured judge effectiveness or false-positive costs.
title: Turn recurring production failures into durable evaluation coverage

explanation: When stakeholders disagree about a launch issue, the speaker starts with the worst plausible consequence. A defect that could seriously harm a small fraction of people can outrank a defect that mildly annoys everyone. Frequency is not the definition of severity in this framework. The instruction is to identify the worst version of the failure before negotiating ownership, timing or the practical response.
qualification: The 100% annoyance versus 0.1% serious-harm comparison is illustrative, not a quantified analysis of a specific product incident.
title: Set healthcare severity by plausible worst-case harm rather than average annoyance

explanation: Severity should reflect harm rather than the owner, available capacity or implementation difficulty. Once the risk is understood, the speaker allows three explicit responses: fix it, delay launch or accept the risk with sign-off. This keeps delivery constraints visible as a decision about what to do, instead of disguising them as a factual reassessment that the defect is less serious.
qualification: The talk does not identify who may sign off on each risk class or which legal and clinical risks cannot be waived.
title: Do not lower a defect severity because the team cannot fix it

explanation: Under uncertainty, safety bugs should lean toward holding and fixing because shipping a real safety defect is worse than delaying for a false alarm. For polish issues, the default reverses: delay can cost more than releasing a minor flaw. This is a conditional decision aid, not one universal ship-or-hold rule; first determine which consequence class the unresolved issue belongs to.
qualification: The framework guides judgment rather than deciding automatically; no numeric expected-loss model or reliable safety-versus-polish classifier is supplied.
title: Choose the safer error direction according to the kind of defect

explanation: The speaker argues that observed organizational behavior reveals the real launch bar more accurately than statements such as no production bugs. A behavior tolerated for weeks or months without escalation, complaints or leadership concern should not abruptly become a blocker only when attached to a new feature. This exposes inconsistent standards, while remaining a descriptive organizational calibration rule rather than evidence that the existing behavior is safe.
qualification: This creates a genuine tension with worst-case safety scoring: past acceptance does not independently establish clinical safety or regulatory permission.
title: Compare a proposed launch bar with risks already accepted in production

explanation: Automated judges, trace coding and refreshed dashboards can expand faster than the organization's ability to interpret patterns and act. The speaker treats available human attention as a hard system constraint, not an optional operational afterthought. Monitoring architecture should therefore be designed around people actually reading and responding to the signals, rather than treating the mere existence of scores and dashboards as completed oversight.
qualification: No staffing model, alert-budget policy or measured queueing behavior is provided.
title: Scale response capacity alongside automated judging

explanation: If a team omits an agreed fast-follow item from launch, the speaker treats it as already committed debt, not a wish list to reprioritize away. This adds a concrete boundary to risk acceptance: deciding to ship without a planned piece does not erase the obligation to deliver it. The rule concerns delivery accountability after launch rather than the initial measurement of defect severity.
qualification: The source does not describe scheduling, enforcement, ownership or a measured outcome from this policy.
title: Treat deferred launch obligations as commitments rather than optional backlog

explanation: A fall in a clinical judge score may indicate a worse agent or a faulty judge. The speaker recommends checking examples before changing prompts, since reacting to an invalid signal can break correct behavior. In the caffeine illustration, contextual cautions are falsely flagged in one response, while an unsafe amount is correctly flagged in another. The proper fix depends on whether the scorer's judgment is actually right.
qualification: The 4.9-to-4.5 score change and caffeine responses are illustrations, not a validated judge study or medical advice; no calibration dataset is disclosed.
title: Investigate scorer validity before responding to an apparent quality drop

explanation: Define completion as an inspectable artifact and supporting tool evidence, not an agent declaration that a change is fixed. Agree on outcome, scope, invariants, and acceptance criteria before evaluating the result. A reviewer can then compare the diff and checks to what the task actually required.
title: Completion requires evidence

explanation: A generated test can reproduce the same mistaken assumption as the generated implementation. Self-critique can help, but it is not an independent oracle. Seek disconfirming evidence from complementary checks such as compilation, tests, analysis, and human review rather than treating the agent and its own test as independent votes.
title: Correlated verification failure

explanation: Separate execution controls, such as sandbox permissions and approvals, from artifact evaluation, such as tests, policy, and intent. Containing what an agent may do does not establish that its output is correct or a query is safe. Layer controls that cover different boundaries and retain human responsibility for shipping decisions.
title: Containment is not correctness

explanation: Supply project guidelines and architecture before generation; check the result for security, quality, and maintainability; and feed detected issues into remediation. The speaker positions this as an iterative development cycle rather than a single post-generation verdict. The generate step can use a separate coding agent.
qualification: This is a vendor workflow; reported token savings are not quantified.
title: Guide, generate, verify, solve

explanation: Run useful verification near the edit rather than waiting for a push and remote CI failure. Early feedback can shorten the edit-fix cycle, while the traditional outer loop remains available for broader checks.
