The demonstrated paid hook analyzes edits server-side, whereas users without it can scan later in CI.
qualification: A vendor demonstration does not establish universal time savings or complete coverage.
title: Shift checks into the edit loop

explanation: The example passes a command-line argument into a query assembled with an f-string and then executes it. The scanner traces the source-to-sink flow across files and the agent replaces the query with a parameterized version. A subsequent analysis reports the targeted rule no longer firing, while distinguishing an older issue.
qualification: A small intentionally vulnerable Python project; the captions garble the command-line variable.
title: Trace untrusted input into SQL execution

explanation: A fake secret in the prompt is blocked in the demonstration, but an audience member asks about reading a secret through a script. The speaker acknowledges that the hook primarily operates at particular tool and prompt invocation points and may not run if bypassed. Treat interception as bounded, not a universal secrecy guarantee.
qualification: The specific bypass was discussed, not shown as a successful exploit.
title: Secret hooks have bypass boundaries

explanation: After an agent changes code, an analysis hook can surface whether a finding was already present instead of forcing unrelated old issues into the current fix. In the demonstration the targeted SQL finding disappears and a preexisting issue remains. This distinction makes feedback actionable without claiming the whole file is clean.
qualification: The observation is from the vendor’s deliberately seeded demo, not a general false-positive or recall measurement.
title: Analyze new issues separately from existing debt

explanation: Compare multi-GPU kernels against communication-aware limits and inspect the communication pattern, not only compute throughput. Bulk collective libraries are tuned for large contiguous transfers and may be less flexible for fine-grained communication and fused collectives. The speaker reports many simple baselines below half their communication-aware roofline.
qualification: Results depend on the benchmark and chosen baseline; figures are speaker-reported.
title: Communication-aware kernel baselines

explanation: Choose a transfer mechanism according to message size, processor and register consumption, and need for in-network computation. The speaker contrasts a host-initiated copy engine for large messages, device-initiated tensor memory acceleration for fine-grained overlap, and register instructions that can exploit in-network reductions. None dominates every workload.
qualification: Hardware-specific discussion focuses on NVIDIA systems.
title: Transfer mechanism resource tradeoffs

explanation: Within-processor overlap can specialize different warps for communication and compute when their data patterns align. When inputs or resource requirements do not align, separate processors can instead specialize across computation, communication, and memory. The suitable schedule also depends on how well it traverses the interconnect.
qualification: The examples and measurements are particular to the discussed GPU architectures.
title: Schedule overlap by data alignment

explanation: Build benchmark tasks from an unoptimized reference implementation plus an explicit topology, then ask for an optimized kernel with the same behavior. Cover representative combinations of parallelism dimensions because each produces different communication patterns. The reported benchmark selects 87 problems from real repositories and optimized implementations.
qualification: Task sourcing is intended to improve relevance; it does not prove generated solutions are production-ready.
title: Representative multi-GPU benchmark taxonomy

explanation: Evaluate whether generated kernels are correct separately from whether correct kernels outperform the reference. The talk describes pass-at-K for correctness and fast-one-at-K for correctness combined with at least baseline speed. A system that compiles or passes tests still may not provide an operationally useful speedup.
qualification: Metric wording and exact aggregation follow the speaker’s description; consult the benchmark paper for formal definitions.
title: Separate correctness and performance

explanation: The speaker reports that additional parallel samples increase correct solutions from 28 to 36, while the fast metric plateaus near 31 percent. This illustrates why test-time sampling should be evaluated against the performance objective as well as validity. Compilation and additional attempts alone may not overcome deeper optimization weaknesses.
qualification: These are speaker-reported results for the tested models and benchmark, not a universal scaling law.
title: Sampling plateaus on speed

explanation: When generated kernels fail to achieve strong speedups, inspect collective ordering, data partitioning, transfer mechanisms, and compute-communication scheduling rather than assuming syntax is the only problem. The speaker reports that repair and sampling often get kernels to compile, yet models still struggle with these hardware tradeoffs.
qualification: The claim is based on the authors’ evaluation and error analysis, not proof that models cannot reason.
title: Diagnose reasoning beyond compilation

explanation: A multi-turn agent with local bash access reportedly solved 35 of 87 problems versus 24 for the compared setup, with 26 faster than the reference. The speaker also reports performance plateauing with more time. Tool access and iteration can help, but should be measured under explicit resource budgets.
qualification: This is one model and one simple harness; the transcript does not specify all budget or statistical details.
title: Agent harness increases correctness but saturates

explanation: Define a domain task narrowly enough that a user can evaluate the result, rather than asking one agent to solve an entire industry workflow. The finance example narrows investment opportunities to a market and industry, then ranks stocks using specified parameters. Pharma workflows can similarly be decomposed into pointed questions.
qualification: Speaker guidance based on experience, not a controlled comparison.
title: Scope vertical agents narrowly

explanation: Identify domain-specific data that is not generally available, including failed experiments and explanations of why trades did or did not work. Existing organizational records may contain useful unstructured material. The speaker argues such data can differentiate a vertical system when public research and generic model access are widely shared.
qualification: The ease of structuring data overnight is an optimistic speaker assertion, not demonstrated.
title: Curate unavailable negative data

explanation: Use the domain practitioner’s way of solving the narrow job as a prompt-design starting point: decompose the task into steps and preserve their logical order. Experts can also refine the questions and identify credible sources. This is a mental model for structuring work, not evidence that the agent replaces the practitioner.
title: Encode expert workflow order

explanation: The speaker describes trying to evaluate specialist outputs with an LLM judge when he lacked trading or scientific expertise, then finding jargon could masquerade as value. In such settings use qualified practitioners to judge substantive utility and identify errors, rather than assuming fluent model-generated grading is sufficient.
qualification: This is an anecdote and strong opinion, not a controlled evaluation of all calibrated judges.
title: Generic judges lack domain grounding

explanation: Involve the target practitioner in prompt refinement, source selection, data curation, decomposition, and final judgment. Repeated user interactions generate examples of what works and what fails, which can feed the next iteration. The speaker reports that hiring a pharma expert changed the direction and perceived relevance of their tools.
qualification: The improvement is a qualitative case study without reported comparative metrics.
title: Build a user-expert learning loop

explanation: Inspect observable traces and logs to identify where the application fails, then correct those failure modes before considering more expensive weight changes. The speaker suggests progressing from error analysis toward supervised training or preference-based methods when justified, and notes that changing the underlying model can impose repeated fine-tuning costs.
qualification: Highest ROI is the speaker’s judgment, not a measured universal ranking.
title: Start with trace-based error analysis

explanation: A human-created rubric can let an AI grade outputs at greater scale, while human preferences can train a reward model. The speaker warns that rubric-based rewards may produce an echo chamber. Preserve a feedback path to domain experts and examine failures rather than treating rubric scores as an independent ground truth.
qualification: The talk provides no numerical comparison of rubric quality or echo-chamber frequency.
title: Human rubrics can echo model errors

explanation: In the speaker’s finance and pharma experience, the expert retains the decision and the AI supplies assistance. A trader can use generated candidate theses but chooses which to pursue; a pharma expert chooses among drug candidates. Evaluate time savings and decision support separately from claims of autonomous decision competence.
qualification: The prediction that this arrangement will last a long time is opinion; no time-savings measurements are provided.
title: AI assists rather than owns domain decisions

explanation: Evaluate an agent’s retrieval trajectory against human-labeled files, lines, and symbols needed for a task, separately from whether the final answer appears successful. This exposes whether the agent found relevant context along the way. The talk uses a context benchmark rather than measuring completed coding-task outcomes directly.
qualification: Labeled context is a proxy: alternative valid paths may be penalized and task success is not directly measured.
title: Benchmark context discovery, not just final answer

explanation: The experiment compares an unmodified coding agent, a version limited to 50-line reads, and the same limited-read setup with semantic search. The read window reduces noise from opening huge files, making file, line, and symbol precision easier to interpret. Changes in both tooling and read policy matter when attributing results.
qualification: The baseline differs in read granularity; results do not isolate semantic search against unmodified agent alone.
title: Control read granularity in retrieval comparisons

explanation: Measure both the fraction of retrieved context that is labeled relevant and the fraction of labeled context retrieved. In this test the default agent had better file recall through broad exploration, while windowed reads plus semantic search improved file precision. High precision alone does not guarantee all needed context was found.
qualification: The speaker reports approximately 65% baseline and 87% semantic-condition file precision across 50 tasks.
title: Precision and recall expose exploration tradeoffs

explanation: Use semantic retrieval for behaviorally related code whose terminology differs, and lexical search for explicit identifiers or import chains. The experiment found tasks where each approach won, even though aggregate recall did not show a uniform semantic-search advantage. Combining tools can cover different information needs rather than replacing one unconditionally.
qualification: The task-level pattern is exploratory and specific to the tested repositories and setup.
title: Semantic and lexical retrieval find different evidence

explanation: Chunk, embed, and index a codebase once so agents can reuse a semantic representation across repeated sessions, instead of repeatedly exploring everything with grep. This may reduce repeated search and token use, but introduces indexing and maintenance costs. The talk frames embeddings as cached semantic computation.
qualification: The presentation does not provide a complete cost accounting or index freshness evaluation.
title: Indexing trades upfront work for repeated retrieval

explanation: Adding a semantic-search tool does not ensure an agent knows when or how to use it. The speaker suggests the tested agent was optimized for grep, whereas another product integrates semantic retrieval more deeply. Tool choice and agent instructions are therefore important experimental variables when comparing retrieval outcomes.
qualification: This explanation is the vendor speaker’s hypothesis, not a controlled ablation of training or tool use.
title: Tool availability is not tool competence

explanation: Code comments can give an embedding model and an agent semantic context that raw implementation details may not express. In audience discussion, the speaker recalls better performance in repositories with useful inline documentation. Consider the information carried by each chunk, not merely whether embedding and indexing succeeded.
qualification: Anecdotal observation, not an isolated controlled measurement; comments may also be stale.
title: Inline comments improve semantic context

explanation: The demonstrated search embeds raw code chunks and query text using a code embedding model. During questions, an audience member suggests parent-child or query-like representations to bridge the mismatch between a natural-language query and raw code. The speaker treats those richer representations as possibilities, not as part of this experiment.
qualification: Statements about another vendor’s indexing approach are speculative and should not be presented as verified.
title: Distinguish raw-code embedding from richer indexing

explanation: Manage prompts, tool access, model routing, memory, autonomy, and child-agent behavior as distinct operational control surfaces rather than assuming one feature-enabled boolean covers all changes. The speaker proposes separate controls for these behaviors and a kill switch. Segmentation allows risky changes to be exposed to selected cohorts.
qualification: The talk inconsistently counts six flag types and lists the kill switch while discussing subagents as a separate surface.
title: Flag independent agent behavior surfaces

explanation: Route a new prompt version to a small beta cohort, observe quality and escalation measures, and promote only when the results remain acceptable. Maintain a stable version for other users. This separates deployment from exposure and gives operators a way to contain regressions before they reach the entire population.
qualification: The 5% cohort and suggested thresholds are starting points, not validated universal values.
title: Canary prompts with explicit promotion criteria

explanation: Place an authorization decision before each tool execution, with policies scoped by user, tenant, or risk class. A tool existing in the codebase should not imply that every agent or customer may invoke it. This matters especially for actions that send messages, move money, delete data, or affect compliance.
qualification: A flag is one operational layer; the talk does not establish that flags alone provide complete authorization.
title: Gate tools independently from prompts

explanation: Design an agent-wide and per-tool stop mechanism before incidents occur. The speaker specifies that the flip should propagate quickly, require no deployment, and be checked by in-flight work at its next decision point. Returning a graceful inability-to-act response can preserve user clarity when a tool is disabled.
qualification: Stopping at the next decision point does not undo an already executed external action.
title: Prewire live kill switches

explanation: Resolve flags and enforce tool, model, autonomy, and kill-switch controls on every spawned agent, not merely at the initial entry point. A child that calls models or tools directly can keep operating after its parent is stopped. Middleware coverage therefore needs to include the entire agent tree.
qualification: The runaway-agent scenario shown in the talk is an illustrative simulation, not a measured incident intervention.
title: Child agents must inherit control middleware

explanation: The proposed rollout order is to wire kill switches first, wrap tool calls with flag checks, and default actions to suggestion. Move toward human confirmation as trust grows and make automatic execution opt-in per tool. Only then add prompt variants and monitor the resulting operational signals.
qualification: This is an advocated rollout sequence, not a tested safety guarantee.
title: Roll out autonomy in stages

explanation: Track kill-switch activations, time to mitigation, canary error-rate delta, and flag audit completeness. The speaker suggests investigation and rollback targets and requires recording who changed what and when. Tune thresholds to the risk, traffic, and severity of the specific surface instead of importing defaults uncritically.
qualification: The numerical thresholds are explicitly presented as suggested defaults.
title: Monitor mitigation and auditability

explanation: Test that in-flight turns and child agents actually see flag changes, that cached responses do not defeat a flip, and that segmentation context remains current. Regularly exercise kill switches and assign owners and removal dates to temporary flags. Multiple prompt variants can interact, so test their combinations rather than each in isolation.
qualification: The transcript’s phrase about testing the Cartesian product is caption-garbled but its intent is supported by surrounding context.
title: Test flag propagation and combinations

explanation: Agent behavior may vary in both result and path even for the same request. Inspecting code or one successful run is therefore insufficient for understanding the operational distribution. Collect many traces, including model calls and tool steps, and examine patterns across runs as well as individual examples.
qualification: This is a practical framing, not a measured coverage guarantee.
title: Use trace distributions to understand agent behavior

explanation: Manual trace inspection can reveal specific failures but becomes a bottleneck at high request volumes. An evaluator can apply a defined notion of success to traces and produce a score; a language-model evaluator may also explain failures. This makes systematic triage possible, but depends on the quality of the success definition.
qualification: Preference for an LLM over code is the speaker’s opinion, not comparative evidence.
title: Compress trace review into explicit evaluations

explanation: When individual evaluation failures are too numerous to read, an agent can examine their explanations and group related failures into recurring signals. Those groups suggest where a fix might affect many requests. A cluster represents a triage hypothesis, not necessarily a verified root cause or a representative prevalence estimate.
qualification: The clustering and autonomous improvement loop are a vendor vision; no accuracy evaluation is presented.
title: Group recurring failures before choosing a fix

explanation: HTTP success or absence of error spans does not establish that a tool provided useful results. In the toy-shopping demonstration the agent inspected quality despite successful spans, and the trace summary highlighted empty search results and overly narrow filtering. Reviewing content and task success can uncover faults hidden from infrastructure health signals.
qualification: Reported percentages come from a small, uncontrolled demonstration.
title: Investigate successful status codes for quality failures

explanation: The coding agent discovered a neighboring pre-solved copy and copied its price-filtering solution rather than independently implementing the fix. The resulting working example still illustrates an assisted repair workflow, but it cannot support a clean claim that the agent solved the problem from the traces and original code alone.
qualification: The speaker explicitly acknowledged the contamination during the live demonstration.
title: Guard against solution leakage in coding demonstrations

explanation: Once a trace reveals a consequential failure, add the example to an evaluation dataset or define a corresponding evaluator. Run existing regression evaluations around proposed changes to check behavior already expected to work. The speaker illustrates this with a check against bomb-making instructions, while also stressing that evaluations consume time and money.
qualification: Regression results provide evidence about covered cases, not a guarantee against all behavior changes.
title: Turn detected failure cases into regression checks

explanation: The proposed monitoring workflow finds patterns, creates an issue with trace context, and can open a pull request if a repository is connected. The presenter describes approving or rejecting those pull requests rather than treating every suggestion as automatically safe. This separates failure discovery and patch generation from the decision to accept a change.
qualification: The repository was not connected in the demonstration; the pull-request feature was described, not demonstrated.
title: Keep proposed agent fixes reviewable

explanation: A monitoring agent is itself an AI system and needs its own evaluation and telemetry. The speaker says their product traces its operations and runs an internal suite using language-model judges to assess proposed pull requests. This applies the same feedback-loop idea recursively, but does not explain judge calibration or empirical reliability.
qualification: This is a vendor description without reported evaluation results or judge validation.
title: Evaluate the agent that diagnoses other agents

explanation: Start by specifying the user, current process, measurable pain and desired outcome without preselecting an agent or other architecture. In the illustrative insurance scenario, reviewers face long claim processing times that delay care. A solution-neutral problem statement keeps architectural choices accountable to an actual operational need.
qualification: The claims scenario and figures are illustrative rather than measured deployment outcomes.
title: Define the business problem before the architecture

explanation: Identify data residency, approved vendors, model availability and mandatory human-review rules before choosing a system design. In the hypothetical claims workflow, complex cases require senior physician review and denials require human review. Those constraints cap autonomy regardless of whether a more autonomous agent is technically possible.
qualification: These review rules are assumptions for the example, not universal legal requirements.
title: Let business constraints determine permissible autonomy

explanation: Inventory each required source, where it lives, its format and how often it changes. Process clinical guidelines and policies on appropriate document-update schedules, while refreshing claim history as new decisions arrive. Stale reference information is especially dangerous when the application makes decisions with consequences for care.
qualification: The annual, quarterly and hourly cadences are illustrative assumptions.
title: Set ingestion cadence from source changes and task needs

explanation: For clinical guidelines and policies, semantic search can be complemented by metadata filters or keyword search to capture exact diagnosis and procedure codes. Patient history instead may use an exact patient identifier. Processing also differs: documents may be chunked and embedded, while structured history may require removal of personal information before model use.
qualification: The proposed retrieval choices were not benchmarked in this talk.
title: Match retrieval methods to the structure of each source

explanation: Avoid selecting an autonomous agent merely because it is fashionable or a coding assistant proposes one. Map the actual task flow, choose the simplest design that can satisfy constraints, evaluate it, and add complexity only where observed gaps justify it. The example combines retrieval, predetermined control flow and human review.
qualification: The insurance architecture is a design exercise rather than a production implementation.
title: Start with the simplest architecture and evaluate gaps

explanation: Design feedback into the user workflow rather than adding it after deployment. Medical reviewers can override a recommended decision, record why, and flag irrelevant citations. Together with the output explanation and sources, this feedback can expose whether a recommendation or its supporting evidence needs investigation.
qualification: A reviewer override is an operational signal, not automatically a ground-truth label.
title: Capture reviewer overrides and citation feedback

explanation: Define input and output guardrails, then measure their behavior separately from response quality, business outcomes and system health. For the example, track rejection rate for invalid inputs, missing citations, faithfulness to retrieved material, processing time and per-recommendation cost. A high rejection rate calls for investigation rather than an automatic quality judgment.
qualification: Presence of citations does not itself establish factual correctness or faithfulness.
title: Measure guardrails separately from response quality

explanation: Continue measuring offline evaluation dimensions in production and add operational signals such as reviewer override frequency and review duration. Rising overrides may signal a change worth investigating, while long review times could reflect verbose or confusing output. These are indirect indicators, so interpret them in context rather than equating them with model accuracy.
qualification: The suggested reasons for long review time are hypotheses, not validated causal findings.
title: Monitor workflow proxies alongside offline metrics

explanation: Two changes can pass CI independently and still break the trunk when combined. The speaker describes a merge infrastructure that tests likely combinations in parallel, removes a predicted breaking change from the queue, and admits changes only after relevant combinations pass. This trades additional testing work for safer parallel throughput.
qualification: The presentation does not quantify the combination strategy or its effectiveness.
title: Test interacting changes before trunk merge

explanation: Agents can create changes faster than human-speed build and review queues can process them. Speeding code generation alone shifts waiting time into those queues, especially when failed checks and follow-up edits create further rounds. Capacity planning therefore needs to cover build, testing, repair and review together rather than optimizing only generation speed.
qualification: Reported growth figures describe the speaker’s company and platform, not a representative industry study.
title: Treat CI and review as coupled capacity constraints

explanation: Run checks locally or otherwise earlier when feasible, so defects can be found before centralized CI and downstream review. The speaker argues that earlier repair can benefit from an agent already holding relevant context and can reduce queue pressure. Not every expensive integration or production check can be moved safely.
qualification: Moving expensive checks after merge improves speed but may increase trunk or production risk.
title: Move feasible checks earlier in the development loop

explanation: The team examined compiler churn, improved cache reuse and invalidation behavior, and sharded work. The speaker reports bringing incremental CI from around ten minutes to under one minute after the cold CI was warmed. This distinction matters: the reported improvement does not establish the same latency for cold builds.
qualification: Vendor-team report without independent methodology or cold-build comparison.
title: Reduce incremental CI time with caching and sharding

explanation: Apply explicit approval criteria that allow some routine or low-risk changes to proceed automatically while requiring human approval for sensitive areas such as payments. The proposed policy also separates the agent that created a change from its approver. Unclassified or exceptional changes should be escalated rather than silently treated as low risk.
qualification: The speaker promotes a vendor product; examples are policy proposals, not proof that autonomous approval is safe.
title: Route approvals according to change risk

explanation: Parallel tests can share setup to save time, but an inadequately guarded shared database can cause cross-contamination and intermittent failures under high concurrency. The speaker reports that an automated review caught this problem before merge and suggested and committed a fix. The example demonstrates a specific failure mode rather than general reviewer accuracy.
qualification: The example is a self-reported vendor case study without comparative evaluation.
title: Preserve isolation when parallelizing tests

explanation: CI logs can expire and force-pushes can change the commit a branch points to. Keep durable records tying each reviewed change to its agent and origin, tested commit, saved test report, finding resolution, independent approver and any named override with its reason. A green status alone cannot reconstruct what was checked.
qualification: Specific retention and control requirements depend on the organization and applicable regulation.
title: Persist commit-specific verification and approval evidence

explanation: A passing build does not establish that a change complies with business or regulatory policies. The speaker describes a feature-flag incident affecting driver checks and says changes affecting London later needed traceable controls. Explicit policy checks and records connect a change to the specific obligation, rather than treating compilation as proof of compliance.
qualification: The historical incident is speaker-reported and not independently documented in the transcript.
title: Check policy compliance beyond build success

explanation: Some design questions become comparatively objective when the context is specified, such as alignment or contrast, while aesthetic preferences can produce genuine expert disagreement. Break a broad design evaluation into narrower properties and choose methods appropriate to each property instead of assuming a single universal taste score.
qualification: The degree of objectivity depends on task context; no expert agreement study is reported.
title: Decompose design into assessable and subjective dimensions

explanation: The speaker describes low-quality generated design through three interacting characteristics: repetition, lack of fit to the context, and weakly expressed or interpreted intent. A pet-shop site and a financial-firm site converging on the same design illustrates why similarity can signal a failure to respond to the specific user and purpose.
qualification: These categories are an interpretive framework, not a validated universal definition.
title: Distinguish repetition, poor fit and weak intent

explanation: The team describes mining website features such as color, typography, layout and audience, then training small classifiers to detect individual characteristics. Co-occurrence and frequency of features are used to predict likely generic AI-generated design. Narrow probes offer interpretable components, but their usefulness depends on how sites and labels were sampled.
qualification: The claimed advantage over LLM judges lacks disclosed metrics, dataset construction and baseline details.
title: Combine narrow design-feature probes to detect repetition

explanation: The speaker says the team analyzed over two million websites over roughly a decade and compared them with synthetically generated sites. They observed visual homogenization before generative AI as well as more repetition across contexts in generated designs. A historical baseline prevents attributing every repeated convention to the current generation system.
qualification: Sampling, quantitative estimates and comparison controls are not provided.
title: Compare generated patterns with historical baselines

explanation: Improving base models alone cannot resolve every design-fit problem because the user’s specific intent is expressed during interaction. The speaker argues for application-level mechanisms that help users articulate intent and carry that context into generation and verification. This complements model training rather than replacing it.
qualification: The claim is the speaker’s architectural position, not a controlled comparison.
title: Elicit context and intent at inference time

explanation: The proposed creativity mechanism would provide inspiration to move beyond default, repetitive outputs. The speaker distinguishes this from simply raising model temperature: creative outputs may deliberately depart from a few conventions while maintaining other expectations appropriate to the task. Novelty without contextual fit can be just another failure.
qualification: The creativity API is described as work in progress, without a demonstrated effectiveness measure.
title: Pursue contextual variation rather than random novelty

explanation: A proposed brand workflow extracts specific components from an existing brand URL into structured context an agent can follow and against which an output can be checked. A slide-deck illustration is presented as more faithful when using the extraction. The same specification serves generation and verification, although shared assumptions may also carry through both.
qualification: The visual comparison is not fully observable in captions and no blinded evaluation is reported.
title: Use structured brand context for generation and checks

explanation: For users without an existing brand, the speaker proposes retrieving a pre-created coherent brand system matching a desired mood, such as dreamy, instead of generating all stylistic choices independently at request time. The intended benefit is fit and internal coherence; the approach still needs to match the user’s actual context.
qualification: This is a proposed product capability, not a measured experiment.
title: Retrieve a cohesive style system when the user lacks one

explanation: A single run can hide changes in an agent’s verdict for the same input. Repeat runs and compare the semantic decisions, not merely wording, to estimate the range and average of observed behavior. This matters operationally when a security alert alternates between benign and suspicious, undermining user trust.
qualification: Repeated runs reveal variability but agreement alone does not establish correctness.
title: Repeat evaluations to expose semantic instability

explanation: The speaker observes that some flip-flopping cases lie near a classification boundary where even experts may disagree. For a borderline hotel review or a failed login attempt, the right label can depend on customer policy and missing information. Clarifying the intended decision rule may be more useful than treating every disagreement as a model defect.
qualification: Not all inconsistent outputs necessarily arise from ambiguity; the talk does not establish a universal cause.
title: Inspect disagreement near ambiguous decision boundaries

explanation: Run several models or repeat the same model, then prioritize items with conflicting verdicts for human labeling and investigation. The speaker favors disagreement over model-reported confidence based on their experience, because confident answers can still be wrong. Review can clarify labels or identify missing features before updating the system.
qualification: This selection strategy can miss consistently wrong outputs; the talk gives no comparative selection benchmark.
title: Use repeated or committee disagreement to select review cases

explanation: When review reveals a general decision rule, record the rule in a knowledge base for the agent to consult. The speaker illustrates customer-specific distinctions between attempted and successful login attacks and between actionable and non-actionable hotel feedback. Such rules make policy explicit and can improve consistent labeling by both humans and agents.
qualification: The particular benign-versus-malicious choices are customer-specific examples, not general security guidance.
title: Store clarified customer rules as semantic memory

explanation: Instead of immediately distilling a general rule, retrieve a similar previously labeled case and use its earlier decision as a reference. This can help handle recurring security-alert patterns with less additional human intervention. It is weaker when no suitable precedent exists or when the retrieved example is not actually comparable.
qualification: The talk does not specify similarity thresholds or methods for verifying a precedent.
title: Use past labeled cases as episodic references

explanation: The proposed loop uses episodic memory to address recurring situations, then sends unresolved cases or those without useful references to human reviewers. Reviewers distill generalizable policy into semantic memory for future decisions. These components complement one another, allocating scarce review attention to cases that remain ambiguous after precedent retrieval.
qualification: The allocation assumes retrieval and escalation correctly identify cases needing attention.
title: Combine episodic recall with semantic rules and human review

explanation: The speaker reports running 93 real cybersecurity alerts three times each: about a quarter initially flipped verdicts, episodic memory made approximately 15 percentage points consistent, and about 10% remained inconsistent. Human review is proposed for the remainder. The result concerns consistency on a small sample, not an independently established accuracy improvement.
qualification: The captions do not provide a control design, uncertainty intervals, or definitive accuracy labels.
title: Report consistency gains with the sample and residual

explanation: The proposed active-learning loop differs from traditional retraining by incorporating clarified rules and relevant precedents into an agent’s memory. The speaker presents this as a lighter-weight way to iterate when fine-tuning is costly, while acknowledging retraining remains an option. The choice depends on whether the missing behavior is accessible through retrieved context.
qualification: No cost, latency, or quality comparison with fine-tuning is provided.
title: Consider memory updates before expensive retraining

explanation: A passing test suite and a clean diff can miss interactions with older behavior. The ticket-transfer example permits the original buyer to cancel a transferred ticket because cancellation logic lives in another file. Review therefore needs repository context and scenarios covering the interaction, not merely the added lines.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Check new behavior against existing code

explanation: Static analysis can trace security flaws across files, while a contextual reviewer can compare changes to feature descriptions and existing business logic. The presenters frame the two layers as complementary, not substitutes, because they identify different classes of mistakes. The source supplies this as a practical observation in its own setting, not as proof that the approach works reliably in every environment.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Combine deterministic analysis with intent-aware review

explanation: A technically valid change may violate a business promise that exists only in documentation or a team member’s head. In the sample ticketing service, a per-ticket fee conflicts with an all-in advertised price rule; supplying that rule enables the reviewer to flag the mismatch. The source supplies this as a practical observation in its own setting, not as proof that the approach works reliably in every environment.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Supply business rules absent from code

explanation: Repository rules can activate when specific pull-request criteria are met. The pricing example inspects customer-facing fields when pricing files change and reports whether they include all fees, turning an implicit convention into a repeatable review step. The source supplies this as a practical observation in its own setting, not as proof that the approach works reliably in every environment.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Trigger targeted review rules on changed files

explanation: The presenters argue that a false review finding costs more than attention: an attempted automated fix consumes tokens and may introduce a change that was never needed. This makes signal quality important when review findings can trigger autonomous edits. The source supplies this as a practical observation in its own setting, not as proof that the approach works reliably in every environment.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Account for the downstream cost of false positives

explanation: A ticket-scanning refactor fails a test because a used ticket can be scanned again. The demonstration reads the failure in CI and describes an agent applying a fix and rerunning verification, with a required passing status check before automatic merge. The source supplies this as a practical observation in its own setting, not as proof that the approach works reliably in every environment.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Inspect failing CI and revalidate proposed fixes

explanation: The workshop enables automatic application and merge separately, with required CI checks and repository-level selection. The presenter associates fuller automation with repositories having extensive guardrails and sophisticated pipelines; the demo does not establish that passing CI guarantees correctness. The source supplies this as a practical observation in its own setting, not as proof that the approach works reliably in every environment.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Match automation settings to repository guardrails

explanation: Two independently passing pull requests may fail when combined, and a change that merges cleanly in one repository can break another. Cross-PR and cross-repository analysis are presented as additional review surfaces for concurrent development. The source supplies this as a practical observation in its own setting, not as proof that the approach works reliably in every environment.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Review changes across repositories and concurrent PRs

explanation: The speaker argues that generator and validator should not be assumed interchangeable. His rationale is that model vulnerability detection is variable across runs and misses issues found by deterministic checks, so security should use independent verification rather than trust a generation model to certify itself.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Separate code generation from security validation

explanation: The vendor describes running models five times on the same vulnerabilities and reports only 50% found consistently across runs, 75% of issues found versus deterministic checks, and 40% F1. The transcript lacks the benchmark construction and denominators needed to generalize these figures. The source supplies this as a practical observation in its own setting, not as proof that the approach works reliably in every environment.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Measure repeatability and coverage of vulnerability detection

explanation: Security risks are not limited to generated code. The speaker identifies poisoned skills and MCP servers alongside unexpected behavior, including an agent copying personally identifying data into an untrusted database. Effective inspection needs visibility into dependencies, tools and actions as well as outputs. The source supplies this as a practical observation in its own setting, not as proof that the approach works reliably in every environment.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Inspect agent environment, outputs and behavior

explanation: The speaker reports that different models performed differently on personal-information extraction and decision override attacks. This suggests selecting and controlling models against the actual failure modes of a task, rather than assigning each model one universal security score. The source supplies this as a practical observation in its own setting, not as proof that the approach works reliably in every environment.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Evaluate model security by attack and failure type

explanation: The speaker says discovery across customer repositories revealed more agentic components than models, and stresses mapping the full landscape before judging risk. The reusable point is that tools and agents can create risk at layers invisible to a model-only inventory. The source supplies this as a practical observation in its own setting, not as proof that the approach works reliably in every environment.
qualification: Reported or proposed in the source; broader effectiveness is not independently established.
title: Inventory agentic components before governance

explanation: In a recorded QR-code dependency demonstration, both candidate packages have no active CVEs, but one is maintained and the other is not. The presenter prefers maintenance because future fixes may arrive sooner, distinguishing current known vulnerability status from ongoing remediation capacity. explanation: The proposed organizational loop groups similar agent runs, distills a skill, and checks for issues including prompt injection and personal information before putting it into a shared library. A gateway then serves that knowledge to other clients. The proposed loop shares procedural knowledge across agents, rather than changing the underlying model weights.
qualification: The speaker does not specify detection accuracy, approval policy, or protection against incorrect procedural content.
title: Screen distilled skills before organization-wide distribution

explanation: The speaker argues that a strong model’s discovered operational knowledge can be saved as reusable playbooks rather than lost when a session ends or a model is deprecated. Such a library can retain organization-specific procedures for later agents. The proposed loop shares procedural knowledge across agents, rather than changing the underlying model weights.
qualification: Durability depends on ongoing maintenance and compatibility; continued correctness is not established by persistence alone.
title: Persist discovered procedures independently of model availability

explanation: Before exposing users, gate a multi-turn agent on an offline suite with explicit criteria. Once deployed, collect execution traces, grade production interactions, and have humans analyze errors and return actionable findings to the development team. The two stages address different risks and should not be conflated.
qualification: The speakers describe their support-agent workflow, not proof that a particular threshold guarantees safety.
title: Gate launches offline and monitor real traces online

explanation: Define a simulated user by intent, relevant world state and a behavioral persona, then let a user model interact with the agent across turns. Supplement synthetic examples with samples of actual production interactions and mutations covering golden paths and edge cases, rather than generating a set of generic queries alone.
qualification: Representative production coverage remains a challenge; simulations are proxies.
title: Build simulated conversations around intent, state, and persona

explanation: A helpful assistant acting as a simulated customer can provide patient, complete explanations unlike frustrated real users. Lyft saw an initially greater-than-90-percent pass rate and made the simulator more realistic by fine-tuning on user utterances and defining personas; the reported score subsequently fell, revealing a harder test.
qualification: A lower score alone does not establish simulator validity; the transcript does not quantify downstream predictive accuracy.
title: Test whether simulated users are unrealistically cooperative

explanation: Complement language-model grading with executable checks for agent actions whose expected outcomes are unambiguous. For a support scenario requiring a concession, compare the actual tool calls with the expected concession outcome. This separates a concrete action failure from more subjective assessments of the interaction. The example concerns an expected concession and does not imply every task can be reduced to tool-call matching.
qualification: The example concerns an expected concession and does not imply every task can be reduced to tool-call matching.
title: Check consequential tool actions with deterministic assertions

explanation: Work with domain experts to define task-specific pass and fail criteria linked to business outcomes. Lyft’s education rubric treats excessive repeated education and premature escalation as distinct failures. Binary outcomes make calibration and error analysis easier than a generic helpfulness number that does not indicate what to fix.
qualification: Binary framing is the speakers’ recommendation for their tasks; richer or multidimensional outcomes may require other approaches.
title: Replace generic scores with actionable success criteria

explanation: Treat each binary judge as a classifier: hand-label approximately one hundred examples, reserve separate examples for few-shot prompting, prompt iteration, and final validation, and report precision and recall against human labels. Keeping the test split out of prompt refinement helps reveal overfitting to development examples.
qualification: The approximate sample size is suggested practice, not a statistical guarantee; label quality is not independently demonstrated.
title: Validate a binary judge on held-out human labels

explanation: Evaluation criteria are discovered and refined while inspecting examples, so quality definitions can change as new model behaviors appear. Co-develop the evaluator and the model rather than assuming the initial rubric is complete; after criteria change, validate the judge against labels reflecting the updated definition.
qualification: Evolving criteria can complicate comparisons over time; the speakers do not specify a versioning protocol.
title: Revise rubrics as real examples expose criteria drift

explanation: Run error analysis as a recurring loop: inspect raw traces, pinpoint concrete failure modes, retain metrics that change decisions and correspond to functional or business requirements, and then revisit the premise. A weekly or biweekly cadence is offered as an example rather than treating review as a one-time audit.
qualification: Cadence and selection depend on the application; no comparative experiment is reported.
title: Use recurring trace review to select decision-changing metrics

explanation: Add confidence intervals, calibration and appropriate sampling when interpreting reported evaluation results. A small apparent difference between evaluators on a sample of fifty traces may be noise, so reserve especially careful analysis for shipping decisions and leadership reporting. Larger effects and paired designs can reduce sample demands.
qualification: The numeric example is illustrative and the caption contains a garbled statement of the difference; no power calculation is given.
title: Reserve statistical rigor for consequential comparisons

explanation: Replace scattered notebooks and scripts with a standardized evaluation harness that lets different contributors define tasks, datasets, personas, model adapters and evaluators. The speakers envision reusable configuration and repeated runs at local development, pre-commit and CI gates, with parallel execution for large suites. The talk explicitly describes the harness as a planned investment; current scripts are scattered and not repeatable.
qualification: The talk explicitly describes the harness as a planned investment; current scripts are scattered and not repeatable.
title: Standardize repeated evaluations through reusable configurations

explanation: Rather than assume one small model replaces a general frontier model on every request, divide a workload into task slices, select candidate open models for each slice, evaluate them, and adapt them as needed. The resulting system may use a fleet of models rather than a single model endpoint.
qualification: The claimed frontier-level performance depends on the task and is not established by a controlled quality comparison here.
title: Evaluate specialized small models by task slice

explanation: Open inference servers are not necessarily tuned for the precise combination of model, hardware and request distribution being deployed. Run parameter sweeps and tune for the actual traffic rather than assuming default settings yield high performance. The speaker describes this as an ongoing research effort rather than a quick installation.
qualification: Specific configurations and reproducible sweep results are not supplied in the transcript.
title: Tune serving stacks for model, hardware, and traffic

explanation: For fleets serving many small, fast requests, the speaker proposes a gateway that annotates requests and places them on a centralized queue. Workers pull requests and form batches themselves rather than relying on a top-down router with stale worker-state information, which he says can leave GPUs underutilized.
qualification: The reported utilization comparison is vendor experience; workload and benchmark settings are not fully described.
title: Let workers pull and form batches from a shared queue

explanation: The described gateway accepts binary multimodal payloads through a common API and moves larger payload pieces into cloud storage while requests wait, preventing the queue from being clogged. It should parse and annotate only enough to route work, since expensive gateway processing itself can serialize and bottleneck requests.
qualification: This is an architecture description, not a controlled comparison of serialization formats.
title: Keep inference gateways lightweight and large payloads off queue

explanation: A worker cannot always know the ideal batch size before pulling requests from a shared queue. Returning excess items across the network adds latency, so the described multi-GPU-machine design adds local queue coordination that lets colocated workers negotiate without incurring that network round trip. The speaker does not specify scheduling correctness, fairness or measured latency for this specific optimization.
qualification: The speaker does not specify scheduling correctness, fairness or measured latency for this specific optimization.
title: Use local coordination when batch-size prediction is uncertain

explanation: Increase offered request load while tracking both achieved throughput and latency. The knee is the point where additional offered traffic stops producing proportional throughput and latency begins to climb, indicating saturation. It provides a more meaningful operating reference than quoting maximum throughput without its latency behavior.
qualification: The exact threshold for acceptable latency still depends on the service and workload.
title: Benchmark serving at the throughput–latency knee

explanation: The speaker contrasts optimized PyTorch workers with a smaller statically linked alternative whose image is much smaller and could reduce cold-start transfer time. Their alternative runtime had not yet approached PyTorch performance, so deployment choices must consider startup costs alongside steady-state inference throughput. Names of runtimes are imperfectly transcribed; image sizes and performance are speaker estimates.
qualification: Names of runtimes are imperfectly transcribed; image sizes and performance are speaker estimates.
title: Balance runtime speed against image size and cold start

explanation: For small models, a dedicated always-warm worker pool per model can waste capacity. The speaker suggests packing multiple models on one GPU while combining pinned models with lazy loading and eviction driven by memory pressure. This makes model residency a scheduling choice rather than a fixed pool assumption.
qualification: The presentation ran out of time and gives no detailed policy, measurements or failure analysis.
title: Combine pinned models with lazy loading under memory pressure

explanation: Synthetic-data and annotation generation can be candidates for locally served task-specific models when the work is controlled and output quality can be inspected. Evaluate the generated labels and the resulting downstream task before substituting an inexpensive model; low serving cost alone does not establish useful annotation quality.
qualification: This is the speaker’s suggested use case, not an evaluation of synthetic label accuracy.
title: Consider local specialized models for controlled annotation jobs

explanation: An automated research workflow reportedly produced a low-cost adapter that improved retrieval on a German legal-text task by 18 percent. This illustrates why specialized adaptation may be worth testing for a narrow retrieval workload, while preserving the distinction between a proof of concept and general performance claims.
qualification: The transcript does not specify the retrieval metric, dataset, baseline, uncertainty or evaluation protocol.
title: Treat low-cost adaptation improvements as task-specific evidence

explanation: Item response theory models the probability of a correct answer as a function of a latent model ability and item parameters. The difficulty parameter locates the midpoint of an item curve, while discrimination describes its slope. The resulting estimate weights item responses according to the fitted model instead of merely counting correct answers.
qualification: The single latent ability is a modeling assumption; the speaker proposes multidimensional models as future work.
title: Model item difficulty and discrimination, not only raw accuracy

explanation: Fit item curves using response data, then combine the likelihood contribution of observed answers to estimate a model’s latent ability and an interval around it. Different items contribute differently according to their estimated properties. The speaker presents this as a richer benchmark analysis than a single uncalibrated raw count.
qualification: The transcript does not provide estimation code or establish calibration of the stated intervals.
title: Combine item response curves into an ability distribution

explanation: Flag questions with significantly negative discrimination, where stronger models under the fitted scale tend to answer incorrectly. Inspect the wording and gold answer before removing or repairing an item. In one illustrated question, the benchmark answer counted passengers plus crew even though the question requested passengers only.
qualification: The presenter also uses another LLM to inspect an item; its answer is not independent proof of a labeling error.
title: Investigate negatively discriminating benchmark items

explanation: Order items by estimated discrimination and evaluate how many are needed to reproduce the original model ranking. In one speaker-reported dataset, about 97 of 484 items reached a 99 percent ranking-correlation target; randomly selected items performed worse. Check the subset against the original ranking before relying on it.
qualification: The speaker notes this does not hold for every benchmark and cites GPQA as a counterexample.
title: Shorten benchmarks by testing informative items first

explanation: Compare each model’s actual response with the probability predicted by the item response model. An unexpectedly correct or incorrect answer is a residual worth investigating, and repeated samples of the same question can help distinguish unstable behavior from a persistent pattern. Residual structure can suggest inference or quantization issues.
qualification: A surprising response by itself does not prove contamination, overfitting, or an infrastructure defect.
title: Use item residuals to locate unexpected responses

explanation: Keep a representative anchor set common across organizations and expose each organization to a different set of particularly hard fingerprint items. Later compare residuals on these sets for new models: unusually high performance on one organization’s exposed items can trigger investigation of possible leakage or training contamination.
qualification: The illustrated leakage analysis uses synthetic data, and the speaker says the technique is not bulletproof.
title: Use hard organization-specific items as leakage fingerprints

explanation: Partition models into groups such as open- and closed-weight systems, fit an item response curve for each group, and inspect items with gaps at the same estimated ability. Clusters of such items can suggest systematic differences in behavior and help focus further investigation of the benchmark.
qualification: The presenter does not reveal the flagged items or establish why group differences occurred.
title: Compare item curves across model groups

explanation: Correlate models’ item residual vectors and visualize their similarity to look for shared patterns of mistakes. The speaker observes clusters involving model families and distillations and proposes this as a way to investigate potential model relationships, including unauthorized distillation, beyond aggregate benchmark scores. Shared residual patterns are suggestive rather than proof of ancestry or unauthorized distillation; examples lack validation detail.
qualification: Shared residual patterns are suggestive rather than proof of ancestry or unauthorized distillation; examples lack validation detail.
title: Explore model relationships through response residuals

explanation: A one-dimensional item response model compresses performance into a single latent scale even though different tasks may require different skills. The speaker proposes multidimensional and hierarchical models and combining benchmarks as future directions that might expose separate skill levels and improve estimation across evaluations. These extensions are research directions, not demonstrated results in this talk.
qualification: These extensions are research directions, not demonstrated results in this talk.
title: Treat a single ability scale as a simplifying assumption

explanation: An agent can both consume a product directly through documentation and APIs and recommend it to a human or install it in a workflow. Evaluate these paths separately: successful discovery does not establish usability, and an agent-friendly interface does not ensure the product will be recommended.
qualification: The speaker presents an advocacy framework, not measured evidence that agents always make purchasing decisions.
title: Evaluate agents as users and recommenders of tools

explanation: Construct tasks reflecting the software development lifecycle, run agents both with and without a candidate tool, and inspect traces to understand not only whether the tool changes outcomes but where the agent experiences friction. The speaker describes hundreds of tasks and thousands of traces from her code-navigation benchmark.
qualification: No effect size or detailed experimental controls are reported in this passage.
title: Compare agent work with and without the tool

explanation: A coding agent attempted a familiar parameter name instead of the tool’s actual name, failed, and recovered because the error message explained the problem. The recovery was useful but consumed an entire turn. Inspect such traces and clarify the interface so the failure need not occur repeatedly.
qualification: The speaker says the exact parameter names approximately; the lesson concerns the mismatch and recovery rather than a specific API.
title: Use trace failures to repair tool-interface expectations

explanation: The speaker tested product recommendation prompts and found the product mentioned around 65 percent of the time in explicitly comparative shopping prompts but not in a pain-focused scenario. Design discovery evaluations around realistic user needs as well as direct product searches, because prompt distribution can change the apparent result.
qualification: A small pilot is described without full sample sizes, uncertainty, or a reproducible prompt distribution.
title: Measure recommendations across user-intent prompt types

explanation: When agents fail to connect a user’s pain to a relevant product, hypothesize that the published messaging does not clearly explain the use case. Update the content and then measure whether agents using web search change their recommendations, distinguishing retrieval-time information from claims about retraining model weights.
qualification: The content campaign is described as planned; no causal lift is reported.
title: Test whether updated content changes agent recommendations

explanation: A newer model in the speaker’s pilot recommended an older product even more often than the older model. This illustrates why model upgrades alone do not guarantee current product information; test versions and retrieval behavior, and provide current authoritative sources with provenance for agent-facing content.
qualification: The proposed explanation of compounding old model-generated content is speculative, not established by the pilot.
title: Audit stale product references across agent versions

explanation: Discoverability in registries is only one stage of adoption. The speaker argues that agents also need a practical path from discovery through setup and use, and that processes requiring multiple sales interactions may obstruct that path. Evaluate agent and human onboarding as a connected experience rather than a recommendation score alone.
qualification: This is a product-design argument; no controlled onboarding experiment is presented.
title: Measure friction from discovery to actual tool use

explanation: Divide responsibility across engineering, product and marketing: instrument and evaluate agent-facing interfaces, turn observed traces into experience rubrics and product changes, and separately assess how users discover the product. Ownership can be mixed across people depending on the organization rather than imposed as one fixed job title.
qualification: The proposed organization is a framework, not an empirically validated team structure.
title: Route agent experience findings to engineering and product

explanation: When people bring agents into developer communities, the agents may record or process conversations that other participants regard as human discussion. Community builders should consider the privacy and data implications while retaining a place for human connection, rather than treating machine-readable interaction as the only requirement.
qualification: The speaker raises a concern but does not provide a specific privacy control or legal analysis.
title: Account for privacy when agents enter human communities

explanation: A prompt change reportedly made an agent run 28 percent cheaper while the agent still failed to use the tool that the experiment sought to assess. Identify the decision and target behavior first; cost changes can motivate further investigation but do not establish that the intended tool-use problem was solved.
qualification: The speaker notes that cost variance still needed investigation; the observed change is not a verified causal saving.
title: Do not confuse an incidental metric gain with task success

explanation: The speaker describes a third-party coding benchmark where changing the harness reversed the relative ordering of two models, with a reported large effectiveness difference. Test the combination of model, tools, prompt and runtime that resembles the intended deployment instead of choosing a model from a leaderboard alone.
qualification: This is a speaker-reported third-party result on roughly 63 tasks; the underlying study and controls are not detailed.
title: Evaluate the model and harness as a configuration

explanation: Public benchmarks provide a standardized reference for the model landscape, but an application evaluation should measure the actual decision and deployment configuration. Use public scores to shortlist candidates, then compare them on relevant internal workloads rather than assuming a coding benchmark predicts performance on unrelated legal work.
qualification: Public benchmarks can still be directly relevant where the deployed workload matches their task and conditions.
title: Use public benchmarks to shortlist, not certify deployments

explanation: Cluster representative tasks into workload families, such as code understanding and bug fixing, and consider multiple runs because agent outcomes vary. Plan comparisons around the variables that may interact, including model and harness, instead of attributing every observed difference to one component without a suitable design.
qualification: The talk gives no required number of repeats or specific experimental design.
title: Cover task families and repeat nondeterministic runs

explanation: Debug a tool-using agent by checking the available context first, then whether the tool was called, what it returned, and whether the final task outcome changed. Track non-use and failed attempts as well as successful calls: a tool can be invoked without its information being used effectively.
qualification: This is a diagnostic workflow, not a guarantee that traces alone establish causality.
title: Trace tool availability, calls, returned values, and outcomes

explanation: The speaker describes a code search that returned 295 files when only six were needed. Recall alone could appear ideal if all relevant material was retrieved, while the volume of irrelevant results imposed a different cost. Choose precision, recall or a combined score according to the actual task objective.
qualification: The example is illustrative; the transcript does not provide the full relevance labels or a numerical F1.
title: Select retrieval metrics for the information burden

explanation: In the speaker’s software-factory experiment an agent noticed that something was wrong, but no mechanism enforced a stop. Build an independent gate that actually blocks unsafe progression and define when the issue escalates to a person; merely emitting a warning or an agent judgment is not an enforcement mechanism.
qualification: The example describes an experimental workflow and does not establish which controls fit every risk level.
title: Separate detection from stopping and escalation

explanation: Estimate how many alerts will reach domain experts when setting a judge threshold and human-review policy. The speaker cites an example in which a one-percent false-alarm rate produces ten thousand reviews, illustrating that even seemingly small error rates can overwhelm operations at high volume. The denominator and full confusion matrix are not given, so the example should not be generalized numerically.
qualification: The denominator and full confusion matrix are not given, so the example should not be generalized numerically.
title: Budget review capacity for false alarms at scale

explanation: For security-sensitive evaluations, consider whether the retained trace can be trusted and compare it with an independently collected record of activity. The speaker recounts a third-party security experiment where a hash-check setup missed seeded issues while a separate traffic and change history detected them. The third-party experiment is summarized briefly; the transcript does not explain enough to reproduce its mechanism.
qualification: The third-party experiment is summarized briefly; the transcript does not explain enough to reproduce its mechanism.
title: Verify sensitive audit records independently of agent traces

explanation: Classify real production interactions into task families and use them to build representative offline comparisons. After deployment, continue measuring the system in its real environment; shadow evaluation may reduce exposure for higher-blast-radius changes. Offline proxies are useful but do not replace evidence of live behavior.
qualification: The speaker describes ongoing work, not a quantified production validation study.
title: Refresh realistic workload proxies with production observations

explanation: The speaker distinguishes an oracle who directly assesses and changes an application, an evaluator who defines and collects quality measures for engineers, and an architect who designs systems to learn and improve. These are organizational roles, not claims that every team needs three separate hires.
title: Three roles for incorporating expert judgment

explanation: When meaningful objective measurement is unavailable and taste dominates, consider an oracle. When measures exist and manual engineering iteration suffices, an evaluator can organize the measurement loop. If manual iteration is too slow and suitable automation exists, an architect approach may become useful as the system scales.
title: Choose the role by measurability and iteration speed

explanation: The Granola example describes a writer reviewing meeting notes and directly improving prompts after extensive user research. The speaker argues that one principal oracle can remain useful when the product has a concentrated output and no objectively perfect note. The company also uses evals and internal prompt tooling.
qualification: Speaker-reported account; see source limitations.
title: One oracle can own a subjective core output

explanation: Tandem reportedly moved from one medical doctor reviewing notes and updating prompts to multiple clinicians handling subsets. Different specialties, geographies and note types required many prompt variations. This decentralized oracle pattern trades single-person simplicity for local expertise and customization; it is presented as a company case rather than comparative evidence.
qualification: Speaker-reported account; see source limitations.
title: Distribute review and prompt ownership across specialties

explanation: At Anterior, the speaker moved from reviewing and changing the product personally to defining failure modes and metrics, building a review dashboard, and hiring clinicians. The resulting information supported engineers making changes. Later variation in policy interpretation made manual fixes too slow and motivated an architect approach.
qualification: Speaker-reported account; see source limitations.
title: Turn prior authorization review into an evaluation system

explanation: Relevant expertise means direct experience with the particular work, not just a broad professional credential. For example, a doctor may not know medical coding or its distinctive failures. Prompting and content engineering can be helpful adjacent skills, but the speaker considers them more learnable than domain insight.
title: Hire expertise matched to the exact workflow

explanation: The speaker advocates one principal domain expert accountable for AI quality and empowered to participate in decisions, rather than two advisory experts with ambiguous authority. He describes slow progress and expert departures at one organization, while acknowledging that the reasons for those departures are his interpretation.
title: Assign accountable expert ownership

explanation: A domain expert who can grow into measurement and systems design may preserve valuable knowledge gained from reviewing real failures. Hire for breadth where practical, but pair the expert with specialists such as a statistician when needed. The role should evolve only if product scale and measurement conditions warrant it.
title: Pair domain expertise with complementary skills

explanation: A benchmark item should be well posed, verifiable and tractable for other experts, not merely accepted by its author. The speaker highlights GPQA’s author, reviewer, adjudicator and revision process, including agreement-linked incentives, as a way to scrutinize demanding tasks that are hard for any single specialist to judge.
title: Adversarial multi-expert review improves task quality

explanation: Build a taxonomy of the target domain and deliberately allocate tasks across it. Depending on the evaluation goal, the distribution may mirror observed production traffic or overrepresent rare but consequential failures. These are different design objectives, so the chosen mix should reflect the decision the benchmark is meant to inform.
title: Design the benchmark distribution intentionally

explanation: A useful frontier benchmark needs tasks that current systems cannot all solve, while remaining solvable enough to discriminate capability. The speaker cites ARC-style human-solvable tasks with low model scores as an example of headroom. Claims about the benchmark’s relationship to broader reasoning progress are his interpretation.
title: Preserve difficulty and headroom

explanation: A benchmark should measure dimensions relevant to deployment rather than reducing everything to end-task accuracy. The speaker cites a simulated travel agent that books the requested flight but violates fare-class policy: successful completion still fails the constraint. Cost, latency, intermediate steps and tool use may also matter depending on the target.
title: Measure policy constraints alongside task success

explanation: A benchmark can state a research hypothesis about which capabilities will become important, not just rank current models. Terminal-oriented tasks exemplify the speaker’s bet that the command line is a general-purpose interface for agents. Whether such a benchmark actually drives adoption is an interpretation rather than an experimentally established causal result.
title: Build benchmarks around an explicit capability thesis

explanation: Make a benchmark straightforward to run, extend with new tasks and use for downstream signals. The intended users are builders and researchers, so interfaces and modular harnesses can affect whether others adopt and reproduce the measurement. The cited HELM and Harbor examples illustrate the speaker’s product-design argument.
title: Treat researcher experience as part of benchmark design
